items.stem: A nurse reinforces teaching for an older adult who uses a single-point cane after a right total knee arthroplasty and must climb four steps to enter the home. Which instruction should the nurse give about going up the steps?
options: Place the cane on the step above first, then step up with the right leg followed by the left leg
Step up with the right leg first, then bring the left leg and the cane up to the same step
Step up with the left leg first, then bring the right leg and the cane up to the same step
Hold the cane in the right hand and lead with the right leg on each step
items.rationale: Going up, the stronger leg leads while the cane and the operative leg stay on the lower step, so the surgical knee carries the least load; the cane and the weaker leg then follow. The cane is held on the stronger side, opposite the surgical knee, which widens the base of support. Leading with the operative leg or moving the cane up first shifts full body weight onto the painful joint.

items.stem: A home health nurse adjusts a new front-wheeled walker for an older adult with balance problems. Which finding indicates that the walker height is correct?
options: The hand grips sit at mid-thigh so the client leans forward over the walker while walking
The hand grips reach the client's lower ribs and the shoulders rise when the client grips them
The hand grips are level with the client's wrist crease when the arms hang at the sides, and the elbows flex about 20 to 30 degrees when the client grips them
The hand grips reach the client's waist and the elbows stay fully extended when the client grips them
items.rationale: A walker set at the wrist crease produces about 20 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion, which lets the arms absorb weight and push the client upright. A walker set too high raises the shoulders and tires the arms, while one set too low forces the client to stoop, moving the center of gravity forward and increasing fall risk. Leaning over the frame also pushes the walker away from the body.

items.stem: A nurse gives a complete bed bath to an adult client who is on bed rest. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Wash the face, cleaning each eye from the inner to the outer canthus with a separate corner of the cloth
Change to clean water and clean gloves and perform perineal care last, cleaning from front to back
Turn the client to the side to wash the back and offer a back rub
Wash the legs and feet, changing the water when it cools or becomes soapy
Check the water temperature and fill the basin with water that is comfortably warm, about 43 C (110 F)
Wash the arms, chest and abdomen, keeping the rest of the body covered with the bath blanket
items.rationale: Bathing moves from the cleanest to the least clean areas, so the face is washed before the trunk, limbs and back, and perineal care is done last with fresh water and gloves to avoid carrying organisms toward the urethra. Water is checked first because skin that is aged or insensate burns easily. The bath blanket keeps the client covered for warmth and privacy, and turning for the back also allows a back rub and a skin check.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who may not bear weight on the right leg is fitted for axillary crutches before discharge. The crutch pads should rest {{1}}, and body weight should be carried {{2}}. When the client reaches a staircase with a handrail, the nurse teaches the client to step up first with {{3}}.

options: at the level of the lower ribs
level with the top of the shoulder
snugly up against the axilla for support
about two to three finger widths below the axilla
on the right leg with the elbows locked
on the hands and arms through the hand grips
on the axillae through the crutch pads
evenly on the axillae and the right leg
the right leg and both crutches together
both crutches lifted to the step above
the left leg
the right leg

items.rationale: Resting body weight on the axillary pads compresses the brachial plexus and causes crutch palsy, so the pads sit about 5 cm (two to three finger widths) below the axilla and the hands bear the weight with the elbows flexed 20 to 30 degrees. On stairs the rule is up with the good and down with the bad: the unaffected leg steps up first, and the crutches with the affected leg go down first.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate complications of immobility requiring follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 0830, postoperative day 3 after open reduction and internal fixation of the left hip.
The client has remained in bed since surgery and says, 'it hurts less if I do not move.'
Incision is dry and intact with staples approximated.
Pain is 3 out of 10 after the scheduled acetaminophen.
Breath sounds are diminished in both bases and the incentive spirometer has not been used since yesterday morning.
No bowel movement in four days; the abdomen is firm and the client reports fullness.
Oral intake 1,400 mL in the past 24 hours.
A 3 cm area of redness over the sacrum does not blanch when pressed.
Heels are supported on a pillow and the skin there is intact.
Voiding 250 to 300 mL each time without difficulty.
Family is at the bedside asking about the rehabilitation plan.

items.rationale: Three days of bed rest produce predictable harm: retained secretions and atelectasis show as diminished bases with unused incentive spirometry, slowed motility shows as four days without stool and a firm abdomen, and unrelieved pressure shows as nonblanchable sacral redness, a stage 1 pressure injury. Controlled pain, an intact incision, floated heels and adequate intake and voiding are expected findings that need no immediate change.

items.stem: A client who had an open cholecystectomy rates incisional pain 6 out of 10 thirty minutes after receiving the prescribed analgesic. Which comfort measures should the nurse offer in addition to the analgesia? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a heating pad set on high directly over the incision
Withhold the next scheduled analgesic dose so the comfort measures can be judged on their own
Offer slow paced breathing and the client's preferred music through headphones
Reposition the client in semi-Fowler position with the knees slightly flexed
Dim the lights and group care activities so the client has an uninterrupted rest period
Support the incision with a folded pillow during coughing and deep breathing
items.rationale: Nonpharmacologic measures work alongside analgesia, not instead of it: splinting reduces the pull on the incision, semi-Fowler with flexed knees relaxes abdominal muscles, and music with paced breathing shifts attention and lowers muscle tension. Clustering care protects rest, which raises pain tolerance. Withholding a scheduled dose leaves pain uncontrolled, and high heat on a fresh incision risks burns and swelling.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to change the dressing on a 4-year-old's healing scald burn. The child received the prescribed analgesic 30 minutes ago. Which additional comfort measure is most appropriate?
options: Ask the parent to wait in the playroom so that the child does not become more upset
Reassure the child that the dressing change will not hurt at all
Let the child blow bubbles and hold a favorite toy while a parent stays at the bedside during the dressing change
Begin the dressing change while the child is asleep so that the child is not frightened
items.rationale: Blowing bubbles gives a preschooler both distraction and slow exhalation, and a familiar object with a parent present lowers distress during a painful procedure. Sending the parent away removes the child's main source of security, false reassurance destroys trust once the dressing is removed, and starting while the child sleeps makes the bed feel unsafe. The playroom is kept a procedure-free space.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the record of a resident in long-term care who has become less interested in drinking. Based on the trended data, which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The changes reflect normal aging and no change to the plan of care is needed
The resident has fluid volume overload and the daily fluid allowance should be lowered further
The weight loss is explained by poor appetite alone, so fluid intake can be considered adequate
The resident is becoming dehydrated and needs a plan of offered fluids and notification of the provider
items.rationale: Intake below 1,000 mL with falling output, darkening concentrated urine and a 2 kg loss over four days is a fluid deficit, since about 1 kg of rapid weight change equals 1 L of body water. Older adults have a blunted thirst response, so fluids must be offered on a schedule in preferred forms rather than left to thirst. Overload would show weight gain and edema, and dehydration is never a normal age change.

items.stem: A nurse plans positioning for several clients on a medical unit. For each nursing action, click to indicate whether it is appropriate or not appropriate.
matrixRows: Keeping the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees for a client receiving a continuous gastric tube feeding
Placing an abduction pillow between the legs of a client after a posterior total hip arthroplasty
Turning a client with a sacral pressure injury fully onto the greater trochanter in a 90-degree side-lying position
Massaging a reddened bony prominence to improve circulation to the area
Supporting the calves on a pillow so that the heels float free of the mattress
Leaving the head of the bed at 60 degrees for several hours for a client at risk for sacral shearing
Setting the repositioning schedule from the client's skin assessment, mobility and comfort rather than a fixed clock alone
items.rationale: Elevating the head 30 to 45 degrees during tube feeding and abducting the legs after hip replacement prevent aspiration and dislocation. Pressure relief follows the 30-degree lateral rule, because a full 90-degree turn loads the trochanter, and reddened prominences are never massaged since friction damages fragile capillaries. Floating the heels removes pressure, prolonged elevation above 30 degrees shears sacral tissue, and turning intervals follow the skin rather than the clock.

items.stem: A nurse assists a client who has dysphagia after a stroke to eat lunch. Which action best reduces the risk of aspiration?
options: Serve the meal in the busy day room so that conversation encourages the client to eat more
Seat the client fully upright, teach a chin tuck with each swallow and check the mouth for pocketed food before offering the next bite
Seat the client at 45 degrees with the head tilted back so that gravity carries the food down
Offer thin liquids through a straw between bites to wash the food down
items.rationale: Sitting fully upright with the chin tucked narrows the airway entrance and widens the path to the esophagus, and checking for pocketed food prevents a bolus from being aspirated later. Tilting the head back opens the airway and is the position most likely to cause aspiration. Straws deliver thin liquid fast and past the tongue's control, and a noisy distracting room interferes with the concentration safe swallowing requires.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with a new gastrostomy tube reports cramping and bloating during every bolus feeding. The nurse should {{1}}, and after each feeding the client should stay {{2}}.

options: flush the tube with 120 mL of cold water before each feeding
raise the syringe higher so the feeding finishes more quickly
chill the formula before the next feeding so the cramping is numbed
slow the feeding so it runs in by gravity over 15 to 20 minutes and use room-temperature formula
upright at 30 to 45 degrees for at least 30 to 60 minutes
flat so the stomach can empty more easily
upright for 5 minutes and then returned to a flat position
flat in a left side-lying position

items.rationale: Cramping, bloating and nausea during a bolus feeding usually mean the formula is going in too fast or is too cold, so the nurse lowers the syringe to slow gravity flow over 15 to 20 minutes and warms the formula to room temperature. Staying upright afterward uses gravity for gastric emptying and lowers the risk of reflux and aspiration, whereas lying flat pushes stomach contents toward the airway.

items.stem: A nurse assists an older adult who is blind to eat lunch on a rehabilitation unit. Which action best supports the client's independence?
options: Describe the position of each food using the face of a clock and guide the client's hands to the utensils and cup
Set the tray down and leave the room so that the client can eat privately without being watched
Arrange for a family member to come to every meal to feed the client so that intake is recorded
Cut all of the food and feed the client each bite so that the meal is eaten while it is still warm
items.rationale: The clock method gives the client the spatial information sight would normally supply, and placing the hands on the utensils and cup lets the client locate them without searching. Feeding a client who can self-feed removes control and dignity for no clinical reason. Leaving the room without orienting the client to the tray leads to spills and poor intake, and family feeding creates dependence rather than skill.

items.stem: A nurse plans care for a resident in long-term care who has hard, infrequent stools and no signs of obstruction. Which measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage 1.5 to 2 L of fluid daily unless fluids are restricted
Keep the resident on a bedpan for 30 minutes at a time until a stool is passed
Increase dietary fiber gradually toward 25 to 30 g per day along with adequate fluids
Offer toileting about 30 minutes after breakfast to use the gastrocolic reflex
Seat the resident upright on a toilet or bedside commode with the feet supported rather than using a bedpan
Give a soapsuds enema every morning so that a routine is established
items.rationale: Fiber only softens stool when fluid intake supports it, so the two are raised together and fiber is increased slowly to avoid gas and cramping. Toileting after a meal uses the gastrocolic reflex, and sitting upright with the feet supported lets gravity and the abdominal muscles work, which a bedpan prevents. Daily enemas create dependence and irritate the mucosa, and prolonged bedpan sitting causes sacral pressure injury and shame without producing stool.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that require follow-up by the nurse.

highlightSegments.text: 1000, day 5 after creation of a descending colostomy.
The stoma is round, moist and beefy red, about 3 cm in diameter.
The skin around the stoma is red, weeping and painful where stool has tracked under the barrier.
The pouch has leaked twice in the past 12 hours.
The client states, 'I cut the opening in the barrier about 2 cm wider than the stoma so it will not rub.'
Output is soft and brown, about 350 mL in 24 hours.
The client emptied the pouch at one-third full while the nurse observed.
Temperature 36.9 C (98.4 F); the abdomen is soft and non-tender.
The client asks how to order pouching supplies for home.
Appetite is improving and the client ate 75% of lunch.

items.rationale: A barrier opening should clear the stoma by only about 3 mm; a 2 cm gap leaves skin bathed in effluent, which explains the weeping painful dermatitis and the repeated leaks, so the barrier is resized and the skin treated before the next pouch is applied. A beefy red moist stoma, soft brown output, emptying at one-third full and questions about supplies are expected findings and signs of learning.

items.topic: Oral Care of the Intubated Client
items.stem: A nurse provides oral care for a client who is unconscious and orally intubated in the intensive care unit. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Lower the bed flat and rinse the mouth with a large volume of mouthwash to loosen debris quickly
Swab the mouth with lemon-glycerin sponges every two hours to stimulate saliva
Instill 30 mL of normal saline into the mouth with a syringe and let the fluid drain onto a towel
Elevate the head of the bed, turn the client's head to the side, brush with a soft suction toothbrush and suction secretions as they pool
items.rationale: An unconscious client cannot protect the airway, so oral care is given with the head elevated and turned to the side while a suction toothbrush removes plaque and pooled secretions, which lowers the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Large volumes of saline or mouthwash flood the pharynx and are aspirated, lying flat removes gravity's protection, and lemon-glycerin swabs dry and erode the mucosa.

items.stem: A rehabilitation nurse reviews care of a new transtibial prosthesis with a client. Which client statement indicates that the teaching has been effective?
options: 'I will wash my residual limb with mild soap and water at bedtime and dry it well before I go to sleep.'
'If a red mark is still there 30 minutes after I take the prosthesis off, I should wear it longer so the skin toughens.'
'I will wear the same limb sock for two or three days so that the fit of the socket does not change.'
'I will rub lotion into my residual limb just before I put the prosthesis on each morning.'
items.rationale: Washing at night gives the skin hours to dry, because a damp or greasy limb macerates and slides inside the socket. Lotion applied before donning has the same effect and is used only at bedtime if at all. Redness that persists beyond about 20 minutes signals a socket that does not fit and is reported rather than pushed through, and limb socks are changed and washed daily to keep sweat and ply thickness consistent.

items.stem: A nurse performs passive range-of-motion exercises for a client who has right hemiplegia after a stroke. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Move each joint slightly past the point of resistance to stretch the tightening muscles
Move each joint quickly through its full range so the exercises are finished before the client tires
Support the limb above and below the joint and move it slowly to the point of resistance, stopping if the client reports pain
Exercise only the unaffected left side so that the weak right arm is allowed to rest
items.rationale: Supporting the limb above and below the joint protects a flaccid shoulder and elbow from subluxation, and slow movement to the point of resistance preserves joint capsule length without tearing tissue. Fast movement triggers spasticity and pain, forcing past resistance injures the joint, and leaving the hemiplegic side unexercised is exactly how contractures form within days of immobility.

items.stem: A client who gave birth vaginally 3 hours ago with a second-degree perineal laceration reports perineal soreness and burning. Which comfort measure should the nurse provide now?
options: Have the client sit upright in a straight-backed chair so that drainage is encouraged
Apply a covered perineal cold pack for about 20 minutes and teach the client to rinse with a peri-bottle of warm water after voiding
Apply a warm moist compress to the perineum for 20 minutes
Assist the client into a warm sitz bath for 20 minutes
items.rationale: During the first 24 hours cold limits edema and hematoma formation and numbs the area, so a covered pack is used for about 20 minutes at a time to protect the skin. Warm applications and sitz baths increase blood flow and are helpful after the first 24 hours, when the goal shifts to healing rather than controlling swelling. Rinsing with the peri-bottle cleans without rubbing the suture line.

items.stem: A nurse plans the first walk for a client on the day after an open colectomy. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Delay walking until the client reports no incisional pain at all
Have the client walk the full length of the hallway right after breakfast so the daily activity goal is met
Keep the client on bed rest until the abdominal drain has been removed so that the incision is protected
Give the prescribed analgesic about 30 minutes beforehand, then sit the client on the edge of the bed and check blood pressure and dizziness before standing
items.rationale: Early walking prevents atelectasis, venous thromboembolism, ileus and deconditioning, and it succeeds when pain is treated first and orthostatic tolerance is checked at the edge of the bed. Waiting for a pain-free client or for drain removal keeps the client in bed for days, where those complications begin. Pushing a full hallway on the first attempt ignores tolerance and risks a fall.

items.stem: A home health nurse reviews foot care with a client who has type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: 'I soak my feet in hot water for 20 minutes each evening to soften the calluses.'
'I dry between my toes and put lotion on the top and sole but not between the toes.'
'I look at the top and the sole of each foot every day and use a mirror for the bottoms.'
'I wear socks and shoes indoors instead of walking barefoot.'
items.rationale: Neuropathy removes the warning of heat and pressure, so hot soaks scald skin the client cannot feel, and prolonged soaking macerates it and invites infection. Daily inspection with a mirror finds injuries the client cannot feel, lotion everywhere except between the toes prevents both cracking and maceration, and footwear indoors prevents the puncture wounds that begin most diabetic foot ulcers.

items.stem: A nurse provides perineal care for an uncircumcised male client who has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Leave the foreskin in place and clean only the exposed shaft with soap and water
Retract the foreskin, clean the glans in a circular motion from the meatus outward, clean the catheter from the meatus downward and then return the foreskin to its position
Clean the catheter tubing first, wiping from the drainage tubing toward the meatus
Retract the foreskin, clean the area and leave the foreskin retracted so the skin can air dry
items.rationale: Cleaning always moves away from the meatus, the cleanest point, so that organisms are not dragged along the catheter toward the bladder, which is how catheter-associated urinary tract infections begin. The foreskin must be returned immediately after care, because a foreskin left retracted constricts the glans and can cause paraphimosis. Cleaning only the exposed shaft leaves smegma and moisture under the foreskin.

items.topic: Sleep and Rest in Hospitalized Children
items.stem: A 7-year-old hospitalized with pneumonia wakes several times each night and is tearful in the morning. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Leave a dim night light on and keep the door partly closed to reduce hallway noise and light
Encourage a parent to stay overnight if able and to be present at bedtime
Follow the bedtime routine the parents use at home, including a story and the child's own blanket
Allow the child to sleep through the afternoon to make up for the sleep lost at night
Cluster vital signs, medications and treatments so the child has longer uninterrupted stretches
Offer the child a favorite caffeinated soft drink with dinner to improve the evening appetite
items.rationale: School-age children sleep best when the hospital routine copies home: the familiar sequence, comfort object and a parent at the bedside reduce the arousal that unfamiliar surroundings cause. Clustering care and controlling light and noise protect the long sleep cycles that restore a child. Long afternoon sleep and caffeine at dinner both push the sleep phase later and worsen the night waking they are meant to fix.

items.stem: A nurse begins a bladder training program with a cognitively intact resident in long-term care who has urge incontinence. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Teach the resident to stop, breathe slowly and contract the pelvic floor when an urge comes, then walk to the toilet
Restrict total fluids to 1,000 mL per day so that there are fewer episodes
Keep the call light within reach and the path to the bathroom clear and well lit
Offer toileting on a set schedule of about every 2 hours while awake and lengthen the interval as control improves
Insert an indwelling catheter at night so that the resident's sleep is not interrupted
Give most of the daily fluid earlier in the day and limit caffeinated drinks
items.rationale: Bladder training works by toileting before the urge becomes urgent and then stretching the interval, while urge suppression with slow breathing and pelvic floor contraction lets the detrusor contraction pass instead of being chased to the toilet. Fluids are timed, not restricted, since concentrated urine irritates the bladder and worsens urgency. An indwelling catheter for convenience introduces infection and abandons continence.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A hospice client with metastatic bone pain rates the pain 5 out of 10 an hour after a scheduled long-acting opioid and says the evenings feel endless. The nurse should {{1}}, and should explain that guided imagery and music help most when they are used {{2}}.

options: offer guided imagery with a scene the client chooses while keeping the prescribed analgesic schedule
wait until the pain reaches 8 out of 10 before starting any comfort measure
explain that relaxation should make the pain medication unnecessary
replace the next opioid dose with guided imagery so that tolerance does not develop
only after the analgesics have failed completely
only during daytime hours when the client is alert
together with analgesia and before the pain becomes severe
in place of breakthrough doses during the night

items.rationale: Guided imagery and music lower the distress and muscle tension that amplify pain, but they raise the pain threshold rather than block nociception, so they are added to the analgesic plan and started while pain is still moderate. Substituting them for a scheduled or breakthrough opioid leaves cancer pain untreated, and waiting for severe pain makes any comfort measure, drug or not, far less effective.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with an indwelling urinary catheter reports lower abdominal discomfort, and no urine has drained into the bag for the past 2 hours. The nurse should first {{1}}. To keep drainage flowing, the nurse also keeps the bag {{2}}.

options: irrigate the catheter with 60 mL of sterile normal saline
ask the provider for a bladder antispasmodic
remove the catheter and insert a new one
palpate the bladder and trace the tubing for kinks, dependent loops or the client lying on it
below the level of the bladder and off the floor
resting on the floor beside the bed
clamped except when it is emptied every 4 hours
hanging from the side rail at the level of the abdomen

items.rationale: Absent drainage with bladder discomfort is far more often mechanical than an obstructed catheter, so the nurse palpates for a distended bladder and follows the tubing for kinks, loops and body weight before any invasive step. Irrigation and reinsertion are late measures that break a closed system. A bag above bladder level allows reflux, and a bag on the floor or clamped invites contamination and retention.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the note that indicate the resident's nutrition and hydration need follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: Quarterly nutrition review for an 84-year-old resident of the long-term care unit.
Weight today is 54.1 kg, down from 57.2 kg one month ago.
Meal records show the resident eats about 25% of most meals.
The resident says, 'My gums hurt when I chew and the bottom denture slips.'
Oral mucous membranes are dry, the tongue is furrowed and the urine is dark amber.
The resident comes to the dining room for meals and enjoys the company there.
Family brings a favorite soup on Sundays, which the resident finishes.
No nausea, vomiting or diarrhea is reported.
Temperature 36.6 C (97.9 F), blood pressure 118/68 mm Hg.
The resident walks to the bathroom with a rolling walker.

items.rationale: A 3.1 kg loss in a month is more than 5% of body weight, a red flag that pairs with intake of only a quarter of meals and with dry mucous membranes, a furrowed tongue and concentrated urine. Painful gums and a loose denture explain why intake fell, so the follow-up is a dental and dietitian referral with preferred, easily chewed foods and offered fluids. Dining-room attendance, family food and stable vital signs are strengths to build on.

items.stem: A client began scheduled oxycodone on day 1 after a spinal fusion. The nurse reviews the trended record. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Offer a large hot meal to stimulate the gastrocolic reflex
Continue to monitor for another day, since bowel patterns often change after surgery
Contact the provider for the prescribed bowel regimen and meanwhile increase fluids and help the client walk
Hold the oxycodone doses until the client has a bowel movement
items.rationale: Opioids slow gut motility for as long as they are taken, and this trend, stools that went from formed to hard to absent with falling fluids, less walking, hypoactive sounds and distention, is heading toward impaction rather than resolving on its own. A stimulant laxative with a softener, more fluid and mobility treat it. Holding analgesia leaves pain untreated, and food alone cannot move a stool that is already hard and retained.

items.stem: A nurse plans heat and cold applications for several clients. For each application, click to indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
matrixRows: Moist heat to the lower back of a client with chronic muscle spasm
A covered cold pack to the knee 6 hours after arthroscopic surgery
A heating pad over the abdomen of a client with right lower quadrant pain and suspected appendicitis
A warm compress over an enlarging hematoma at an intravenous site removed 1 hour ago
A cold pack to the hands of a client with Raynaud phenomenon
A warm sitz bath for a client 2 days after hemorrhoidectomy
A heating pad placed underneath a client who has reduced sensation from diabetic neuropathy
items.rationale: Heat relaxes spasm and, once bleeding and swelling have settled, brings blood flow that speeds healing, which is why it suits chronic back spasm and a sitz bath on the second postoperative day. Heat over an inflamed appendix can hasten rupture, and heat over a fresh hematoma increases bleeding. Cold limits early swelling after surgery but provokes vasospasm in Raynaud, and any device left under a client or on insensate skin causes burns and pressure injury.

items.stem: A nurse assists a client with left knee osteoarthritis to move from the bed to a chair using a front-wheeled walker. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Have the client grasp the walker grips and take small steps, turning toward the chair
Lower the client into the chair while the hands stay on the armrests
Place the walker directly in front of the client within arm's reach with the wheels forward
Have the client push up from the mattress with both hands to stand, then pause to check for dizziness
Have the client back up until both legs touch the chair and reach back for the armrests
Assist the client to sit on the edge of the bed with both feet flat on the floor in non-skid footwear
items.rationale: Sitting on the edge of the bed with the feet flat lets orthostatic blood pressure settle before weight bearing, and the walker is positioned before standing so it is never used as a pulling point. The client pushes up from the mattress rather than from the walker, which would tip, and only grasps the grips once standing and steady. Feeling the chair against both legs before reaching back for the armrests prevents sitting down short of the seat.

items.stem: A nurse in long-term care assesses an 88-year-old resident who has passed frequent small amounts of liquid brown stool for 2 days after 5 days with no bowel movement. The abdomen is distended with hypoactive bowel sounds, and the resident reports rectal fullness and cramping. There is no fever and no recent antibiotic use. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Withhold all oral fluids until the liquid stools stop
Place the resident on contact precautions and send a stool specimen for C. difficile toxin
Check the rectum for hard stool as facility policy permits and report the findings to the provider
Administer the prescribed oil-retention enema and assist the resident onto a bedside commode
Give an antidiarrheal medication and continue to monitor the stool output
bowtieParams: Passage of formed stool and relief of rectal fullness
Pupil size and reaction to light
items.rationale: Liquid stool seeping around a hardened mass after days without a bowel movement, with distention and rectal fullness, is overflow diarrhea from impaction rather than infection, which would bring fever or recent antibiotics. The nurse confirms hard stool in the rectum, notifies the provider and gives the ordered oil-retention enema; an antidiarrheal or withheld fluids would harden the mass further. Progress shows as formed stool, a softer abdomen and returning bowel sounds.

items.stem: A home health nurse visits a client with Parkinson disease whose spouse reports that the client coughs during most meals and sounds 'wet and gurgly' afterward. The client has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb) in one month. Which referral should the nurse initiate first?
options: Speech-language pathology for a swallowing evaluation
Physical therapy for a trunk strengthening program
Occupational therapy for adaptive feeding utensils
Registered dietitian for calorie supplementation and weight monitoring
items.rationale: Coughing with meals and a wet, gurgly voice are cues for dysphagia, and the speech-language pathologist is the discipline that evaluates the swallow and sets the safe diet texture and feeding strategies. Weight loss here is a consequence of an unsafe swallow, so a dietitian consult alone does not address the airway risk. Adaptive utensils help a client who cannot bring food to the mouth, and strengthening addresses mobility, not swallowing.

items.stem: A client recovering from a stroke walks safely with a cane but cannot fasten buttons, open toothpaste, or manage a razor with the affected hand. Which member of the interdisciplinary team should the nurse consult?
options: Social worker for a home aide referral
Physical therapist for lower extremity strengthening
Speech-language pathologist for cognitive retraining
Occupational therapist for retraining in activities of daily living
items.rationale: Occupational therapy addresses fine motor skill, self-care performance and adaptive equipment for activities of daily living such as dressing and grooming. Physical therapy focuses on gross motor function, gait and transfers, which this client already performs safely. Speech-language pathology covers communication, cognition and swallowing, and a home aide substitutes for the skill rather than restoring it.

items.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes tells the clinic nurse, 'I skip my insulin on some days because I cannot afford the copay until payday.' The client demonstrates correct injection technique and accurate carbohydrate counting. Which referral is most appropriate?
options: Home health nurse for daily insulin administration
Diabetes care and education specialist for injection technique review
Social worker for prescription assistance and coverage review
Registered dietitian for carbohydrate counting review
items.rationale: The barrier is financial, not knowledge or skill, so the social worker is the discipline that screens for benefits, manufacturer assistance programs and lower-cost coverage options. Repeating dietary or injection teaching addresses skills the client has already demonstrated and leaves the real cause of missed doses untouched. A home health nurse is neither necessary nor a solution to cost.

items.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility receives a telephone order from the on-call provider. Which action best meets the standard for accepting a telephone order?
options: Ask the prescriber to spell the drug name and then enter the order from memory
Repeat the order aloud to a second nurse who listens on the line
Enter the order into the record and read it back to the prescriber at the end of the shift
Write the order down, read it back to the prescriber, and obtain confirmation
items.rationale: The accepted standard is write down, read back, and receive verbal confirmation from the prescriber during the same call, which catches sound-alike drug names and misheard numbers before the order is carried out. A second listener does not replace read-back by the person who took the order, and a read-back delayed to the end of the shift allows the wrong order to be acted on first. Entering an order from memory removes the verification step entirely.

items.stem: A nurse is preparing to telephone the provider about a client whose urine output has been 15 mL/hr for 4 hours. Which statement belongs in the recommendation portion of the SBAR report?
options: 'The urine output has been 15 mL/hr for 4 hours and the blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg.'
'I think the client needs an order for a fluid bolus and a repeat basic metabolic panel now.'
'I am calling about the client in room 412 whose urine output has dropped.'
'This client is 1 day post bowel resection and has a history of heart failure.'
items.rationale: Recommendation states what the nurse is asking the provider to do or order, which makes the request explicit instead of leaving the provider to infer it. Identifying the client and the problem is Situation, relevant history is Background, and current vital signs and findings are Assessment. Naming the ask is the part nurses most often omit, and it is what turns a report into a decision.

items.stem: A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is being discharged home on continuous oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which action by the nurse best supports a safe transition?
options: Send the client home with the hospital's portable oxygen cylinder
Give the client the oxygen prescription to take to a supplier after discharge
Teach the family to call a supplier if the client becomes short of breath at home
Confirm with the durable medical equipment supplier that the concentrator and tubing will be delivered to the home before the client arrives
items.rationale: Durable medical equipment must be in place and working when the client walks through the door; confirming delivery with the supplier closes the most common gap in oxygen discharges. Handing the client a prescription shifts the coordination to a client who may be unable to arrange it, and hospital cylinders are not a home oxygen supply. Waiting until the client is dyspneic makes a preventable readmission likely.

items.stem: While preparing to give a scheduled medication, the nurse finds that the client's wristband barcode is worn and will not scan. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Verify the client's identity using two identifiers, apply a new wristband, and scan it
Use the system override function and document that the scanner failed
Enter the client's room number into the scanner to complete the task
Ask a second nurse to confirm the client's name and then give the medication
items.rationale: An unreadable wristband is fixed, not bypassed: the nurse confirms identity with two identifiers such as name and date of birth, prints a new band, and scans it so the safety check still occurs. Overrides and workarounds defeat the barcode system and are a leading contributor to wrong-client errors. A room number is a location, not a client identifier, and a colleague's recognition is not an approved identifier.

items.stem: A nurse notices that the pharmacy has dispensed heparin 10,000 units/mL when 1,000 units/mL was ordered. The nurse returns the vial before any dose is drawn up. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Document the pharmacy's dispensing error in the client's medical record
No report is needed because the vial was returned and no client was harmed
Ask the pharmacy manager to counsel the technician who filled the order
Complete an occurrence report describing the near miss
items.rationale: A near miss is reported precisely because it reveals a system weakness, such as look-alike heparin concentrations, while there is still time to fix it without a client being harmed. Occurrence reports are internal quality documents and are not filed in or referenced from the medical record, which contains only the client's care. Individual counseling is a manager's decision after review, not the nurse's first step, and a just culture examines the process before the person.

items.stem: An 82-year-old client who lives alone is being discharged after surgical repair of a hip fracture. The client ambulates with a walker, has four steps at the entrance to the home, and has lost 4 kg (8.8 lb) during the admission. Which referrals should the nurse include in the discharge plan? Select all that apply.
options: Registered dietitian for a nutritional assessment
Physical therapy for gait training and stair safety
Case management to arrange home health services
Occupational therapy for evaluation of activities of daily living and home safety
Chaplain services for spiritual distress
Speech-language pathology for a communication evaluation
items.rationale: Discharge planning matches each identified need to the discipline that resolves it: stairs and a walker call for physical therapy, self-care and home hazards for occupational therapy, unintended weight loss for the dietitian, and arranging home health visits for case management. Nothing in the scenario suggests a communication or swallowing problem or spiritual distress, and referrals made without an identified need consume resources and delay the discharge.

items.stem: A nurse manager audits documentation on the unit. Which entries meet accepted documentation standards? Select all that apply.
options: '0930 Client reports pain 7/10 in the right hip; ibuprofen 400 mg given as ordered.'
'1400 Late entry for 1100: client ambulated 15 m (50 ft) with a walker and tolerated it well.'
'1600 Provider notified of blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg; no new orders received.'
'Client appears to be doing fine; will continue to monitor.'
'Dressing changed; see occurrence report for details.'
'Client was uncooperative and difficult all morning.'
items.rationale: Acceptable entries are timed, objective, and describe what was observed, what was done and the response, including notification of the provider and the outcome of that call. A late entry is legitimate when it is clearly labeled with both the time of the entry and the time of the care. Labels such as 'uncooperative' or 'difficult' are conclusions rather than behavior, vague reassurance documents nothing, and the record must never reference an occurrence report.

items.stem: A nurse receives a new order for morphine 10 mg IV push every 2 hours for a 78-year-old opioid-naive client with a serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Give the dose as written because the prescriber is accountable for the order
Hold the medication until the order is clarified
Contact the prescriber to question the dose and the dosing interval
Ask another nurse to administer the dose instead
Review the client's opioid history, age and renal function before contacting the prescriber
Document the clarification request and the prescriber's response
items.rationale: A nurse who carries out an order known to be unsafe shares accountability for the harm, so the dose is held and clarified before administration. Gathering the client's age, opioid history and renal function first makes the call specific and gives the prescriber what is needed to adjust the order. Passing the task to a colleague transfers the risk without resolving it, and the clarification and the response must be documented to show the concern was raised and answered.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse in a rural emergency department receives a telephone order for hydralazine 10 mg IV now for a client whose blood pressure is 210/118 mm Hg. Before ending the call the nurse should {{1}}. The entry in the record must identify the prescriber, the date and time, and the order must then be {{2}}.

options: enter the order and verify it with the pharmacist afterward
repeat the order to the charge nurse for a second check
summarize the order in the nurse's own words
write the order down and read it back to the prescriber exactly as written
countersigned by the prescriber within the time frame set by facility policy
transcribed onto a paper medication record as a backup
witnessed by a second nurse before the dose is given
reported to the nursing supervisor at the end of the shift

items.rationale: Read-back of the written order in the prescriber's exact words is what catches misheard doses and sound-alike drug names, and paraphrasing defeats that purpose. Telephone orders are documented with the prescriber's name, the date and time and a read-back notation, and facility policy sets the window, commonly 24 to 48 hours, for the prescriber to countersign. A second listener, a supervisor report or a duplicate paper record none of them verify the order with the person who gave it.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with heart failure has been readmitted twice in 30 days and cannot say which of the two 'water pills' at home should be taken. The nurse should involve {{1}} in the discharge plan. The intervention most likely to prevent another readmission is {{2}}.

options: the infection preventionist
occupational therapy
the facility chaplain
a transitional care manager
a prepared low-sodium meal delivery service
medication reconciliation with teach-back before discharge and a follow-up call within 48 hours
a repeat echocardiogram before discharge
a longer inpatient stay to observe the client

items.rationale: Duplicate or confused diuretic regimens are a classic cause of heart failure readmission, and a transitional care manager owns the handoff between settings: reconciled medications, an early follow-up appointment and a post-discharge call. Reconciliation confirmed by teach-back verifies what the client will actually do at home. Extra inpatient days, repeat imaging and meal delivery do not correct the medication confusion that is driving the readmissions.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A home health nurse learns that a client has been buying sterile dressing supplies out of pocket because the covered supply order was never renewed. The nurse should {{1}}. Selecting supplies that are covered by the client's plan and meet the wound's needs is an example of {{2}}.

options: wait until the recertification visit to raise the issue
advise the client to buy a larger quantity to lower the unit cost
substitute clean gauze from the client's household supplies
notify the agency case manager so the covered supply order is renewed
delegation of nursing responsibility
cost-effective resource management
utilization review performed by the provider
benchmarking against national quality data

items.rationale: An expired supply order is a coordination failure the case manager can correct, and an out-of-pocket cost the client cannot sustain predicts that the dressing changes will simply stop. Cost-effective care means achieving the same clinical outcome with resources the client can obtain, not lowering the standard of the dressing. Substituting nonsterile household supplies introduces infection risk, and delaying to the next recertification leaves the wound undertreated for weeks.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the nurses' note that do not meet documentation standards.

highlightSegments.text: 1900 Client admitted to room 214 from the emergency department; oriented to the room and call light.
Vital signs: temperature 37.1 C (98.8 F), heart rate 88, blood pressure 132/76 mm Hg.
Client is a poor historian and seems to be drug seeking.
Reports pain 6/10 in the lower back; oxycodone 5 mg by mouth given at 1915.
1930 Peripheral IV started in the left forearm on the second attempt; client tolerated the procedure.
Wrong-size catheter used by the float nurse; see the occurrence report sent to risk management.
2000 Client ambulated to the bathroom with one-person assistance and returned to bed.
Client seems comfortable and is probably fine for the night.
2100 Spouse at the bedside; call light and water within reach; bed in the lowest position.
The 2000 entry was changed with correction fluid to read 2030.

items.rationale: Documentation must be objective, factual and permanent. Labeling a client 'drug seeking' or 'a poor historian' records an opinion, and 'probably fine' records nothing measurable. Correction fluid destroys the original entry; an error is corrected with a single line, initials and the time. Referencing an occurrence report pulls an internal quality document into the legal record. The timed entries about vital signs, medication, the IV and ambulation meet the standard.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the discharge planning note that require additional coordination before the client can safely go home.

highlightSegments.text: 1000 Discharge planning note: 71-year-old client, hospital day 4 for community-acquired pneumonia.
Temperature has been 36.8 C (98.2 F) for 48 hours and the client is eating 75% of meals.
Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air at rest but falls to 86% after walking 30 m (100 ft).
Client lives alone in a second-floor apartment with no elevator.
Discharge prescriptions include levofloxacin and a new inhaler.
Client states, 'I have never used an inhaler and no one has shown me how.'
Client states, 'I stopped filling my prescriptions last year because of the cost.'
Daughter is able to visit on weekends and has the discharge instructions.
Follow-up appointment is scheduled for Thursday and the client has transportation to it.
Client ambulates independently without a device on level ground.

items.rationale: Exertional desaturation to 86% means home oxygen may be needed before the client leaves, and stairs to a second-floor apartment compound that risk. A new inhaler with no teaching and a history of not filling prescriptions because of cost predict that the treatment will not happen at home, so teach-back and a social work or pharmacy referral belong in the plan. Stable temperature, intake, transportation and weekend family support are strengths, not gaps.

items.stem: A nurse on the unit practice council reviews the quality data after a fall-prevention bundle was introduced in January. Which conclusion is supported by the trended data?
options: The improvement is a chance finding because only four months of data are available
The unit can stop screening clients for fall risk because no injuries occurred in April
The fall rate is declining as hourly rounding compliance rises, so the bundle should be sustained and re-audited
Hourly rounding compliance is unrelated to the number of falls on the unit
items.rationale: The fall rate drops in every month that rounding compliance rises, and injuries fall with it, which is the pattern a quality team looks for when judging whether an intervention is working. A sustained improvement is a reason to hardwire and keep measuring the process, not to stop the screening that identifies at-risk clients. Dismissing four consecutive months of concordant process and outcome data as chance ignores the dose-response relationship in the table.

items.stem: A quality improvement team reviews the unit's urinary catheter data. Which action should the team take first based on the trend?
options: Require a second nurse to witness every catheter insertion
Begin routine surveillance urine cultures on every client with an indwelling catheter
Change the antiseptic solution used during catheter insertion
Reinforce the daily review of catheter necessity so catheters are removed as soon as they are no longer indicated
items.rationale: Infection risk rises with each catheter day, and the table shows catheter days climbing while documented necessity reviews fall, pointing at duration rather than insertion technique. The highest-yield first action is restoring the daily necessity review, often as a nurse-driven removal protocol. Surveillance cultures detect colonization and lead to unnecessary antibiotics, and changing antiseptic or adding a witness addresses insertion, which the data do not implicate.

items.stem: For each client need identified during interdisciplinary rounds, select the discipline the nurse should consult.
matrixRows: Client needs a home exercise program to improve balance after two falls.
Client with expressive aphasia after a stroke needs strategies to communicate needs.
Client newly diagnosed with celiac disease asks for help planning gluten-free meals.
Client is uninsured and has no way to pay for follow-up care.
Client coughs and chokes when drinking thin liquids.
Client is being discharged to a shelter and needs community placement resources.
items.rationale: Referrals are matched to the discipline whose scope covers the need: physical therapy for balance and gait, speech-language pathology for both communication and swallowing, the dietitian for therapeutic diet planning, and social work for financial barriers and community placement. Sending every need to the same discipline delays care and wastes limited consult capacity. Noticing that one discipline may own two different problems is part of knowing the team's scope.

items.stem: A nurse answers a call from the on-call provider who wishes to give a telephone order. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Enter the order in the record with the date, time, prescriber's name and the notation 'telephone order, read back and verified.'
Write the order down completely as the prescriber states it.
Obtain confirmation from the prescriber that the read-back is correct.
Read the order back to the prescriber word for word.
Open the client's record and confirm the client's name and date of birth with the prescriber.
items.rationale: Confirming the client first prevents an order being placed on the wrong record, which is the error a read-back cannot catch. The order is then written as it is spoken, read back word for word and confirmed by the prescriber before the call ends, because verification after the fact does not prevent a wrong dose from being given. Entering the order with the read-back notation last creates the record that the verification actually occurred.

items.stem: A client admitted for a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation fires two puffs from a metered-dose inhaler in rapid succession while breathing through the nose and does not use the prescribed spacer. The nurse has reviewed the technique twice with no change. Which consult is most appropriate?
options: Respiratory therapist to reteach inhaler technique and evaluate the delivery device
Physical therapist for pulmonary rehabilitation exercises
Provider for an order to change to an oral bronchodilator
Case manager to arrange a home nebulizer
items.rationale: Respiratory therapists specialize in aerosol delivery and can both reteach technique and recommend a device the client can actually use, such as a spacer or a breath-actuated inhaler. Switching to a nebulizer or an oral drug because technique is poor escalates cost and side effects before the simpler problem is solved. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves endurance but does not correct how the medication is delivered.

items.stem: A resident in a long-term care facility has a sacral pressure injury with full-thickness tissue loss, visible subcutaneous fat and undermining at the 3 o'clock position. The wound has not changed in size in 2 weeks on the current dressing regimen. Which referral should the nurse make?
options: Provider for an order to culture the wound surface
Wound, ostomy and continence nurse for reassessment and a revised treatment plan
Infection preventionist to review isolation precautions
Physical therapist to increase the resident's mobility
items.rationale: A stalled full-thickness wound with undermining needs expert reassessment of staging, debridement need, dressing selection and pressure redistribution, which is the wound care nurse's scope. Mobility and nutrition matter but do not substitute for a treatment plan that is no longer working. Surface swabs of an open wound grow colonizing organisms and are not used to diagnose infection, and there are no cues suggesting a transmissible infection requiring the infection preventionist.

items.stem: The evening before surgery a client says, 'I keep thinking I will not wake up from this. I would like to make peace with God, but my minister is out of the country.' Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Notify the provider and request an order for an anxiolytic
Refer the client to social work to review the advance directive
Offer to contact the facility chaplain or the client's preferred spiritual care provider
Reassure the client that this surgery is routine and rarely has complications
items.rationale: The client has named a specific spiritual need and a barrier to meeting it, and chaplaincy is the discipline that provides or arranges that support regardless of the client's faith tradition. False reassurance closes the conversation and dismisses a fear the client has just risked voicing. Sedation treats a symptom the client did not report, and an advance directive review, while reasonable later, answers a legal question rather than the spiritual one.

items.stem: A client receiving continuous enteral feeding through a gastrostomy tube has had four loose stools in 12 hours, and capillary glucose values have trended from 150 to 268 mg/dL. The tube site is clean and dry and residuals are minimal. Which team member should the nurse consult about the feeding regimen?
options: Speech-language pathologist to evaluate the swallow
Registered dietitian to review the formula, rate and osmolality
Physical therapist to increase activity and glucose use
Wound care nurse to assess the gastrostomy site
items.rationale: Loose stools with rising glucose during continuous feeding point to the formula itself: osmolality, carbohydrate load, fiber content or infusion rate, all of which the dietitian recalculates with the team. A swallow evaluation is irrelevant for a client who is not taking food by mouth, and the site is described as intact, so wound care has nothing to treat. Activity is beneficial in general but will not resolve formula intolerance.

items.stem: While verifying new orders in the electronic health record, the nurse receives a clinical decision support alert that the newly ordered ciprofloxacin interacts with the client's warfarin. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Override the alert, since the prescriber ordered both medications
Contact the prescriber and pharmacist to review the interaction and the monitoring plan before the first dose
Hold both medications until the provider rounds in the morning
Document the alert in the record and give the ciprofloxacin as ordered
items.rationale: Interaction alerts are decision support, not decisions: the nurse closes the loop with the prescriber and pharmacist so the plan, such as more frequent international normalized ratio monitoring or a different antibiotic, is explicit before the drug is given. Clicking through alerts is how alert fatigue turns a safeguard into noise. Holding the anticoagulant on the nurse's own initiative creates a second risk, and documenting an alert without acting on it does not protect the client.

items.stem: A handwritten order reads 'insulin glargine 10 U subcut at bedtime,' and the nurse cannot tell whether the number is 10 or 100. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the dose the pharmacy dispensed in the client's drawer
Contact the prescriber to clarify and have the order rewritten using the word 'units'
Administer 10 units because it is the lower and therefore safer amount
Ask the charge nurse to interpret the prescriber's handwriting
items.rationale: 'U' is on the do-not-use abbreviation list precisely because it is misread as a zero, and an order the nurse cannot read with certainty is not a valid order. Only the prescriber can clarify intent, and the corrected order should be rewritten with 'units' spelled out. Guessing low still risks an incorrect dose, a colleague's interpretation of handwriting is not verification, and pharmacy may have made the same misreading.

items.stem: The electronic health record will be unavailable for 4 hours during a planned upgrade. Which action should the nurse take during the downtime?
options: Delay nonurgent care and medications until the system is available
Wait until the system returns and reconstruct the shift's documentation from memory
Document care on the facility's downtime forms and enter it into the record once the system returns
Keep personal notes during the shift and shred them after charting from memory
items.rationale: Planned downtime is managed with the facility's downtime packet: paper forms, printed medication administration records and a defined process for back-entry once the system is restored, so care is documented contemporaneously and nothing is lost. Care itself continues on schedule, because a system upgrade is not a clinical reason to delay treatment. Charting from memory hours later produces inaccurate records, and informal personal notes are not part of the legal record.

items.stem: During a scheduled video visit, a client with known coronary artery disease reports crushing substernal chest pain that began 20 minutes ago and appears diaphoretic on camera. Which action should the telehealth nurse take first?
options: Send a message to the provider through the electronic health record
Schedule an urgent in-person appointment for later in the day
Advise the client to take sublingual nitroglycerin and call back in 5 minutes
Activate emergency medical services to the client's location and stay on the call with the client
items.rationale: Ongoing chest pain with diaphoresis is a possible acute coronary syndrome, and the telehealth nurse's first responsibility is to get the client into the emergency system, which is why the client's physical location is verified at the start of every virtual visit. Remaining on the call keeps the nurse assessing and coaching until help arrives. Nitroglycerin, a later appointment or an electronic message all delay definitive care during the window when reperfusion matters most.

items.stem: A client received a medication prepared for a different client. Which statements reflect a just-culture approach to reviewing the event? Select all that apply.
options: The nurse is asked to walk through each step so the process can be mapped
The names of the staff involved are posted with the findings so others learn
The nurse involved is suspended while the investigation is completed
Look-alike packaging and interruptions during the medication pass are examined
The event is reported and reviewed even though the client was not harmed
The review focuses on the system factors that allowed the error to reach the client
items.rationale: Just culture separates human error and system failure from reckless behavior, so the review maps the process the nurse actually followed and looks for the conditions, such as look-alike packaging or interruptions, that made the error possible. Reporting is expected whether or not harm occurred, because unharmed events carry the same system lessons at no cost to a client. Automatic suspension and public naming punish reporting and drive the next error underground.

items.stem: A unit council is choosing nurse-sensitive quality indicators to track on a med-surg unit. Which outcomes are nurse-sensitive indicators? Select all that apply.
options: Hospital-acquired pressure injuries
Time from emergency department arrival to the provider's first order
Central line-associated bloodstream infections
Surgical instrument cost per case
Falls with injury
Catheter-associated urinary tract infections
items.rationale: Nurse-sensitive indicators are outcomes that change when nursing care, staffing or process reliability changes: pressure injuries, falls with injury, central line infections and catheter-associated urinary tract infections all respond directly to nursing assessment and bundle adherence. Instrument cost per case is a supply chain and surgical practice measure, and door-to-order time reflects provider availability and department throughput rather than nursing care.

items.stem: A nurse is completing a home health referral for a client discharged after a total knee arthroplasty with a surgical wound and a new anticoagulant. Which information must the referral include? Select all that apply.
options: The wound care and dressing change orders
The emergency contact and the name and date of the follow-up provider visit
The skilled need and the reason the client is homebound
The current medication list, including the anticoagulant dose and schedule
The client's employer and job title
The client's complete hospital billing summary
items.rationale: A home health agency cannot open a case without a documented skilled need and homebound status, and the visiting nurse must arrive with the reconciled medication list, the wound orders and the follow-up plan so care continues without a gap. Anticoagulant details matter most, because dosing and laboratory monitoring errors after discharge are a leading source of harm. Billing summaries and employment details are not clinical handoff information and share more than the agency needs.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse scans a client's wristband and a medication barcode, and the system displays the alert 'dose exceeds maximum for client weight.' The nurse should {{1}} before the drug is given, because barcode scanning and alerting systems are {{2}}.

options: ask the client whether the dose looks like the usual one
override the alert and document the reason in the record
stop and verify the ordered dose and the client's documented weight with the pharmacist
give half of the ordered dose and reassess the client
primarily a way to record medication pass productivity
a legal substitute for an independent double check
a safeguard that supports, but never replaces, the nurse's own verification
required only for high-alert medications

items.rationale: A weight-based maximum dose alert most often means either the dose or the recorded weight is wrong, and both are verified with the pharmacist before administration. Technology narrows the chance of error but the nurse remains the last check before the drug reaches the client, so an override without verification simply moves the error forward. Halving a dose on the nurse's own authority creates a new unordered dose, and clients cannot be expected to validate their own therapy.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A remote monitoring program reports that a client with heart failure has gained 2.3 kg (5 lb) in 3 days and is now sleeping on two extra pillows. The telehealth nurse should first {{1}}, and should then contact {{2}} for further orders.

options: schedule the client for the next routine visit in 2 weeks
advise the client to restrict all fluids to 500 mL daily
assess the client's symptoms, daily weights and diuretic adherence by video or phone
instruct the client to double the next dose of furosemide
the hospital admitting department
the heart failure provider, using an SBAR report
the durable medical equipment supplier
the client's insurance case reviewer

items.rationale: A gain of more than 0.9 kg (2 lb) in a day or 2.3 kg (5 lb) in a week with new orthopnea signals fluid overload, but the nurse first confirms the weights, symptoms and adherence, because scale errors and missed doses are common explanations. The findings then go to the provider in SBAR form with a specific request. Nurses do not independently adjust diuretic doses, and a routine visit in 2 weeks allows a preventable admission.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that the nurse should report to the provider.

highlightSegments.text: 0400 Postoperative day 1 after open colectomy; client resting in bed.
Temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), up from 37.2 C (99 F) at midnight.
Heart rate 118 and regular, up from 86 at midnight.
Blood pressure 98/56 mm Hg, down from 124/70 mm Hg on admission to the unit.
Respiratory rate 22; oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula.
Abdominal dressing is dry and intact.
Urine output 90 mL over the past 4 hours for a client weighing 80 kg (176 lb).
Pain rated 3/10 with the epidural infusion running at the ordered rate.
Nasogastric tube draining bilious fluid, 150 mL this shift.
Client is alert and oriented to person, place and time.

items.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, a falling blood pressure and urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hr together form an early sepsis picture on the first postoperative day and belong in an SBAR call made now, not at morning rounds. Controlled pain, an intact dressing, expected nasogastric output, normal mentation and a saturation of 95% give context rather than urgency. Reporting the trend, not the single value, is what makes the deterioration visible.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the home visit note that indicate a need for a social work referral.

highlightSegments.text: 1400 Routine home visit for a client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Client states, 'I do my breathing exercises twice a day.'
Client states, 'My electricity was shut off last week, so the oxygen concentrator has not been running.'
Oxygen saturation 90% on room air, unchanged from the previous visit.
Client states, 'I ran out of my inhaler because I had to choose between that and groceries.'
Client's daughter states, 'I have missed so much work caring for him that I may lose my job.'
Weight is unchanged and the client reports a good appetite.
Client states, 'I have no way to get to the pulmonary clinic next week.'
Client ambulates to the bathroom without dyspnea.
Home is clutter free with clear walkways and working smoke detectors.

items.rationale: Utility shutoff, choosing between medication and food, caregiver strain and lack of transportation are social determinants that no amount of teaching will fix; the social worker connects the client with utility assistance, prescription programs, caregiver support and transportation benefits. Recognizing them as referable problems rather than nonadherence changes the plan. Stable saturation, weight, exercise tolerance and a safe home are monitored, not referred.

items.stem: A unit-based quality team reviews data collected after hand hygiene coaching began and dispensers were moved to every doorway. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Compliance is rising and unit-acquired infections are falling, so the changes should be sustained and monitoring continued
Compliance data should be collected only in months when infections increase
Auditing can be discontinued now that compliance is above 90%
The decrease in infections is unrelated to the change in hand hygiene compliance
items.rationale: The process measure and the outcome measure moved together across four months with a constant number of observations, which supports continuing both the intervention and the measurement. Improvement decays quickly when auditing and feedback stop, so success is a reason to hardwire the change rather than to stop watching it. Collecting data only after infections rise removes the early warning that makes prevention possible.

items.stem: A care transitions team reviews outcomes after starting a heart failure discharge program. Which conclusion about the program is supported by the trended data?
options: The decline reflects fewer heart failure admissions rather than the program
Readmissions are falling as post-discharge calls and early appointments increase, supporting continuation of the program
The program has had no effect because readmissions continue to occur
Follow-up appointments should be moved from 7 days to 30 days after discharge
items.rationale: Readmissions fall steadily as the two process measures rise, which is the expected relationship when the transition itself, rather than the inpatient stay, is what is being improved. Expecting a program to drive readmissions to zero misreads the purpose of the measure. Nothing in the table reports total admissions, so attributing the change to lower volume is unsupported, and pushing follow-up out to 30 days removes the early visit that is doing the work.

items.stem: For each nursing action, select whether it is appropriate or not appropriate practice.
matrixRows: Accepting a verbal order during a code while the prescriber is performing chest compressions.
Accepting a telephone order for an intravenous chemotherapy agent.
Copying yesterday's assessment forward into today's note to save time.
Documenting 'telephone order, read back and verified' with the prescriber's name, date and time.
Letting a float nurse chart under the unit's shared computer login because a password was not issued.
Using the record's secure messaging function to send a nonurgent question to the provider.
items.rationale: Verbal orders are limited to emergencies in which the prescriber cannot write or enter the order, and they are still read back and documented afterward. Chemotherapy is excluded from verbal and telephone orders because a misheard agent or dose can be fatal. Copied-forward assessments record care that was never performed, and a shared login destroys the audit trail; secure messaging is the right channel for nonurgent questions.

items.stem: A client's condition has changed and the nurse must escalate the concern. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Document each notification with the time, the person contacted and the response received.
Activate the rapid response team when the provider has not returned the call within the time set by policy.
Escalate to the nursing supervisor and the attending provider according to the chain of command.
Telephone the covering provider and give an SBAR report of the change in condition.
Reassess the client and gather current vital signs, intake and output, and recent laboratory results.
items.rationale: Escalation starts with current data, because an SBAR report built on four-hour-old vital signs invites a delayed response. The covering provider is called first, and when that call is not returned within the policy window the nurse uses the rapid response team, which exists precisely so a deteriorating client is not waiting on a callback. Moving up the chain of command follows, and documenting every notification with times creates the record that the concern was raised and escalated.

items.stem: A home health nurse visits a client on postoperative day 7 after an abdominal hysterectomy. The incision edges are red and warm with purulent drainage, and the temperature is 38.5 C (101.3 F). Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieConditions: Allergic reaction to the dressing adhesive
bowtieActions: Notify the surgeon with an SBAR report and request orders for a wound culture and antibiotics
Instruct the client to stop oral fluids until the surgeon calls back
Apply a heating pad to the incision to increase circulation
Document the findings and reassess at the next routine visit in 1 week
Arrange a wound, ostomy and continence nurse visit through the agency
bowtieParams: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Amount, color and odor of wound drainage
items.rationale: Purulent drainage with erythema, warmth and fever a week after surgery is a surgical site infection; clot formation, dehiscence and contact dermatitis do not produce pus and fever together. Home health care depends on coordination: the surgeon is notified in SBAR form with a specific request for culture and antibiotic orders, and the agency's wound care nurse is brought in for the treatment plan. Progress is judged by defervescence and by drainage becoming less purulent.

items.stem: A resident of a long-term care facility who was on bed rest for 6 days during treatment for pneumonia now requires two-person assistance to stand and takes short shuffling steps with a walker. The resident dresses and grooms independently while seated. Which referral should the nurse initiate?
options: Speech-language pathology for a cognitive screen
Occupational therapy for adaptive dressing equipment
Social work to discuss a change in level of care
Physical therapy for strengthening, transfer training and gait retraining
items.rationale: Deconditioning after even a few days of bed rest is reversible with targeted strengthening, transfer practice and gait training, which is physical therapy's scope. Self-care is already independent, so occupational therapy has no identified deficit to treat, and nothing suggests a cognitive or communication problem. Moving to a higher level of care before rehabilitation is attempted removes function the resident could regain.

items.stem: The utilization reviewer informs the nurse that a client's insurer has denied further inpatient days. The client still requires intravenous antibiotics twice daily for another 10 days and cannot self-administer them. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Request that the provider change the antibiotic to an oral formulation
Inform the client that discharge must occur today because coverage has ended
Ask the provider to document that the client is refusing to leave the hospital
Notify the case manager to arrange home infusion services and to initiate an appeal
items.rationale: A payer denial is a coverage decision, not a clinical one, and the case manager arranges the next safe setting, here home infusion with a visiting nurse, and files the appeal when continued inpatient care is warranted. Discharging a client who cannot administer the therapy guarantees an incomplete course and a readmission. Changing the route is a prescriber's clinical judgment, not a workaround, and documenting refusal misrepresents the situation.

items.stem: A charge nurse on a med-surg unit has been assigned a float nurse from the postpartum unit for the shift. Which assignment is most appropriate for the float nurse?
options: A newly admitted client with sepsis receiving a vasopressor infusion
Two clients with chest tubes placed earlier this morning
