Total-care needs have outgrown the assistive personnel staffing, so the charge nurse should request added support and build repositioning into tonight's assignment
Registered nurse staffing is the problem, so one nurse should be replaced by an assistive personnel
The pattern is normal for weekends and requires no change
items.rationale: Total-care clients more than doubled while assistive personnel were cut from two to one, and missed turns rose in step, which is a staffing-mix problem rather than a charting problem. The charge nurse escalates the resource request and redistributes the repositioning work so pressure injury prevention is explicitly assigned. Trading a registered nurse for unlicensed staff would remove assessment capacity, and calling the pattern normal accepts preventable harm.

items.stem: A charge nurse on a medical-surgical unit is assigning the clients below between a registered nurse and an LPN/LVN. Indicate the most appropriate staff member for each client.
matrixRows: A client who arrived 20 minutes ago and needs the admission assessment
A client with a chronic wound needing the daily dressing change per protocol
A client receiving a nitroglycerin infusion titrated for chest pain
A client with stable diabetes needing scheduled subcutaneous insulin
A client receiving the first dose of intravenous immune globulin
A client with an established gastrostomy tube needing a scheduled feeding
items.rationale: The registered nurse keeps the initial admission assessment, any titrated infusion, and a first dose of a product that can cause an infusion reaction, because each requires ongoing assessment and dose decisions. Protocol wound care, scheduled subcutaneous insulin and feeding through an established tube are predictable procedures within LPN/LVN practice. Assignments are built on the judgment a client's care demands, not on how many tasks it involves.

items.stem: A nurse manager reviews delegation decisions made by a nurse during one shift. Indicate whether each decision was appropriate or inappropriate.
matrixRows: Delegating a 24-hour urine collection to assistive personnel after explaining how the specimen is stored
Asking assistive personnel to obtain the first set of vital signs on a client just returned from the operating room
Asking the LPN/LVN to reinforce dietary teaching the registered nurse began
Asking assistive personnel to apply a condom catheter for a client with incontinence
Asking the LPN/LVN to decide whether a client is ready to be discharged home
Asking assistive personnel to stay with a client who has a nasogastric tube and report any vomiting
items.rationale: Specimen collection with clear instructions, reinforcing teaching already started, applying an external catheter and observing with defined report-back parameters are all correctly delegated. The first set of vital signs after surgery is part of the registered nurse's postoperative assessment, and deciding readiness for discharge is evaluation of the plan of care. The pattern to learn is that collecting data may be delegated while interpreting it and deciding on it may not.

items.stem: A nurse plans to delegate collection of a midstream urine specimen to assistive personnel who recently joined the unit. Place the steps of the delegation process in the correct order.
options: Observe part of the collection and stay available for questions.
Give specific directions, including when the specimen is needed and what to report back.
Verify that the assistive personnel has been trained to collect a midstream specimen.
Assess the client's stability and decide that the task is appropriate to delegate.
Evaluate whether the specimen was obtained correctly and give feedback.
items.rationale: Delegation begins with the right task and right circumstance, which means judging that this client and this task are suitable, and then confirming the right person by checking training. Specific direction follows, then supervision while the task is performed, and finally evaluation with feedback so practice improves. Skipping the early steps is what produces the errors that show up later as a supervision failure.

items.stem: A nurse believes the night assignment is unsafe because two clients require continuous observation and no extra staff are available. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Discuss the specific concern and possible solutions with the charge nurse.
Notify the nursing supervisor on duty when the charge nurse cannot close the staffing gap.
Follow up with the nurse manager during business hours about a longer-term staffing solution.
Provide care for the assigned clients, prioritizing those at highest risk, and never leave them unattended.
Document the concern on the facility's assignment-despite-objection or safety report form.
items.rationale: Concerns go up the chain of command one level at a time, beginning with the charge nurse who can reallocate staff, then the supervisor who controls resources across the facility. Filing the written objection creates the record that protects the nurse and triggers review. The nurse still provides care, because refusing an assignment already accepted is client abandonment, and systemic fixes are pursued with the manager afterward.

items.stem: In a long-term care facility, assistive personnel tell the nurse that a resident who received the morning insulin 'refused breakfast and now seems shaky and sweaty.' The nurse finds the resident diaphoretic, tremulous and confused but able to swallow, with a point-of-care glucose of 44 mg/dL, heart rate 110/min and blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Give 15 g of a fast-acting oral carbohydrate now, since the resident can swallow safely
Have the assistive personnel walk the resident until the shakiness passes
Withhold all treatment until the provider returns the call
Recheck the point-of-care glucose 15 minutes after treatment
Administer the scheduled correction dose of insulin
items.rationale: Insulin given without the expected meal produces hypoglycemia, and diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia and confusion with a glucose of 44 mg/dL confirm it. A conscious resident who can swallow receives 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, with the glucose rechecked in 15 minutes and repeated until it is above 70 mg/dL. Glucose and level of consciousness show whether treatment is working; insulin, delay and exertion would all deepen the episode.

items.stem: A nurse on a medical unit programs an IV heparin infusion into a smart pump. When the rate is entered, the pump displays a hard-limit alert stating that the dose exceeds the maximum allowed for the unit. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Override the alert, since a provider wrote the order and the pump is only a guide
Recheck the order, the bag concentration and the pump programming with a second nurse before starting the infusion
Start the infusion at the ordered rate and document that the alert was displayed
Program the infusion in mL/hr outside the drug library so the alert does not reappear
items.rationale: A hard limit is a dose the pump will not deliver because it falls outside safe practice, and the most common cause is a programming or concentration error, so the nurse stops and verifies the order, the bag and the entries with an independent double check. Overriding the alert, bypassing the drug library or simply documenting the alert all defeat the dose-error reduction software that exists to catch exactly this mistake.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health visit note that require the nurse to intervene.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit 1030: client with COPD receiving oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula from a concentrator.
Client reports sleeping better since the concentrator was delivered.
A lit candle is burning on the end table beside the concentrator.
Spare cylinder is stored upright and strapped into a stand in the hallway.
The concentrator is plugged into a power strip that also supplies a space heater and a television.
The client's son smokes on the back porch with the door closed.
A "No smoking - oxygen in use" sign is taped to the front door.
Client applies petroleum jelly to the nares several times a day for dryness.
Tubing is 7.6 m (25 ft) long and is coiled on a hook when not in use.
The hallway smoke alarm has been chirping for a week and the client has not changed the battery.

items.rationale: Oxygen makes any fire burn faster and hotter, so an open flame, a petroleum-based product at the nares and an overloaded power strip feeding a space heater are all ignition risks that must be corrected at once, and a chirping smoke alarm means the household's early warning is failing. Secured upright cylinders, posted signage, smoking outdoors and neatly stored tubing are the safe practices this home is already following.

items.stem: A fire starts in a wastebasket in a client's room on a medical-surgical unit. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Close the doors of the client rooms along the corridor
Move the client in that room and the roommate out into the hallway first
Use the elevator to move clients to the floor below
Open the windows at the end of the hall to let the smoke out
Use the extinguisher on the wastebasket once the clients are out and the alarm has sounded
Activate the nearest fire alarm pull station
items.rationale: RACE sets the order: rescue anyone in immediate danger, activate the alarm, contain the fire by closing doors, then extinguish a small fire that is still confined. Opening windows feeds the fire oxygen and draws smoke through the unit, and elevators may open onto the fire floor or lose power, so stairwells and horizontal movement behind fire doors are used instead.

items.stem: A nurse is using a fire extinguisher on a small, contained fire after the clients have been moved and the alarm has been activated. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Pull the pin out of the extinguisher handle
Aim the nozzle at the base of the flames
Squeeze the handle slowly and evenly
Stand about 1.8 m (6 ft) from the fire with an exit at your back
Sweep the nozzle from side to side across the base of the fire
items.rationale: The nurse positions first, keeping a clear escape route behind, then follows PASS: pull the pin, aim at the base of the flames, squeeze the handle and sweep side to side. Aiming at the tops of the flames wastes the charge because the fuel burning at the base is never reached, and standing without an exit behind you can leave the nurse trapped if the fire grows.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client on the oncology unit has a low-dose-rate cesium implant in place for cervical cancer. When providing care the nurse should {{1}}. If the implant is found in the bed linens, the nurse should {{2}} and then {{3}}.

options: move the client into a double room so another client can provide company
cluster tasks, stay at the foot of the bed and limit time in the room to 30 minutes per shift
provide unhurried total care at the bedside every hour to reduce the client's isolation
ask the staff nurse who is 12 weeks pregnant to take the assignment for continuity
leave it in the linens and send the bed made up to the laundry
flush it down the client's toilet as contaminated waste
pick it up with gloved hands and return it to the radiation department
pick it up with the long-handled forceps and place it in the lead container kept in the room
ask the client to hold the container until transport arrives
document the finding in the chart at the end of the shift
notify the radiation safety officer and the provider immediately
wait until the implant is due to be removed and report it then

items.rationale: Exposure is controlled by time, distance and shielding, so tasks are clustered, care is given from the foot of the bed and time in the room is capped; pregnant staff and visitors are never assigned. A dislodged sealed source is handled only with long-handled forceps and placed in the lead container that stays in the room, never with hands, never flushed, and the radiation safety officer is notified at once so the source can be recovered and accounted for.

items.stem: A glass thermometer breaks on the tile floor of a long-term care dining room and beads of mercury scatter across the floor. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Pour warm water over the beads to keep them from moving
Vacuum the beads quickly so no one steps in them
Sweep the beads into a dustpan and place them in the regular trash
Move residents and staff away from the area, close the door, and call the facility's hazardous materials spill team
items.rationale: Mercury vaporizes at room temperature and the vapor is what harms the lungs and nervous system, so the first action is to clear and close the space and let a trained spill team use the mercury kit. Vacuuming aerosolizes the metal and contaminates the machine, sweeping breaks the beads into smaller droplets that spread further, and water neither contains the beads nor stops the vapor.

items.stem: A nurse is caring for a client 24 hours after an infusion of IV cisplatin. The client has used a urinal and asks the nurse to empty it. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Wear two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves and a disposable gown, then discard the personal protective equipment in the chemotherapy waste container
Empty the urinal with clean gloves only, since the drug was given the day before
Rinse the urinal in the client's sink and return it to the bedside
Ask unlicensed assistive personnel to empty it wearing a mask and face shield
items.rationale: Hazardous drugs and their metabolites are excreted in urine, stool, sweat and emesis for at least 48 hours, so anyone handling those fluids wears double chemotherapy-tested gloves and a disposable gown, and that personal protective equipment goes into the yellow chemotherapy waste stream. Clean gloves alone are permeable to many agents, a mask and face shield do not protect the hands, and rinsing in an open sink splashes contaminated fluid into the client's environment.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the safety round note that require the nurse to intervene.

highlightSegments.text: 0700 safety round, intensive care bed 12: client is sedated on mechanical ventilation.
Bed is in the low position with the brakes locked.
The ventilator high-pressure alarm volume has been turned down to zero.
Suction is set up at the head of the bed with a Yankauer within reach.
A portable oxygen cylinder is lying loose on the floor next to the bed.
The norepinephrine pump is plugged into a red emergency outlet.
A personal fan under the bed is powered through an extension cord run across to the wall.
Call light is clipped to the pillow within the client's reach.
The wall-mounted sharps container is two-thirds full.
A manual resuscitation bag with a mask hangs at the head of the bed.

items.rationale: A silenced ventilator alarm removes the only warning of a disconnection or obstruction in a sedated client, an unsecured cylinder can fall and shear its valve into a projectile, and a household extension cord is not rated for continuous hospital use and creates a fire and shock hazard. The locked low bed, red-outlet pump, ready suction and resuscitation bag, reachable call light and a sharps container still below the three-quarter mark all meet standard.

items.stem: A charge nurse reviews monitor data for a 24-bed telemetry unit. Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trend?
options: Alarm fatigue is developing: alarms are tripling while actionable alarms stay flat and response times climb
The monitors are defective and the vendor should replace the telemetry system
The unit is caring for sicker clients, so the rise in alarms is expected and needs no action
Staff are responding well, because the number of actionable alarms has not increased
items.rationale: When total alarms climb sharply while the number of true alarms stays flat, almost all the added noise is non-actionable, and the lengthening response time is the measurable sign that staff are tuning it out. The fix is fewer false alarms: default limits customized to each client, daily electrode changes with skin preparation, and review of self-resetting alarms. Sicker clients would raise actionable alarms too, and working monitors are reporting exactly what they are set to report.

items.stem: Two nurses prepare to move a client who weighs 125 kg (275 lb) from the bed to a chair with a ceiling lift. The sling hanging at the bedside is labeled with a maximum capacity of 90 kg (200 lb). Which action should the nurses take?
options: Use the sling that is available and add a third staff member at the client's hips
Transfer the client with a gait belt and two staff members instead
Double the sling straps through the spreader bar to increase the capacity
Obtain a bariatric sling rated for the client's weight before beginning the transfer
items.rationale: A sling rated below the client's weight can tear or release the client mid-transfer, and the rating is a property of the sling fabric and straps that no amount of extra staff or strap looping changes. The nurses obtain equipment rated for the load. Falling back on a gait belt puts the client's full weight on the staff members' backs, which is what safe client handling programs exist to prevent.

items.stem: A nurse feels a tingling sensation while touching the metal frame of a client's electric bed. The client is alert and reports no symptoms. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Complete the shift and report the bed to engineering at the end of the day
Unplug the bed from the wall outlet without touching the client and the frame at the same time
Place a folded blanket over the frame so staff do not touch the metal
Ask the client whether they also feel the tingling before doing anything
items.rationale: A tingle means current is leaking to the chassis, and a hospitalized client can be far more vulnerable to that current than the nurse, so the power source is removed at once, the bed is tagged out of service and biomedical engineering is notified. Touching the client and a live frame together could make the nurse the path to ground. Asking the client to test the frame, insulating it with a blanket, or waiting until the end of the shift all leave a faulty device in use.

items.stem: A nurse is reviewing sharps safety with a group of new graduate nurses. Which practices should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a sharps container within arm's reach at the point of use
Recap a used needle with two hands before carrying it to the container
Replace the sharps container when it reaches the three-quarter fill line
Dispose of the needle and syringe as one unit without separating them
Press down on the contents of a full container to make room for one more syringe
Activate the needle's safety device immediately after withdrawing it from the client
items.rationale: Most needlestick injuries happen between use and disposal, so the safety device is engaged at the bedside, the device goes into the container in one piece, and a container is kept at the point of use so a used sharp is never carried. Containers are exchanged at three quarters full because overfilled containers cause injuries at the opening. Two-handed recapping and pushing down contents are the two classic ways nurses stick themselves.

items.stem: A specimen container of formalin is knocked off the back table in an operating room between cases and breaks, and staff begin coughing and report burning eyes. Which action should the circulating nurse take first?
options: Pour isopropyl alcohol over the spill to neutralize the formaldehyde
Move everyone out of the room, close the door, and follow the safety data sheet for a formaldehyde spill
Mop the spill with water and open the sterile supply cabinet to air the room
Cover the spill with sterile towels and continue preparing the room for the next case
items.rationale: Formaldehyde vapor irritates the eyes and airway at very low concentrations, so people leave the area before anything is cleaned and the room is closed until the spill team works from the safety data sheet, which names the required respirator, absorbent and disposal route. Mopping and opening cabinets spread the vapor and contaminate sterile stock, alcohol does not neutralize formaldehyde, and towels leave staff breathing the vapor while they work.

items.stem: A client in the emergency department waiting area has been told the wait is another two hours. The client is pacing, clenching both fists, standing close to the triage desk and shouting at staff, and a colleague reports the client punched a wall in the corridor. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieConditions: Escalating aggression with imminent risk of assault
bowtieActions: Warn the client that security will remove them if they do not sit down
Leave the client alone in the room until the anger passes
Step closer and place a hand on the client's shoulder to reassure them
Keep an unobstructed path to the door and maintain at least two arm lengths of space
Call the behavioral emergency response team
bowtieParams: Ability to accept redirection and choose from offered options
Pacing, clenched fists and rising voice volume
items.rationale: A client in the emergency department who is pacing, clenching the fists and shouting at staff is escalating toward assault, and the nurse's own safety comes first: keep the exit behind you, stay outside striking distance and bring trained help rather than handling it alone. Crowding or touching the client and issuing ultimatums escalate the encounter, and abandoning the client removes the chance to de-escalate. Progress is judged by the behavioral cues settling and the client's ability to be redirected, not by laboratory values.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Staff on a rehabilitation unit must move a client who weighs 118 kg (260 lb) up toward the head of the bed. To protect themselves from injury they should {{1}}, and each staff member should {{2}}.

options: lower the bed and have one nurse lift under the shoulders while another lifts the hips
flatten the bed, raise it to waist height and use a friction-reducing sheet with staff on both sides
raise the head of the bed and pull the client up by the arms
ask the client to grab the head of the bed and pull while one nurse lifts
reach across the bed and twist at the waist to move the client
hold the breath during the move to brace the spine
keep the load close to the body, bend at the hips and knees and pivot with the feet
lock the knees and lift with the arms fully extended

items.rationale: Sliding rather than lifting is the principle: a flat bed removes gravity, waist height keeps the work between shoulders and hips, and a friction-reducing sheet lets the load glide instead of being carried. Keeping the weight close to the body and turning with the feet protects the lumbar spine, while twisting, reaching, locked knees and pulling on the client's arms concentrate force on the back and can dislocate the client's shoulders.

items.stem: An infant abduction alert is announced overhead while a nurse is charting on the postpartum unit. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Call the security office for instructions and continue caring for the assigned clients
Search every room on the postpartum unit and report the results to the charge nurse
Gather the other parents in the lounge and explain what has happened
Go to the assigned exit or stairwell and watch everyone leaving, noting anyone carrying a bag or package large enough to hold an infant
items.rationale: Facility abduction plans assign every staff member a monitoring post the moment the alert sounds, because an abductor leaves within minutes and usually conceals the infant in a bag, a box or under a coat rather than carrying it openly. Searching only the unit lets the abductor pass an unwatched exit, phoning security adds delay to a plan that is already written, and gathering families pulls staff away from the exits.

items.stem: A resident with moderate Alzheimer disease in a long-term care facility has twice been found trying to open the stairwell door, saying it is time to go to work. Which interventions should the nurse add to the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Use signs, contrasting paint or a curtain to camouflage the exit door
Apply a wander-alert bracelet that triggers the exit door alarms
Provide a structured walking program at the times the resident usually seeks the door
Keep a current photograph and physical description in the record for use if the resident elopes
Confine the resident to the room with the door closed during staff shift change
Tell the resident each time that they are retired and no longer go to work
items.rationale: Wandering is met with monitoring and redirection rather than confinement: an alarming bracelet and a current photo shorten the time to locate a resident, scheduled walking meets the need that drives the pacing, and visual camouflage reduces how often the exit draws attention. Shutting the resident in a room is seclusion and increases agitation, and repeatedly correcting the resident's belief about work provokes distress without changing the behavior.

items.stem: For each item, select the container the nurse should use for disposal.
matrixRows: IV bag and tubing used to infuse cyclophosphamide
A dressing saturated with blood that would drip if squeezed
A used insulin syringe with the needle attached
The plastic wrapper from a sterile dressing package
An empty glass ampule of ondansetron that broke while being opened
The disposable gown worn while hanging a chemotherapy infusion
items.rationale: Waste is segregated by the hazard it carries: anything contaminated with a hazardous drug, including the tubing, the bag and the personal protective equipment worn to give it, goes in the yellow chemotherapy stream, while dressings soaked enough to release blood go in red biohazard bags. Anything that can puncture, including broken glass ampules as well as needles, belongs in a rigid sharps container. Clean packaging is ordinary trash, and treating it as biohazard waste wastes costly disposal capacity.

items.stem: An apartment building fire sends casualties to a community emergency department. The nurse leader reviews the hourly data. Which action should the nurse leader take first?
options: Move the clients who left without being seen to the top of the triage list when they return
Ask each nurse to take two additional clients and keep the current assignment structure
Close the waiting room doors until the current clients have been treated
Activate the emergency operations plan and request additional staff through the labor pool
items.rationale: Census nearly tripling while staffing is unchanged, triage times stretching past half an hour and clients leaving untreated are the signals that demand has outrun the department's normal capacity, which is exactly what the emergency operations plan and its staff labor pool exist for. Simply adding clients to each assignment stretches the same nurses further, refusing arrivals is not lawful under emergency treatment requirements, and tracking those who left does nothing about the backlog creating the risk.

items.stem: A storm knocks out utility power to the hospital and the emergency generator starts. Which action should the nurse on the intensive care unit take first?
options: Reassure each client that the generator supplies the whole hospital
Turn off the overhead lights in every room to reduce the load on the generator
Chart on paper until the electronic record comes back online
Verify that the ventilator and the vasoactive drip pumps are plugged into the red emergency outlets
items.rationale: Emergency generators supply only the red outlets, and they carry a brief gap before the generator picks up the load, so the nurse immediately confirms that life-sustaining equipment is on emergency power and that battery-backed devices are charging. Conserving lighting, moving to paper documentation and reassuring clients all matter, but none of them keeps a ventilated client breathing or a vasopressor infusing in the next few minutes.

items.stem: While walking past an empty soiled utility room, a nurse sees flames in a linen hamper. No one is in the room. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Begin moving the clients in the two nearest rooms to the far end of the hall
Pull the fire alarm at the station beside the utility room door
Find the charge nurse to confirm there is a fire before alerting anyone
Take the extinguisher off the wall and try to put out the hamper fire
items.rationale: RACE begins with rescuing anyone in immediate danger, and because the room is empty the nurse moves straight to activating the alarm, which summons help and triggers the building's fire response. Extinguishing comes after the alarm, never before it, since a fire that grows while one nurse fights it alone leaves no one warned. Moving unthreatened clients or hunting for a colleague only delays the alarm.

items.stem: A fire in an adjoining wing requires a medical unit to evacuate. No client is in immediate danger from flames or smoke. Which client should the nurse direct staff to move first?
options: The client receiving a blood transfusion who needs a wheelchair
The client who is ambulatory and waiting for discharge instructions
The client in skeletal traction who must be moved on a rescue sheet
The client on a ventilator who requires two staff and a transport bag
items.rationale: Ambulatory clients are evacuated first because they can be directed out in groups with minimal staff, which clears the unit and frees every remaining pair of hands for the clients who must be wheeled, carried or moved with equipment. Starting with the most dependent client ties up the whole team while clients who could have walked out remain in the smoke path.

items.stem: A fire on a hospital unit forces an evacuation. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Move the clients who need a wheelchair or stretcher through the fire doors
Move the ambulatory clients through the fire doors into the adjoining wing
Move the remaining clients using rescue sheets or carries
Take the clients down the stairwell to the ground floor if the fire doors no longer hold
Account for every client, visitor and staff member in the safe area
items.rationale: Evacuation moves horizontally first, taking clients behind the fire doors of an adjoining compartment, and it works from the most mobile to the least: those who can walk, then those who can be wheeled, then those who must be dragged or carried. A head count in the safe area is what proves no one was left behind. Vertical evacuation down a stairwell is used only if the fire compartment fails, because moving dependent clients down stairs is slow and dangerous.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse in a long-term care dining room sees flames and smoke coming from a toaster oven on the counter. Following the RACE sequence, the nurse first {{1}} and activates the alarm, then contains the fire by {{2}}.

options: asks a resident to watch the oven while help is summoned
helps the residents seated nearest the counter move away from the area
returns to the nurses' station to look up the fire policy
unplugs the toaster oven and carries it to the sink
propping the corridor fire doors open so staff can move quickly
turning the ventilation system to its highest setting
closing the dining room doors and windows
opening the windows so the smoke can escape

items.rationale: Rescue comes before every other step, so residents in the immediate area are moved away from the flames before anything is done about the fire itself. Containment then means closing doors and windows to starve the fire of oxygen and hold smoke in one compartment. Opening windows, boosting ventilation or propping fire doors open all spread smoke and flame through the building, and carrying a burning appliance risks a spill of burning material.

items.stem: A nurse answers the unit telephone and the caller states that a bomb has been placed in the hospital. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Use a two-way radio to broadcast a warning to the other units
Keep the caller talking while writing down the exact words and any background sounds, and signal a colleague to notify security
Begin searching the unit's storage rooms for an unfamiliar package
Hang up immediately and pull the nearest fire alarm
items.rationale: The person taking the call is the only source of information police will have, so the caller is kept on the line while the exact wording, voice characteristics and background noise are recorded and another staff member alerts security and the operator. Hanging up loses that information, the fire alarm sends people into corridors that have not been cleared, and two-way radios and cell phones are avoided because their transmissions can trigger some devices.

items.stem: Gunshots are heard in the lobby of an outpatient clinic. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Gather the clients in the hallway so staff can account for them
Evacuate by the route farthest from the sound, leaving personal belongings behind
Pull the fire alarm so that everyone in the building evacuates
As a last resort, when life is in immediate danger, use whatever is at hand to disrupt the attacker
Call 911 as soon as it is safe and report the location, number of shooters and description
If escape is not possible, lock and barricade the door, turn off the lights and silence all phones
items.rationale: Run, hide, fight is the sequence: escape by a route away from the threat if one exists, otherwise shelter behind a locked, barricaded door with lights off and phones silenced, and call for help once it is safe. Fighting is a last resort only when the attacker is upon you. Pulling the fire alarm drives people into open corridors toward the shooter, and gathering clients in a hallway leaves a group with no cover.

items.stem: Which event should the nurse expect to trigger activation of the hospital's internal disaster plan?
options: An outbreak of foodborne illness at a community festival fills the waiting room
A water main break floods the hospital pharmacy and sterile processing department
A multivehicle crash on the interstate sends 20 casualties to the emergency department
A hurricane makes landfall 300 km away and community shelters open
items.rationale: An internal disaster is an event inside the facility that damages the building or disables the services the hospital runs on, such as flooding, fire, a hazardous spill or a loss of the electronic record, and its plan deals with relocating services and protecting the people already inside. An external disaster happens in the community and sends casualties in, so the crash, the hurricane and the outbreak all activate the external plan and its surge capacity.

items.stem: Engineering reports a leak that requires the piped oxygen zone valve for a medical unit to be closed within minutes. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask engineering to delay the shutoff until every client can be transferred off the unit
Place clients on portable cylinders, beginning with the client on a ventilator and those at the highest flow rates
Notify each client's provider before any oxygen source is changed
Chart the flow rate each client is receiving so the settings can be restored later
items.rationale: When piped oxygen is about to be lost, the nurse's task is to guarantee an alternative source before the valve closes, and the clients who will decompensate first are the ventilated client and those on high flow, so cylinders go to them first. Documentation and provider notification follow once oxygen delivery is secure. Delaying a shutoff for a leak leaves an ignition and asphyxiation hazard in place and is not the nurse's decision to make.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the environmental log for the unit's sterile supply room. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The readings are acceptable because the temperature has stayed within range
The humidity rise will correct itself once the room is restocked
The packages stored in this room may no longer be sterile; the supplies should be removed from use and facilities notified
Only the air exchange rate matters for sterile storage, and it remains adequate
items.rationale: Sterile storage is kept below about 60% relative humidity with at least four air exchanges per hour, because moisture wicks through wrappers and paper-plastic pouches and carries microorganisms to the contents, a process called strike-through. Humidity climbing past that ceiling while ventilation falls means the packages can no longer be assumed sterile, so they are pulled and the ventilation problem is reported. A temperature within range does not compensate for a failing humidity control.

items.stem: A client with spina bifida who has had 11 previous operations is scheduled for a urologic procedure. Which action should the perioperative nurse take?
options: Have the surgical team wear powdered latex gloves and change them frequently
Premedicate the client with diphenhydramine and proceed with standard supplies
Schedule the client as the first case of the day and set up the room with a latex-free cart
Schedule the client as the last case of the day so the room can be cleaned afterward
items.rationale: Repeated procedures make latex sensitization common in clients with spina bifida, so these clients are treated as latex allergic and scheduled first, before airborne latex particles from other cases accumulate in the ventilation system, with a dedicated latex-free cart at hand. Going last exposes the client to a day of aerosolized allergen, powdered gloves are the main source of that airborne latex, and antihistamines do not prevent anaphylaxis.

items.stem: A client admitted to a medical unit has a documented latex allergy. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Use IV tubing with needleless, non-latex ports for medication administration
Wear powdered latex gloves when caring for other clients on the unit
Draw medications through the rubber stoppers of multidose vials as usual
Apply an allergy identification band and post latex-free signage on the door
Ask nutrition services to omit banana, kiwi and avocado from the client's tray
Remove latex gloves and latex tourniquets from the room and the supply cart
items.rationale: A latex-safe environment means removing the allergen from the room and the supply chain, flagging the allergy so no one reintroduces it, and using non-latex ports and stoppers, since repeated needle punctures of a latex stopper shed particles into the drug. Latex-fruit cross-reactivity makes banana, kiwi, avocado and chestnut worth avoiding. Powdered gloves anywhere on the unit aerosolize latex protein that travels on air currents to the client.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the preoperative note that suggest the client is at risk for a latex reaction.

highlightSegments.text: Preoperative interview, 0645: 34-year-old client scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Works as a dental hygienist and wears gloves for most of the working day.
Reports itching and hives on both hands by the end of a shift, which resolve overnight.
Takes a daily multivitamin; no prescription medications.
Describes lip tingling and throat itching after eating avocado and kiwi.
Denies tobacco use; drinks alcohol socially.
Had a tonsillectomy at age 9 with no complications.
Reports facial swelling after a dental examination two years ago.
Vital signs: blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats/min, temperature 36.8 C (98.2 F).
States the anesthesia team has not asked about allergies yet.

items.rationale: Frequent occupational glove use is the single strongest risk factor for latex sensitization, and hand urticaria at the end of a gloved shift, facial swelling after a gloved dental examination and oral symptoms with avocado and kiwi together form the classic pattern of latex allergy with latex-fruit cross-reactivity. Recognizing it before induction lets the team convert the room to latex-free instead of managing anaphylaxis under drapes.

items.stem: A client has a low-dose-rate sealed implant in place. The client's family asks about visiting. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Visitors may sit at the bedside and hold the client's hand but must not touch the linens
Visits are limited to 30 minutes each day at a distance of at least 1.8 m (6 ft), and no children or pregnant visitors may come
Visitors may stay as long as they like as long as they wear a lead apron
Visits are not permitted at any time while the implant is in place
items.rationale: Visitor exposure is managed by the same three principles used for staff: limited time, maximum distance and shielding where practical. Children and pregnant visitors are excluded because dividing cells are the most radiosensitive. Lead aprons do not make unlimited exposure safe and are not stocked for visitors, close bedside contact defeats the distance rule, and banning visits altogether isolates the client without any added protection.

items.stem: A client is admitted to a private room with an internal radiation implant. For each nursing action, select whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
matrixRows: Wear a dosimeter badge for every entry into the room
Keep a lead container and long-handled forceps in the room
Assign the staff nurse who is 12 weeks pregnant to the client for continuity
Hold all linens, dressings and trash in the room until the radiation safety officer clears them
Allow the client's 6-year-old grandchild to visit for 15 minutes
Organize supplies before entering so care can be given in one brief visit
items.rationale: Radiation safety rests on time, distance and shielding: a dosimeter measures each staff member's cumulative dose, planning care before entry shortens time at the bedside, and a lead container with long forceps must be in the room so a dislodged source can be secured without handling it. Everything leaving the room is held until it is surveyed, because a source can travel out in the linens. Pregnant staff and children are never assigned or allowed to visit, since rapidly dividing cells are most vulnerable.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse sustains a hollow-bore needlestick while withdrawing a needle from a client with untreated human immunodeficiency virus. The nurse should first {{1}}, then {{2}}, so that postexposure prophylaxis can be started {{3}}.

options: scrub the site with undiluted bleach
wash the puncture site with soap and running water
apply a tourniquet above the puncture site
squeeze the site to force blood out of the puncture
wait for the client's consent before telling anyone
finish the medication pass and report at the end of the shift
report the exposure to occupational health without delay
ask the charge nurse to decide whether it should be reported
only after the source client's laboratory results return in three days
only if the nurse develops symptoms
within hours of the exposure
at the nurse's next scheduled shift

items.rationale: First aid is simple washing with soap and water; squeezing the wound and caustic agents such as bleach damage tissue and do not reduce transmission. Immediate reporting matters because prophylaxis for human immunodeficiency virus is most effective when started within hours, and it is begun on the basis of the exposure rather than held until source testing returns. Waiting for symptoms means waiting until prophylaxis can no longer work.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A family member in the emergency department waiting area begins shouting and pointing at the triage nurse about the wait. The nurse should {{1}}, speak in {{2}}, and {{3}}.

options: turn away and continue triaging the next client
stand between the family member and the doorway to block the exit
move in close and take the family member's hands
stand nearest the door with a clear path out and keep an arm's length of space
a firm voice matched to the family member's volume
a whisper so the person has to stop shouting to hear
a calm, low, unhurried voice
a raised voice to regain control of the area
ignore the outburst so it is not reinforced
promise that the client will be taken back immediately
name what the person seems to be feeling and offer a realistic choice
tell the person that security will remove them if they do not stop

items.rationale: De-escalation begins with the nurse's own safety: keep the exit accessible and respect personal space, because crowding or blocking someone who is already aroused invites a physical response. A calm, low voice lowers the volume of the whole exchange, while matching the person's volume escalates it. Acknowledging the feeling and offering a genuine choice restores some control, whereas threats, impossible promises and ignoring the person all intensify the anger.

items.stem: A nurse enters a room and finds the spouse of a postoperative client pressing the patient-controlled analgesia button while the client sleeps, saying "I want to stay ahead of the pain." Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Assess the client's level of sedation and respiratory rate, then teach that only the client may press the button
Thank the spouse for helping and document the family's participation in pain management
Increase the lockout interval on the pump so extra doses cannot be delivered
Remove the pump and request an order for intramuscular analgesia
items.rationale: The safety feature of patient-controlled analgesia is that a client too sedated to press the button cannot dose again, and analgesia by proxy defeats it, so the nurse first checks sedation and respiratory rate for early opioid-induced respiratory depression and then teaches the family why only the client presses. Praising the behavior reinforces the hazard, and changing pump settings or the route of a medication requires a provider order.

items.stem: A hospital introduced safety-engineered needle devices in January. The safety committee reviews the quarterly data. Which conclusions are supported by the trend? Select all that apply.
options: Container-related injuries have not improved and now make up half of the injuries reported
Rising training coverage tracks with the fall in total injuries
The data show that staff have stopped reporting injuries
Sharps injuries cannot be reduced further and the program should be discontinued
The device conversion is working, since injuries from devices without safety features have fallen sharply
trendHeaders: Injuries from devices without safety features
Injuries at an overfilled sharps container
Staff trained on the new devices (%)
items.rationale: Total injuries fell by more than half as training coverage rose and injuries from unprotected devices dropped from 19 to 4, which is the expected signature of a successful device conversion. Container-related injuries did not move at all, so they now account for about half of what remains and become the next target: exchanging containers at three-quarters full and mounting them within reach. Nothing in the data suggests underreporting, and a plateau in one injury type is a reason to redirect the program, not to end it.

items.stem: A client on a rehabilitation unit brings in a personal recliner heating pad, a laptop and a small lamp from home. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Grasp the plug rather than the cord when unplugging a device
Run the cords under the carpet and across the doorway to keep the walkway clear
Use only three-prong grounded plugs for devices in the client care area
Provide a two-prong adapter for the lamp, since the outlet has no ground
Remove from service and tag any device that sparks, feels hot or produces a shock
Have biomedical engineering inspect each personal device before it is used
items.rationale: Personal equipment enters a clinical area only after biomedical engineering verifies grounding and insulation, and grounded three-prong plugs keep stray current out of the client. Pulling on a cord separates the wire from the plug and creates a shock hazard, and any device that sparks, heats or tingles is tagged and removed at once. Cords under carpet are crushed until the insulation fails, and an adapter that removes the ground pin defeats the very protection the third prong provides.

items.stem: Click to highlight the information in the handoff note that requires the nurse to act on the facility's security plan.

highlightSegments.text: 2200 handoff, emergency department observation unit.
32-year-old client admitted for observation after an assault by a former partner.
Vital signs stable; pain 4 out of 10, controlled with ibuprofen.
The client asks that no one be told they are in the hospital.
A caller has telephoned the unit twice this evening asking which room the client is in.
The unit clerk gave the room number to the second caller.
The client's sister visited and was on the approved visitor list.
The client is in the room directly across from the nurses' station.
A court protective order is with the client's belongings in the unit safe, and security has not been told it exists.
Client sleeping at present, call light within reach.

items.rationale: A request for confidentiality is a security order, not a preference: the client is registered as no-information status so the hospital neither confirms nor denies the admission, and repeated calls fishing for a room number are a warning sign that must be reported. Releasing the room number is a breach that has to be escalated at once so the client can be moved and monitored, and security cannot enforce a protective order it has never been shown. Stable vitals, an approved visitor and a room near the station are appropriate.

items.stem: About 50 mL of cyclophosphamide spills onto the floor of an oncology infusion room when tubing separates from the bag. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Restrict access to the area and post a hazardous drug spill sign
Report the spill and any exposure to the supervisor and complete an exposure record
Cover the spill with the absorbent pads from the kit, working from the outer edge inward
Seal all contaminated material in the chemotherapy waste bag from the spill kit
Clean the area three times with detergent solution, then rinse it with water
Put on the gown, two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves, the respirator and the face shield from the spill kit
items.rationale: The area is isolated first so no one walks through the drug or tracks it out of the room, and the responder does not approach the spill until the kit's personal protective equipment is on. Absorbing from the outside edge inward keeps the spill from spreading, and everything used goes into the chemotherapy waste bag before the surface is cleaned three times with detergent and rinsed. Reporting closes the loop so exposed staff receive follow-up.

items.stem: A nurse is taking a client to the radiology department on a stretcher with a portable oxygen cylinder. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Secure the cylinder upright in the carrier attached to the stretcher
Stand the cylinder unsupported on the floor of the elevator during the ride
Lay the cylinder on the mattress beside the client's legs
Carry the cylinder by the valve stem while a colleague pushes the stretcher
items.rationale: A cylinder holds gas at roughly 2,000 psi, so if it falls and the valve stem shears off, the cylinder becomes a projectile; it is therefore always secured upright in a rack, cart or stretcher carrier. Lying loose on a mattress it can roll onto the floor, carrying it by the valve stem puts the full weight on the weakest point, and standing it free in a moving elevator invites exactly the fall the carrier prevents.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to suction a client's tracheostomy because secretions are audible and the oxygen saturation has fallen to 91%. The wall suction regulator will not generate any negative pressure. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Use the portable suction unit kept at the bedside, then tag the regulator and report it for repair
Increase the oxygen flow and wait for engineering to replace the regulator
Instill sterile saline into the tracheostomy and ask the client to cough the secretions out
Take the regulator from the wall unit in the empty room next door and install it
items.rationale: A backup suction source is kept at every airway client's bedside precisely so a failed regulator never delays airway clearance; the nurse uses it now and takes the faulty regulator out of service afterward. Waiting on engineering leaves secretions obstructing the airway, saline instillation is no longer recommended because it pushes organisms distally and worsens oxygenation, and hunting for another regulator wastes time the client does not have.

items.stem: A unit council is writing an alarm management policy for a telemetry unit. Which practices should the policy include? Select all that apply.
options: Change electrocardiogram electrodes daily and prepare the skin before applying them
Set alarm parameters to each client's own baseline rather than leaving the unit defaults
Turn off an alarm that keeps sounding for the same reason
Lower alarm volumes overnight so that clients can sleep
Use the pause or suspend function for a defined interval while providing care
Make sure alarms are audible from wherever the assigned staff are working
items.rationale: Alarm fatigue is reduced by cutting the number of meaningless alarms rather than by making alarms harder to hear. Individualized limits, daily electrode changes with skin preparation and a timed pause during care all remove false alarms at the source, and audibility where staff actually work is what makes a real alarm effective. Lowering volume at night and switching off a repeating alarm both leave a deteriorating client unmonitored, which is how alarm-related deaths occur.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: An infusion pump delivers an unintended bolus of insulin and the client's blood glucose falls to 38 mg/dL. After treating the hypoglycemia, the nurse should {{1}}, then {{2}}, and report the event to {{3}}.

options: reset the pump and return it to the clean equipment room
discard the tubing and send only the pump for testing
take the pump out of service with the tubing and cassette still attached
flush the tubing and restart the infusion on the same pump
label the pump so it cannot be reused and send it to biomedical engineering
have a second nurse test the pump on a bag of saline
leave the pump at the bedside for the next shift to try
give the pump to the manufacturer's representative on the next visit
pharmacy, because the medication involved was insulin
the client's family, since they witnessed the event
risk management, which reports device-related harm to the manufacturer and the Food and Drug Administration
the unit educator at the next staff meeting

items.rationale: A device suspected of causing harm is evidence: it is removed from service with its tubing and cassette intact, because the fault is often in the set rather than the pump, and it is labeled so no one puts it back into use before engineering examines it. Testing it on the unit or discarding the tubing destroys the evidence. Reporting through risk management is how device-related harm reaches the manufacturer and the Food and Drug Administration so other clients are protected.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the preincision briefing that increase the risk of a surgical fire.

highlightSegments.text: Preincision briefing 0730: client scheduled for excision of a facial lesion under monitored anesthesia care.
Oxygen is running at 6 L/min through an open nasal cannula beneath the drapes.
The surgeon plans to use the electrosurgical pencil for hemostasis at the lesion site.
The alcohol-based skin preparation was applied two minutes ago and draping is starting now.
A basin of sterile saline and a fire extinguisher are on the back table.
The electrosurgical pencil is stored in its insulated holster whenever it is not in use.
Anesthesia reports the client's beard has been coated with a petrolatum-based ointment.
The drapes are being tented so that gases do not collect under them.
The scrub nurse confirms the instrument and sponge counts with the circulator.
The team states the fire risk score aloud during the time out.

items.rationale: A surgical fire needs an oxidizer, an ignition source and fuel, and all three are present here: open oxygen pooling under drapes near the face, an electrosurgical pencil at the same site, alcohol prep that has not been allowed to dry, and petrolatum in the beard. The saline basin, holstered pencil, tented drapes and a spoken fire risk score are the controls that reduce risk rather than create it.

items.stem: Flames appear at the surgical site during a tracheostomy in which electrocautery is being used. Which action should the team take first?
options: Continue the procedure while the circulating nurse brings the extinguisher
Pour the basin of sterile saline over the surgical field before anything else is done
Activate the fire alarm and evacuate the operating room
Stop the flow of all airway gases and remove the burning drapes and materials from the client
items.rationale: An airway fire is fed by the oxygen and anesthetic gases flowing to the client, so the gas flow is stopped and the burning drapes, tube and sponges are pulled away from the client in the same motion; saline is then used on any remaining flame and the client is reassessed for airway burns. Reaching for saline or an extinguisher first leaves oxygen feeding the fire, and evacuating with an anesthetized client on the table abandons the person who is burning.

items.stem: For each event, select the emergency plan the hospital should activate.
matrixRows: A tornado tears the roof off the hospital's east wing
A commuter train derails and 40 injured people are en route
Ransomware takes the electronic health record offline across the hospital
Wildfire evacuation of a nursing home brings 25 residents to the emergency department
A single client falls in the bathroom and fractures a wrist
A chlorine leak in the hospital's own water plant forces the basement to be cleared
items.rationale: Internal disasters damage the building or disable the hospital's own systems, so structural damage, a hospital-wide record outage and a chemical release inside the facility all call for relocating services, downtime procedures and evacuation of an area. External disasters occur in the community and send casualties in, which is what the derailment and the nursing home evacuation do, activating surge capacity and the labor pool. A single client fall is managed through routine incident reporting.

items.stem: Clients begin arriving at the emergency department entrance after a chemical release at a nearby factory, with the liquid still on their clothing and skin. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Have the clients wait in the waiting room until the chemical has been identified
Give each client a gown and a mask and escort them to the nearest sink to wash
Direct the clients to the decontamination area outside the entrance and have their clothing removed before they come inside
Bring the clients into the treatment rooms and begin triage while awaiting the hazardous materials team
items.rationale: Decontamination happens outside the department because a contaminated client will otherwise expose staff, other clients and the ventilation system, and closing an emergency department for decontamination removes the community's only receiving facility. Removing clothing eliminates the majority of the contaminant before copious water rinsing. Triage, waiting rooms and interior sinks all bring the chemical inside, and care begins once the client is decontaminated.

items.stem: Twenty minutes into a procedure, a client develops generalized flushing and hives, audible wheezing, a heart rate of 128 beats/min and a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. The team is wearing latex gloves and a latex urinary catheter has just been inserted. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Administer intramuscular epinephrine per the anaphylaxis protocol
Document the skin changes and complete the procedure as planned
Give an oral antihistamine and reassess the client in one hour
Stop the procedure and remove every latex item in contact with the client
Apply a cool compress to the areas of redness
bowtieParams: Airway patency, work of breathing and oxygen saturation
items.rationale: Hives, bronchospasm, tachycardia and hypotension within minutes of latex contact are systemic anaphylaxis, not a local or vasovagal event, and malignant hyperthermia presents with rigidity, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide and hyperthermia instead. Treatment is to remove the allergen and give intramuscular epinephrine at once; oral antihistamines act far too slowly for a reaction that closes an airway. Recovery is judged by the airway opening and the blood pressure and heart rate normalizing.

items.stem: A nurse is reviewing infant security measures with staff on a mother-baby unit. Which measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Teach parents to check the photograph identification badge of anyone who takes the infant
Position the bassinet on the far side of the room, away from the doorway
Leave the bassinet in the hallway while helping the parent to the bathroom
Release the infant to any staff member in scrubs whom the nurse recognizes
Transport infants only in the bassinet, never carried in a staff member's arms
Verify each shift that the infant's security tag and matching identification bands are in place
items.rationale: Abductions succeed when an infant is out of a parent's sight with someone who looks like staff, so infants move only in bassinets, are never left unattended, and are handed over only after a photograph badge is verified. Keeping the bassinet away from the doorway removes the easy reach from the corridor, and checking the security tag each shift catches a tag that has been removed or has failed. Recognition is not identification, and a bassinet in a hallway is unguarded.

items.stem: Two staff members must move a client on a loaded stretcher down a long corridor to the procedure suite. Which technique best protects the staff from injury?
options: Lift the head end of the stretcher slightly to steer around the corners
Lock the elbows and lean the upper body into the stretcher to get it moving
Push the stretcher, keeping it close to the body and driving with the leg muscles
Pull the stretcher while walking backward so the client stays in view
items.rationale: Pushing lets the large muscles of the legs and gluteals do the work with the spine in neutral alignment, while pulling loads the lumbar spine and shoulders and means walking backward into an unseen corridor. Lifting any part of a loaded stretcher adds the weight to the staff member's back, and locking the elbows to lean into the load transfers force straight through the joints rather than using the legs.

items.stem: Two nurses are transferring a client from the bed to a chair with a full-body mechanical lift. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Explain the procedure to the client and lock the brakes on the bed and the chair
Attach the sling straps to the spreader bar and check every attachment point
Move the lift to the chair with the second nurse guiding and supporting the legs
Raise the client just clear of the mattress and pause to confirm the sling is secure
Roll the client from side to side to position the sling smoothly under the body
items.rationale: Explaining the transfer and locking the brakes prevent the bed or chair from moving under the load, and the sling is positioned by rolling the client rather than by lifting them. Straps are attached and every hook checked before any weight is taken, and the pause just above the mattress is the point at which a poorly seated sling can be corrected safely rather than mid-air. The second nurse guides the client during the move so the legs do not swing into the lift.

items.stem: A nurse is struck in the face by a client with hyperactive delirium during morning care and sustains a bruised cheekbone. Which action reflects the facility's workplace violence program?
options: Ask the charge nurse to describe the event in the client's chart instead of filing a report
Report the injury through the event reporting system and to occupational health even though the client did not intend harm
Say nothing, since being hit is an accepted part of caring for confused clients
Report the event only if the injury requires the nurse to miss work
items.rationale: Workplace violence programs depend on complete reporting, because unreported events make the hazard invisible and no unit can staff, train or redesign around injuries no one has counted. Reporting is required whether or not the client was capable of intent and whether or not time is lost. Treating assault as part of the job is exactly the norm these programs exist to change, and a chart entry describes the client's condition rather than the staff injury.

items.stem: A behavioral health unit introduced de-escalation training and a behavioral emergency response team a year ago. The safety committee reviews the quarterly data. Which conclusion should the committee draw?
options: Training can now stop, because nearly all staff have completed it
The rise in behavioral emergency calls shows that the training has made clients more violent
The program has had no measurable effect and should be replaced
Staff are summoning help earlier, and assaults and lost-time injuries have fallen as training coverage grew
items.rationale: More behavioral emergency calls alongside fewer assaults is the pattern of a program that is working: staff are calling for a trained team while a situation is still verbal instead of waiting until someone is struck. Assaults fell by more than half and lost-time injuries reached zero as training coverage tripled. Training also has to continue for new hires and as a refresher, since a trained workforce decays with turnover.

items.stem: A nurse manager observes practices on a medical unit. For each observation, select whether the practice is safe or unsafe.
matrixRows: A full oxygen cylinder is stored lying on its side on the equipment room floor
An infusion pump is plugged directly into a grounded three-prong wall outlet
The ventilator alarm is suspended for two minutes while the nurse suctions at the bedside
Tape is placed over the pulse oximeter speaker to quiet a frequent alarm
The defibrillator and crash cart are checked at the start of every shift
The call light cord is routed under the wheels of the bed
A pump that alarmed repeatedly is sent to biomedical engineering with a description of the fault
items.rationale: Cylinders are stored upright and secured so the valve cannot shear, and a call light cord crushed under bed wheels can fail when the client most needs it. Muffling an alarm speaker silences every future alarm from that device, including a true one, whereas a timed suspension during suctioning ends by itself. Grounded outlets, shift checks of resuscitation equipment and sending a faulty pump for repair with a description of the fault are all standard safe practice.

items.stem: A new graduate nurse describes what they would do in a unit fire. Click to highlight the statements that require correction.

highlightSegments.text: "First I would move anyone who is in immediate danger out of the room."
"Then I would pull the nearest alarm and call the emergency number with the exact location."
"I would prop the corridor fire doors open so we could move people through faster."
"I would close the doors of the client rooms as I passed them."
"I would take the clients who can walk into the next wing beyond the fire doors first."
"If the fire were small and everyone was out of the room, I would use an extinguisher."
"I would aim the extinguisher at the top of the flames."
"I would use the elevator to take the clients who cannot walk down to the lobby."
"I would keep a count of everyone who reaches the safe area."
"I would only go down the stairwell if the fire doors stopped protecting us."

items.rationale: Fire doors are the barrier that holds smoke and flame in one compartment, so propping them open destroys the protection that makes horizontal evacuation possible. An extinguisher is aimed at the base of the flames, because the fuel is burning there and the charge is wasted on the flame tips. Elevators may lose power or open onto the fire floor and are never used in a fire. The remaining statements correctly describe rescue, alarm, containment, mobility order and head counting.

items.stem: A nurse working in an endoscopy suite develops burning eyes, a sore throat and a dry cough while scopes soak in an uncovered basin of glutaraldehyde. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Add water to the basin to dilute the glutaraldehyde solution
Leave the room and have the basin covered and the room ventilation checked before anyone returns, then report the symptoms to occupational health
Put on a surgical mask and finish processing the scopes
Prop the door to the corridor open to clear the vapor out of the room
items.rationale: Eye, throat and airway irritation are the warning signs of glutaraldehyde vapor exposure, so the nurse leaves the area first, and the engineering controls that should have prevented it, a covered basin and adequate local exhaust ventilation, are restored before work resumes. A surgical mask filters droplets, not vapor, diluting the solution makes the basin an even larger evaporating surface, and opening the door spreads the vapor into the corridor.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client is being discharged after receiving oral iodine-131 for thyroid cancer. For the first several days at home the client should {{1}}, and household members should {{2}}.

options: collect all urine in a container and bring it to the clinic
flush the toilet twice with the lid down and wash the hands each time
use the family bathroom in the usual way
limit fluid intake so that less urine is produced
sleep in a separate bed and limit close contact, especially children and anyone who is pregnant
make no changes, because the dose is completely absorbed by the thyroid
avoid the client entirely for six weeks
wear gloves whenever they are in the same room as the client

items.rationale: Iodine-131 is an unsealed source that leaves the body in urine, saliva and sweat, so the precautions are about containing body fluids and limiting close contact: double flushing with the lid down, thorough handwashing and generous fluid intake to clear the isotope faster. Sleeping apart and keeping distance from children and pregnant household members applies the distance and time principles at home. Complete avoidance is unnecessary, and gloves do nothing about proximity.

items.stem: A nurse works in the cardiac catheterization laboratory, where fluoroscopy is used during most procedures. Which action demonstrates correct use of the dosimeter badge?
options: Wear the badge at the collar outside the lead apron and never wear anyone else's badge
Wear the badge under the lead apron so that it records the dose the body actually receives
Leave the badge on a sunny windowsill between shifts so the reading resets
Share one badge with the colleague who works the same shifts to simplify tracking
items.rationale: The collar badge worn outside the apron measures the dose reaching unshielded tissue such as the thyroid, eyes and head, which is the exposure the apron does not cover, and it is assigned to one person because the record is that individual's lifetime dose. A badge under the apron underestimates true exposure, a shared badge makes both records meaningless, and heat and sunlight damage the badge and produce false readings.

items.stem: A client scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 1 hour tells the nurse, 'I signed the paper, but I still do not know whether they are taking my gallbladder out or just looking at it.' Which action should the nurse take?
options: Notify the surgeon that the client needs further explanation before the procedure
Document that the client is anxious and continue with preoperative preparation
Ask the client to sign a second consent form after reviewing the operative permit
Explain the difference between a diagnostic laparoscopy and a cholecystectomy to the client
items.rationale: The provider performing the procedure is responsible for disclosing its nature, risks, benefits and alternatives; the nurse witnesses the signature and confirms that the client understands. A signature given without understanding is not informed consent, so the nurse stops and notifies the surgeon. Explaining the surgery personally exceeds the nurse's role, a second signature does not create understanding, and charting anxiety leaves the client uninformed.

items.stem: A nurse signs a surgical consent form as the witness to the client's signature. The nurse's signature attests to which of the following?
options: The surgeon has answered all of the client's remaining questions
The client is the person named on the form and signed it voluntarily
The client understands every possible risk of the procedure
The nurse explained the surgical procedure and its alternatives to the client
items.rationale: Witnessing a consent means verifying the identity of the signer, that the signature is genuine, and that it was given voluntarily and without coercion. Disclosure of the procedure, its risks and alternatives belongs to the provider performing it, so the witness signature cannot certify the client's depth of understanding or that every question has been answered. The nurse does confirm understanding and reports gaps to the provider.

items.stem: A client in the preoperative area received IV midazolam 15 minutes ago for anxiety. The nurse then notices that the operative consent form has not been signed. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Have the client sign the consent now while still able to hold the pen
Hold the consent and notify the surgeon that the client has been sedated
Ask the adult child waiting in the lobby to sign the consent for the client
Document that the client gave verbal consent and send the client to the operating room
items.rationale: Consent obtained after a sedating or mind-altering medication is not valid, because the client can no longer weigh risks and alternatives; the surgeon must be told so the procedure can be delayed until the drug wears off. A family member cannot consent for an adult who has decision-making capacity, and documenting verbal consent does not repair a consent the client could not legally give.

items.stem: The charge nurse audits consent forms on a surgical unit. Which situations indicate that the consent is not valid and requires follow-up before the procedure? Select all that apply.
options: A client read the form, asked two questions the surgeon answered, and then signed
A client signed after the surgeon reviewed the risks, benefits and alternatives
The form for a client who speaks only Vietnamese was explained by the client's 12-year-old grandchild
A client who has a court-appointed guardian signed the form independently
A client signed the form 10 minutes after receiving IV morphine for pain
A 16-year-old client who lives with and is supported by parents signed the form alone
items.rationale: Consent is invalid when the signer is not legally able to give it or cannot understand the information. A non-emancipated minor needs a parent or guardian, an opioid impairs the capacity to weigh risks, a child is never an acceptable interpreter for medical information, and a client under guardianship no longer holds the authority to consent. A signature that follows the provider's disclosure and the client's questions is exactly what a valid consent looks like.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 17-year-old client who is married, employed and living independently comes to the urgent care clinic alone for treatment of a wrist injury. The nurse recognizes that this client is considered {{1}}, so consent for the treatment should be obtained from {{2}}.

options: a ward of the state
a minor who cannot consent to any care
an emancipated minor
a client who requires a court order for treatment
a child protective services caseworker
either parent by telephone
the clinic manager
the client

items.rationale: A minor who is married, in military service or declared emancipated by a court makes health care decisions as an adult does, so the client signs the consent personally. Calling a parent would disclose information the client controls and delay needed care. Guardianship and court orders apply only when no legal decision maker exists, which is not the case here.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the preoperative nurse's note that require follow-up before the client is taken to the operating room.

highlightSegments.text: 0630 Preoperative assessment of a 74-year-old client scheduled for a right total hip arthroplasty at 0800.
The signed and dated consent form lists a left total hip arthroplasty.
The surgeon marked the operative site on the right hip at the bedside.
Identification band and allergy band verified with the client.
Client states, 'My son holds my power of attorney papers, but I still make my own decisions.'
Client asks, 'Will they be putting me to sleep? No one has talked with me about the anesthesia.'
Last oral intake was a sip of water with morning medications at 0500.
Blood pressure 128/74, heart rate 78, respirations 16, temperature 36.8 C (98.2 F).
The witness signature line on the consent form is blank.
Dentures and eyeglasses are at the bedside and labeled.
Latex allergy reported; the operating room has been notified.

items.rationale: A consent that names the wrong side does not match the marked site and must be corrected by the surgeon before surgery, and an unwitnessed form is incomplete. Anesthesia carries its own risks, so the anesthesia provider obtains a separate consent; a client who has not discussed it is not yet informed.
