A client with capacity still decides even when an agent is named, and the fasting status, vital signs, personal items and communicated allergy are expected findings.

items.stem: A client admitted to the medical unit tells the nurse, 'I have a living will at home and my daughter keeps a copy of it.' Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document that the client reports having a living will and take no further action
Have the client complete a new advance directive form before any treatment begins
Ask that a copy be brought in so it can be reviewed and placed in the medical record
Ask the provider to write a do-not-resuscitate order based on the client's statement
items.rationale: An advance directive guides care only when the team can read it, so the admitting nurse documents that one exists and arranges for a copy to be placed in the record. Making the client sign a new form ignores the existing document and the client's stated wishes. A living will is not an order; only a provider can write a do-not-resuscitate order, and only after the client's wishes are known.

items.stem: A client who is alert and oriented has a durable power of attorney for health care naming a nephew as the agent. The client refuses a recommended blood transfusion, and the nephew tells the nurse, 'I hold the power of attorney, so I am consenting to it.' Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: 'The provider will decide which of you should be followed in this situation.'
'Because you hold the power of attorney, your decision is the one we follow.'
'Your authority to decide begins only when the client can no longer make decisions.'
'I will ask the ethics committee to determine who has the right to consent.'
items.rationale: A durable power of attorney for health care takes effect only when the client loses decision-making capacity; until then the client's own refusal governs, which is the principle of autonomy. Letting the agent override an alert client, deferring to the provider, or convening the ethics committee all treat a clear legal question as if it were unresolved and risk an unconsented transfusion, which is battery.

items.stem: A client is being admitted to a long-term care facility. Which nursing actions meet the facility's obligations regarding the client's right to make health care decisions? Select all that apply.
options: Tell the client that a do-not-resuscitate order is a condition of admission
Ask whether the client has an advance directive and document the answer
Place a copy of the client's existing advance directive in the medical record
Offer information about how to prepare an advance directive if the client has none
Give the client written information about the right to accept or refuse treatment
Require the client to complete an advance directive before the admission is finalized
items.rationale: Facilities must ask about advance directives, document the answer, provide written information about the right to accept or refuse treatment, keep any existing directive in the record and offer help in creating one. Care may never be conditioned on signing a directive or accepting a do-not-resuscitate order; making either a requirement is coercion and defeats the purpose of self-determination.

items.stem: A nurse in an outpatient dialysis unit reviews the record of a client with end-stage kidney disease. Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trend?
options: The client is consistently expressing a wish to stop dialysis and needs a goals-of-care discussion
Transportation should be arranged so the client does not miss the next scheduled session
The client is nonadherent and should be reminded of the consequences of missing treatment
The client's decision-making capacity is impaired and the health care agent should now decide
trendRows: Stopped after 90 minutes at the client's request
'I do not see the point in this anymore.'
Declined to come to the chair
'I want to stop dialysis for good.'
items.rationale: A competent adult may withdraw from any treatment, including dialysis, and three consecutive entries of the same wish are a decision rather than a lapse. The nurse arranges a goals-of-care conversation, screens for treatable depression or pain, and offers palliative options. Labeling the client noncompliant is a judgment, not a fact, and capacity is not lost simply because a choice differs from the team's recommendation.

items.stem: A client in a long-term care facility who has a do-not-resuscitate order begins choking during lunch, cannot speak and cannot cough. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Call the provider to clarify the do-not-resuscitate order before intervening
Perform abdominal thrusts to relieve the airway obstruction
Position the client side-lying and wait for the family to be reached
Remain with the client and provide comfort measures only
items.rationale: A do-not-resuscitate order directs the team not to attempt resuscitation after cardiac or respiratory arrest; it does not withhold treatment of a reversible problem such as a foreign-body airway obstruction. Do not resuscitate never means do not treat. Waiting for clarification or for the family while the client is obstructed allows a preventable arrest and is abandonment of care.

items.stem: A client with metastatic cancer is enrolled in home hospice and has a do-not-resuscitate order with a comfort-focused plan of care. For each intervention, click to indicate whether it is consistent or inconsistent with the client's do-not-resuscitate order.
matrixRows: Administering morphine sulfate for dyspnea
Applying oxygen by nasal cannula for comfort
Starting chest compressions when the client is found pulseless and apneic
Treating a symptomatic urinary tract infection with oral antibiotics
Performing endotracheal intubation for respiratory arrest
Repositioning and giving mouth care every 2 hours
items.rationale: A do-not-resuscitate order limits cardiopulmonary resuscitation and intubation at the time of arrest; every other treatment continues unless the client has also declined it. Symptom relief, oxygen, antibiotics for a symptomatic infection and hygiene all support comfort and are fully consistent with the order. Compressions and intubation are precisely the interventions the client has declined.

items.stem: A hospitalized client says to the nurse, 'I want to read what is in my chart.' Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the client to explain the reason for the request before taking any action
Follow facility policy to arrange access with someone available to answer questions
Explain that the record is hospital property and cannot be shown to clients
Tell the client that the record may be requested in writing after discharge
items.rationale: Clients have the right to see and obtain a copy of their own health information; the paper or server belongs to the facility, but the information belongs to the client. The nurse follows the policy that governs timing, copying and supervision, and offers to have someone present to interpret unfamiliar terms. Refusing, demanding a reason or delaying access until discharge all obstruct a right the client already holds.

items.stem: A client in the emergency department who is alert and oriented says, 'I am done waiting, I am leaving,' and begins to dress. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Document what the client was told, the client's own words and the condition at departure
Notify the provider that the client intends to leave before treatment is complete
Provide discharge instructions, prescriptions and clear reasons to return for care
Ask what is prompting the decision to leave and resolve the concern if possible
Explain the risks of leaving and offer the against-medical-advice form for signature
items.rationale: Many departures are driven by a fixable problem such as pain, a long wait, child care or fear, so the nurse asks first and may keep the client in care. The provider is then notified, the risks of leaving are explained and the form is offered, and the client still receives instructions, prescriptions and return precautions because refusing treatment does not forfeit safe care. Documentation of the exchange is completed last and protects both the client and the staff.

items.stem: A client with pneumonia who is alert and oriented refuses the ordered IV antibiotic, stating, 'I have decided that I do not want any more IVs.' Which action should the nurse take?
options: Explore the reason for the refusal and notify the provider that the dose was refused
Give the antibiotic in juice without telling the client it is the same medication
Chart that the client refuses all care and withhold further treatment
Ask the client's spouse to persuade the client to accept the treatment
items.rationale: A client with capacity may refuse any treatment, and the nurse's role is to learn why, correct any misunderstanding, and tell the provider so an alternative such as an oral antibiotic can be offered. Disguising a medication is deception and administration without consent. Recruiting family to pressure the client is coercive, and treating one refusal as a refusal of all care abandons a client who still wants to be treated.

items.stem: An 82-year-old client is brought to the emergency department by an adult child after a reported fall. The client has bruises in several stages of healing on both upper arms, weighs 4 kg less than at a clinic visit 6 weeks ago, and glances at the adult child before answering each question. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Chart that the client was struck by the adult child
Tell the client that the adult child will be removed from the home today
Report the suspicion to adult protective services as a mandated reporter
Interview the client privately, away from the person who accompanied the client
Ask the adult child to describe how each bruise happened while the client listens
bowtieParams: Pattern, location and stage of healing of any injuries at each encounter
Pain rating during ambulation in the hallway
Body weight and hydration status over time
Number of visitors the client receives on the unit
items.rationale: Injuries of differing ages, unexplained weight loss and deferring to a caregiver before speaking are classic cues of mistreatment, and nurses are mandated reporters who act on reasonable suspicion rather than proof. A private interview lets the client speak freely, while questioning the caregiver in front of the client can silence or endanger them. Injury patterns and weight track whether the situation is improving; potassium, visitor counts and ambulation pain do not.

items.stem: A nurse manager observes unit practices during a privacy audit. Which practices are breaches of client confidentiality and require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: A nurse discusses a client's new cancer diagnosis with a colleague in a crowded elevator
A nurse gives change-of-shift report in a conference room with the door closed
A nurse posts online, 'We lost our sweet 92-year-old in room 12 today.'
A nurse opens the electronic record of a neighbor who was admitted overnight
A nurse leaves a workstation logged in and unattended at the nurses' station
A nurse faxes a discharge summary to the client's primary care clinic at the client's request
A nurse tells a telephone caller, 'I am not able to confirm whether anyone by that name is here.'
items.rationale: Confidentiality is breached whenever protected information is disclosed, accessed or left exposed without a treatment-related need, including curiosity lookups and posts that identify a client by room, age and date. Reporting behind a closed door, declining to confirm a client's presence to a caller and sending records the client has authorized are all appropriate uses of protected information.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse photographs a client's leg wound with a personal phone and posts the image online with the caption 'worst one I have seen in 10 years' and no name attached. This is a breach of confidentiality because {{1}}. The nurse's first action should be to {{2}}.

options: only photographs that show a client's face are protected
the caption expressed a personal opinion about the wound
the phone used was not owned by the facility
images and details can identify a client even when no name is used
delete the photograph from the phone and take no further action
remove the post and report the disclosure to the nurse manager
ask the client for permission now that the image has been posted
add a comment stating that the image is not of a real client

items.rationale: Tattoos, scars, wounds, room details and the timing of a post can identify a client as surely as a name can, so posting clinical images without written authorization violates privacy regardless of the platform or the device used. Removing the post limits the exposure, and self-reporting to the manager starts the required investigation and notification. Quietly deleting the image, seeking consent afterward or denying the client is real conceals a disclosure that has already occurred.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health nurse's note that support a report of neglect to adult protective services.

highlightSegments.text: 1400 Home visit for an 88-year-old client with heart failure who lives with an adult grandchild.
The apartment is cold; the client states the heat was shut off 2 weeks ago.
Client is dressed in a sweater with a blanket over the legs.
Weight is 6 kg less than at the visit 1 month ago.
The refrigerator holds only condiments; the client states, 'I eat when my grandchild remembers to shop.'
The weekly pill organizer is full; no furosemide has been taken since the last visit.
Blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 82, lungs clear to auscultation.
The grandchild keeps the client's bank card and states the pension check is 'for the household.'
Client states, 'I do not want anyone to get in trouble.'
Client is oriented to person, place and time and answers questions without hesitation.
Skin is intact with no bruising or pressure injuries.

items.rationale: Withheld heat, food and prescribed medication, unexplained weight loss and a caregiver controlling the client's money are cues of neglect and financial exploitation. A nurse is a mandated reporter who acts on reasonable suspicion and does not need proof, the client's permission or the caregiver's agreement to make the report. Normal vital signs, intact skin and the client's wish that no one get in trouble do not cancel the duty to report.

items.stem: The night nurse reviews the record of a client on a medical unit. Which action should the nurse take first based on the trend?
options: Obtain a PRN order so the restraints may be reapplied if agitation returns
Document that the client tolerated the restraints throughout the night
Assess the client and release the restraints, since the behavior that required them has resolved
Continue the restraints until the provider rounds in the morning
trendRows: Pulling at the abdominal drain; verbal redirection and family at bedside
Pulled the drain dressing off; provider order obtained for soft wrist restraints
Circulation, skin and range of motion checked
Calm and oriented; asks to have arms freed
items.rationale: Restraints are an intervention of last resort that ends at the earliest possible moment, and two consecutive hours of calm, oriented behavior show the danger has passed. Monitoring must also be documented at the required intervals, so the blank entries need correction. Leaving a client restrained for staff convenience is false imprisonment, PRN restraint orders are prohibited, and charting tolerance does not justify continuing an intervention that is no longer needed.

items.stem: A client is found on the bathroom floor on a medical unit. After assessing the client and notifying the provider, which entry should the nurse make in the medical record?
options: 'Client fell because the bed alarm had been turned off by the previous shift.'
'Unwitnessed fall; variance report completed and forwarded to risk management.'
'Client found sitting on the bathroom floor at 0915, states, "My legs gave out." No visible injury, vital signs and neurologic check at baseline, provider notified.'
'Client is careless about safety and needs frequent reminders to call for help.'
items.rationale: Charting is factual and objective: what was observed, the client's own words, the assessment findings and who was notified. Assigning a cause blames a colleague and records a conclusion the nurse cannot prove. Naming the variance report in the chart pulls an internal quality document into the legal record, and calling a client careless is a judgment rather than an observation.

items.stem: A nurse completes a variance (incident) report after a client receives a dose of a medication intended for another client. Which statement about the report is accurate?
options: It is an internal quality-improvement document used to find and correct system problems
It takes the place of charting the event and the client's response
It becomes a permanent part of the client's medical record
It is used by the manager to document disciplinary action against the nurse involved
items.rationale: A variance report is an internal risk-management and quality-improvement tool that lets the facility find the system failure behind an error; it is not filed in the chart and is not a disciplinary form. The client's assessment, the notification of the provider and the client's response are still documented in the medical record, but the record never refers to the report itself.

items.stem: The nurse manager reviews with staff which situations require a variance (incident) report. Which events require one? Select all that apply.
options: A client declines a bath and the refusal is documented in the record
A client's peripheral IV infiltrates and the site is treated per protocol
A client asks to reschedule a physical therapy session and it is moved to the afternoon
A nurse catches a tenfold dose error in an order before the medication is given
A visitor slips on a wet hallway floor and reports no injury
The controlled substance count at shift change does not match the record
A client receives a scheduled dose of insulin 3 hours after the ordered time
items.rationale: A variance report is completed for any event that departs from expected care or facility routine, including harm, potential harm to clients or visitors, medication and timing errors, controlled substance discrepancies and near misses that were caught in time. Documented refusals and schedule changes made at the client's request are ordinary, expected care and need no report.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse finds a heparin infusion running at twice the ordered rate, corrects the rate immediately, and the client shows no change in condition. Even though no harm occurred, the nurse should {{1}}, because the purpose of the report is to {{2}}.

options: tell the oncoming nurse in report and make no written report
complete a report only if the client later develops bleeding
chart the event and note in the record that a report was filed
complete a variance report and chart the assessment findings in the record
create a record of which staff member made the error
fulfill the client's right to be told about the mistake
build the facility's defense if a lawsuit is filed
identify the system failure so it can be corrected before someone is harmed

items.rationale: Near misses are reported precisely because no one was hurt; they reveal the pump programming, labeling or verification failure while there is still time to fix it. The chart holds the clinical facts and the client's response but never mentions the report. Reporting is not a disciplinary record, a substitute for disclosing an error to a client, or a legal strategy.

items.stem: A school nurse examines an 8-year-old who has a looped, linear bruise across the back and says, 'I got in trouble about my grades.' The child asks the nurse not to tell anyone. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Report the suspicion to child protective services as required by law
Honor the child's request and keep the information private
Wait for a second injury so the pattern can be confirmed
Telephone the parents to ask how the injury happened before deciding
items.rationale: A patterned bruise that matches an object and an explanation of punishment are reasonable grounds to suspect abuse, and nurses are mandated reporters who must report suspicion, not proof. Confidentiality does not extend to reportable abuse. Questioning the parents can place the child at greater risk and may allow the story to be changed, and waiting for a second injury means waiting for further harm.

items.stem: A new graduate nurse asks the preceptor about the duty to report suspected abuse. Which statements by the preceptor are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: 'You must have the family's agreement before a report is made.'
'Document the objective findings and the client's own words in the record.'
'Failing to report suspected abuse can carry disciplinary or criminal penalty.'
'A nurse who reports in good faith is protected from civil liability.'
'The report is made whether or not the provider shares your concern.'
'You report when you have a reasonable suspicion; you do not have to prove it.'
items.rationale: Mandated reporting rests on reasonable suspicion, and good-faith reporters are shielded from liability so that concern for the client outweighs fear of being wrong. The duty belongs to the nurse personally, so it is not waived by a family's objection or a provider's disagreement, and not reporting carries its own penalty. Objective documentation with direct quotes supports the report and any later investigation.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the emergency department note that support a report of suspected child abuse.

highlightSegments.text: 1930 A 14-month-old is brought to the emergency department by a parent for 'not using the left arm.'
The parent states the toddler 'rolled off the couch this morning' and has been fussy since.
By the parent's account, the injury occurred about 10 hours before arrival.
Radiographs show a spiral fracture of the left humerus.
Radiology also reports a healing posterior rib fracture of unknown origin.
Temperature 37.1 C (98.8 F), heart rate 138, respirations 30.
Three round, symmetric burns about 1 cm across are noted on the right forearm.
Immunizations are documented as up to date.
The child cries during the examination and is consoled by the parent.
Weight is at the 45th percentile, unchanged from a visit 2 months ago.
The parent asks how long the visit will take.

items.rationale: An injury that does not match the reported mechanism, a delay in seeking care, a healing fracture no one can explain and small round burns of uniform size are classic physical abuse cues, and together they meet the threshold for a report. Normal vital signs, current immunizations, expected growth and a consoling parent are reassuring but never cancel out physical findings that cannot be explained by the history given.

items.stem: A nurse beginning a shift in a long-term care facility finds a stage 3 pressure injury on a resident's sacrum that appears in no previous documentation and was not mentioned in handoff. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Complete a variance report and wait for risk management to investigate the omission
Ask the nurse from the previous shift why the wound was never reported
Photograph the wound with a personal phone so there is proof of the finding
Assess and measure the wound, document the findings and notify the provider and the manager
items.rationale: The client comes first: a full wound assessment, factual documentation and notification of the provider start treatment, and telling the manager begins the facility and state reporting an unreported stage 3 injury requires. A variance report follows but never precedes care. Confronting a colleague delays treatment, and a personal phone photograph is an unauthorized disclosure of protected information.

items.stem: A client with limited English proficiency is scheduled to begin chemotherapy and says through an adult child, 'I do not know what this medicine will do to me.' Which nursing actions demonstrate client advocacy? Select all that apply.
options: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter before any further teaching
Hold the first dose until the client can describe the treatment and its effects
Ask the adult child to interpret the discussion so the appointment stays on schedule
Document the client's stated concern and the follow-up that was arranged
Ask the oncologist to return and review the treatment plan with the interpreter present
Reassure the client that the oncologist would never order anything harmful
items.rationale: Advocacy means making sure the client's voice and understanding shape the plan, which starts with a qualified interpreter rather than a family member who may edit, soften or misunderstand clinical terms. The provider returns because disclosure is the provider's duty, the concern and the plan are documented, and treatment waits until consent is genuinely informed. Blanket reassurance substitutes the nurse's trust for the client's own understanding.

items.stem: A nurse on a psychiatric unit reviews the events of the afternoon. Which action is appropriate at 1500?
options: Direct the other clients to stay in their rooms and continue to document the behavior
Initiate restraint for immediate safety and obtain the provider order and face-to-face evaluation within the required time
Continue verbal de-escalation alone, because restraints are never permitted on a psychiatric unit
Place the client in seclusion for the remainder of the shift so there are no further outbursts
trendRows: Pacing the hallway and speaking loudly
Quiet room and PRN lorazepam offered; both declined
Shouting at another client with fists clenched
Verbal redirection; other clients moved away from the area
Threw a chair toward the nursing station
Advancing toward staff with fists raised
items.rationale: Less restrictive measures were offered and failed across three escalating episodes, and the client now poses an immediate danger to others, which is the only justification for restraint. A nurse may initiate emergency restraint with the provider order and the face-to-face evaluation obtained within the time frame policy requires. Restraint or seclusion ends when the danger ends, so ordering it for the rest of the shift is punishment, and documenting alone leaves staff and clients unprotected.

items.stem: A nurse reviews new restraint orders on a medical unit. Which order should the nurse question?
options: Soft wrist restraints for a nonviolent client, with the order renewed every 24 hours per policy
Restraint now for behavior that is an immediate danger, with a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour
A vest restraint PRN for agitation during the night shift
Bilateral soft wrist restraints for up to 4 hours for pulling at the endotracheal tube
items.rationale: Restraint may never be ordered PRN, because each application must be justified by the client's condition at that moment and covered by a current, time-limited order. Time-limited orders for tube protection, daily renewal for nonviolent restraint and a prompt face-to-face evaluation after emergency application all meet accepted standards. A standing PRN order lets staff restrain at will, which is false imprisonment.

items.stem: A nurse in a memory care unit reviews a resident's record. Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trend?
options: A one-to-one sitter is needed 24 hours a day until the behavior stops
The exit-seeking follows a predictable late-afternoon pattern and calls for structured activity and a wander-alert device
A vest restraint should be applied each evening to keep the resident from leaving
The bed alarm is working and the plan of care does not need to change
trendRows: Found at the exit door wearing a coat
Found at the exit door asking to 'go home and make dinner'
Found in the parking lot by a visitor
items.rationale: Three episodes at nearly the same hour, each with a purposeful explanation, point to a late-day pattern that responds to routine, activity and environmental cues rather than to force. Restraints for wandering increase falls, injury and agitation and may not be used for staff convenience. Around-the-clock observation is more restrictive than the pattern requires, and a night-only bed alarm plainly does not address behavior that occurs before dinner.

items.stem: A client on a medical unit is in bilateral soft wrist restraints for repeatedly pulling at a nasogastric tube. For each nursing action, click to indicate whether it meets or does not meet the requirements for safe and lawful restraint use.
matrixRows: Releasing the restraints every 2 hours for range of motion, skin care and toileting
Securing the restraint straps to the side rails so they are within easy reach
Documenting the behavior that required restraint and the alternatives tried first
Leaving the restraints on after the client is calm so the next shift does not have to reapply them
Obtaining a new provider order when the current order reaches its time limit
Tying the straps with a quick-release knot that one staff member can undo with one hand
items.rationale: Lawful restraint use requires periodic release for circulation, skin and elimination needs, a current time-limited order, documentation of the behavior and the less restrictive measures that failed, and knots that release instantly in an emergency. Straps tied to a side rail tighten or injure the client when the rail is moved, and keeping a calm client restrained for staff convenience is false imprisonment rather than a clinical decision.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: An older adult in a long-term care facility calls out repeatedly during the night, and a staff nurse asks the provider for a sedative so the unit can 'get through the shift.' A medication given for that purpose is considered {{1}}. Before any medication is requested, the nurse should {{2}}.

options: a nursing action outside the restraint policy
an acceptable PRN intervention
a chemical restraint
a routine comfort measure
document that the resident is disruptive to the rest of the unit
look for an unmet need such as pain, toileting, hunger or fear and address it
give the smallest dose of sedative that is available on the unit
move the resident to a room farther away from the other residents

items.rationale: A drug used to control behavior or restrict movement, rather than to treat the client's diagnosed condition, is a chemical restraint and carries the same order, monitoring and documentation requirements as a physical one. Calling out is usually communication, so the nurse looks first for pain, a full bladder, hunger, cold or fear. Moving or labeling the resident manages the staff's inconvenience, not the resident's need.

items.stem: A client with an infected diabetic foot ulcer and osteomyelitis refuses the recommended below-the-knee amputation, saying, 'I would rather take my chances.' The surgeon asks the nurse to 'talk some sense into' the client. Which action by the nurse best supports the principle of autonomy?
options: Confirm that the client understands the options and their consequences, then support the decision
Ask the client's spouse to sign the surgical consent form instead
Repeat the likely outcome of refusing surgery until the client agrees to the procedure
Request a psychiatric evaluation, since refusing a limb-saving procedure is not rational
items.rationale: Autonomy means an informed client with capacity decides, even when the team believes the decision is unwise. The nurse's work is to make sure the decision is informed, to document it, and to keep offering care such as wound management and pain control. Repeating warnings until the client yields is coercion, a spouse cannot consent for a capable adult, and a refusal the team dislikes is not by itself evidence of mental illness.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse tells a client, 'I will be back at 1400 to change your dressing,' and returns at that time despite a heavy assignment, which demonstrates {{1}}. Later the nurse tells the client honestly that the wound culture has grown a resistant organism, which demonstrates {{2}}.

options: justice
non-maleficence
autonomy
fidelity
justice
fidelity
veracity
beneficence

items.rationale: Fidelity is faithfulness to commitments made to the client, and keeping a small promise is what makes a client trust the larger ones. Veracity is the duty to tell the truth, including news the client may not want to hear, because informed decisions rest on accurate information. Beneficence is doing good, non-maleficence avoiding harm, and justice fair treatment, none of which name what these two actions illustrate.

items.stem: During a mass casualty event, the charge nurse assigns the last available ventilator using the facility's triage protocol rather than giving it to the client who arrived first. This decision reflects which ethical principle?
options: Justice, the fair distribution of limited resources
Veracity, the duty to tell clients the truth
Fidelity, keeping commitments made to a client
Autonomy, the client's right to choose treatment
items.rationale: Justice governs how burdens and scarce resources are shared, and a triage protocol applies the same criteria to everyone instead of rewarding arrival order or social standing. Autonomy concerns the client's own choices, veracity concerns truthfulness, and fidelity concerns promises kept; none of them decides who receives a resource that cannot be given to all.

items.stem: A client in the intensive care unit has a nonsurvivable brain injury and death is expected. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Confirm with the organ procurement organization whether the client is listed in the donor registry
Let the trained requestor from the organ procurement organization approach the family about donation
Support the family's decision and continue care that preserves organ function if donation is chosen
Notify the organ procurement organization of the imminent death, as required for every death
Ensure the provider has discussed the client's condition and prognosis with the family
items.rationale: The facility must notify the organ procurement organization of every imminent death, and that organization, not the bedside staff, screens for suitability and checks the donor registry. The family first hears the prognosis from the provider; the donation request follows separately, from a trained requestor, so grief is not mixed with a request. The nurse then supports whatever the family decides and maintains care that keeps organs viable.

items.stem: The family of a client who has been declared brain dead asks the nurse, 'Should we donate the organs?' Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: 'Most families choose to donate, and I think it would be a good decision.'
'Since no donor card was signed, donation is not an option now.'
'You have to decide before the ventilator can be turned off.'
'I will arrange for the organ procurement coordinator to discuss the options with you.'
items.rationale: The request for donation is made by a trained requestor from the organ procurement organization, who can answer questions about the process without any stake in the family's decision. The nurse provides presence, comfort and factual information rather than an opinion, because steering a grieving family undermines a voluntary choice. Absence of a donor card does not end the option, since the legal next of kin may authorize donation.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate the client may not be able to give informed consent for the planned surgery.

highlightSegments.text: 1000 A 79-year-old client admitted yesterday with a left hip fracture is scheduled for surgical repair this afternoon.
Client states the year is 1962 and calls the nurse 'the girl from the bakery.'
Temperature 38.1 C (100.6 F), heart rate 96, blood pressure 132/78.
Client cannot state the reason for being in the hospital or name the planned operation.
Hydromorphone 1 mg IV given 20 minutes ago for pain rated 8 of 10.
Family reports the client was 'sharp as a tack until this week.'
When handed a pen, the client signs the consent form without reading it or asking a question.
Urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase.
The daughter is documented in the record as the health care agent.
Skin over the left hip is intact with no bruising.

items.rationale: Capacity requires the client to understand the problem and the proposed treatment, weigh alternatives and communicate a choice. Disorientation to time and person, inability to name the problem or the operation, a recent opioid dose and a signature given without reading anything show that this is not informed consent. Fever and a positive urinalysis point to a delirium that may be reversible, so the provider assesses capacity and the agent decides only while the client cannot.

items.stem: A client whose religious beliefs prohibit blood transfusion has a hemoglobin of 6.4 g/dL after a gastrointestinal bleed. The client is alert, oriented and signs a refusal-of-blood form. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Notify the provider so alternatives such as volume expanders, iron and erythropoietin can be considered
Transfuse the unit of packed red blood cells, since the hemoglobin level makes this an emergency
Ask the hospital chaplain to persuade the client to accept the transfusion
Ask the client's adult child to authorize the transfusion on the client's behalf
items.rationale: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, including one the team considers lifesaving, and a signed refusal is honored. The nurse's role is to make sure the refusal is informed, document it, and work with the provider on bloodless alternatives so the client is still treated. Transfusing anyway is battery, and using clergy or family to pressure or override the client replaces the client's values with someone else's.

items.stem: A 6-year-old is brought to the emergency department by a neighbor after being struck by a car. The child has a rigid abdomen, a blood pressure of 72/40 and requires immediate surgery. The parents cannot be reached. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
options: The neighbor who brought the child signs the operative consent form
Treatment proceeds under implied consent while efforts to reach the parents continue
All treatment is held until a parent gives consent by telephone
A court order is obtained before any treatment is started
items.rationale: When a delay in treating a life-threatening emergency would cause death or serious harm and no legal decision maker can be reached, consent is implied because a reasonable parent would agree to the care. Staff continue trying to reach the parents and document those attempts. A neighbor has no legal authority to consent, and waiting for a court order in a hemorrhaging child converts a legal formality into a fatal delay.

items.stem: A client who speaks only Somali is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization, and the consent form is unsigned. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Document the interpreter's name or identification number and how the service was provided
Witness the client's signature and place the completed form in the medical record
Have the interpreter confirm that the client can restate the procedure, its risks and the alternatives
Notify the cardiologist that the client is ready for the consent discussion with the interpreter present
Obtain a qualified medical interpreter through the facility's interpreter service
items.rationale: A qualified medical interpreter is arranged first, because nothing said before that point can be verified as understood; family members and bilingual staff without interpreter credentials are not acceptable for consent. The provider then makes the disclosure through the interpreter, the client demonstrates understanding by restating it, and only then does the nurse witness the signature. Recording who interpreted and how completes the legal record.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who lacks decision-making capacity needs emergency surgery, and the health care agent lives 300 km away, so the surgeon obtains consent by telephone. Facility policy requires that this consent be witnessed by {{1}}. The nurse then documents {{2}}.

options: the unit secretary who placed the telephone call
a member of the hospital's legal department
the client's assigned nurse alone
two staff members who both hear the provider's discussion with the agent
that the surgeon accepted responsibility for the consent
the name of the person consenting, the relationship to the client, the date and time, and both witnesses
the agent's home address and telephone number
only that verbal consent was obtained before surgery

items.rationale: Telephone consent is valid when the provider makes the full disclosure and two staff members listen on the line and sign as witnesses, which is the usual facility standard because no signature can be obtained. The surgeon, not the nurse, describes the procedure, risks and alternatives. Documentation must show who consented, by what authority, when, and who witnessed it, so the consent can be verified later.

items.stem: A client with advanced heart failure has a valid advance directive declining resuscitation and intubation, and a matching provider do-not-resuscitate order. The client becomes unresponsive with agonal respirations, and the adult child at the bedside says, 'I want everything done.' Which action should the nurse take?
options: Follow the advance directive and the do-not-resuscitate order, and call the provider to support the family
Begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation because a family member present is requesting it
Start chest compressions but withhold intubation as a compromise
Have the adult child sign a form rescinding the client's advance directive
items.rationale: A client's own documented wishes govern, and family members cannot revoke an advance directive or a do-not-resuscitate order; only the client may do that while capable. The nurse provides comfort measures, honors the order, and brings the provider, chaplain or palliative team to help the family through a grief reaction that is real but does not change the plan. A partial code performed to appease a family is neither what the client chose nor sound care.

items.stem: For each statement about advance directives, click to indicate whether it describes a living will or a durable power of attorney for health care.
matrixRows: Puts in writing which treatments the client would want or refuse near the end of life
Names a person who is authorized to make health care decisions for the client
Guides the team through situations the client never wrote about
Takes effect only in the circumstances the document defines, such as a terminal condition
Lets the designated person consent to a treatment the client never addressed in writing
Is a written statement of the client's preferences with no decision maker named
matrixColumns: Durable power of attorney for health care
items.rationale: A living will is a written statement of treatment preferences that applies only to the conditions it names, so it cannot answer questions the client did not foresee. A durable power of attorney for health care appoints a person, which is why it covers unanticipated decisions and is the more flexible document. Many clients have both, and the named agent is expected to decide in keeping with the written preferences.

items.stem: A client is admitted voluntarily to an inpatient psychiatric unit. Which rights does the client retain during the admission? Select all that apply.
options: The right to keep all personal belongings, including a lighter and a razor, at the bedside
The right to leave the unit whenever desired without telling staff
The right to refuse a specific medication
The right to request discharge, subject to the review period allowed by state law
The right to confidentiality of the treatment record
The right to send and receive sealed mail
The right to be free from restraint or seclusion used as punishment
items.rationale: Voluntary admission does not surrender civil rights: the client may refuse medication, communicate privately, request discharge and expect confidentiality, and restraint may never be used for punishment or convenience. Items that can be used for self-harm are secured under unit safety policy, and movement off the unit is controlled for safety, so those two are limits every client on the unit shares rather than rights that were taken away.

items.stem: A client has been in bilateral soft wrist restraints for 6 hours for pulling at a surgical drain. The client is now calm, oriented and no longer reaching for the drain. The provider is in the operating room and cannot be reached. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Reapply the restraints more loosely until the order can be renewed
Leave the restraints on until the provider can be reached to discontinue the order
Release one wrist at a time every 2 hours until the order expires
Discontinue the restraints and document the assessment and the time of release
items.rationale: A restraint order sets a maximum duration, never a minimum, and the nurse is expected to release the restraint as soon as the behavior that justified it has resolved; no new order is needed to stop. Keeping a calm, oriented client restrained because the prescriber is unavailable is false imprisonment. Loosened straps create a strangulation and entrapment hazard rather than a compromise.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the nurses' note that require follow-up before the client leaves the unit.

highlightSegments.text: 1830 Client admitted this morning with cellulitis of the right leg states, 'I have to get home to my dog, I am leaving now.'
Hydromorphone 1 mg IV was given at 1805 for pain rated 7 of 10.
Client is alert and oriented to person, place, time and situation.
Client states the plan is to drive home alone.
A peripheral IV catheter remains in the left forearm.
The provider has been notified that the client intends to leave.
Client declines to sign the against-medical-advice form.
No prescription for oral antibiotics has been provided to the client.
Temperature 37.6 C (99.7 F), heart rate 88, blood pressure 126/78.
Client was told the risks of leaving before the antibiotic course is finished.
Client's spouse is waiting in the lobby.

items.rationale: An opioid given 25 minutes earlier impairs judgment and makes driving unsafe, so the plan to drive must be addressed, and the IV catheter has to come out before the client leaves. Leaving without antibiotics defeats the treatment the client still needs, so prescriptions and return precautions are given even for a departure against advice. Refusing to sign the form is simply documented and does not keep the client from leaving.

items.stem: An adult sibling of a hospitalized client stops the nurse in the hallway and asks, 'Did the HIV test come back positive? We live in the same house, so I have a right to know.' The client has not authorized any disclosure. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: 'Household members are entitled to the results, so I can tell you what the test showed.'
'The chart is at the bedside if you want to look through it yourself.'
'I will ask the provider whether the result can be released to you.'
'I cannot share any information without the client's permission, but I will let the client know you have questions.'
items.rationale: Protected health information is disclosed only with the client's authorization or for treatment, payment and operations; sharing a home does not create a right of access, and communicable disease follow-up is handled through public health channels rather than by telling relatives at the bedside. Offering to pass the question to the client keeps the decision where it belongs. Pointing to the chart and asking the provider both treat a settled privacy rule as negotiable.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A police officer comes to the emergency department and asks the nurse for a client's blood alcohol result and a copy of the record, presenting no warrant or court order. The nurse should {{1}}. Protected health information is released to law enforcement only {{2}}.

options: give the officer the result verbally but not a copy of the record
confirm only whether the result was above the legal limit
refer the officer to the facility privacy officer or administrator without disclosing anything
release the record because the officer is investigating a crime
whenever an officer states that an investigation is under way
when a law requires it or a warrant, subpoena or court order authorizes it
when a nursing supervisor gives verbal approval
if the client is in police custody at the time

items.rationale: A badge is not authorization. Disclosure to law enforcement requires a legal basis such as a statute, warrant, subpoena or court order, and the privacy officer decides whether one exists, which protects both the client and the nurse. Confirming a result verbally or narrowing it to a yes-or-no answer still discloses protected information, and a supervisor cannot approve what the law does not permit.

items.stem: A nurse receives a social media friend request from a client discharged from the unit last week, along with a message asking the nurse to explain recent laboratory results. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Accept the request and answer only about results that were already discussed in the hospital
Decline the request and direct the client's questions about results to the provider's office
Ask the nurse manager to reply to the client's message on the nurse's behalf
Accept the request but send the results in a private message so nothing is public
items.rationale: Online friendship with a client blurs the professional boundary, and clinical questions answered outside the record leave no documentation and no one accountable for the advice. Declining while redirecting the question keeps the boundary and still helps the client get an answer. A private message is just as much an unauthorized disclosure on an unsecured platform, and handing the exchange to the manager does not fix the channel it is happening in.

items.stem: A 29-year-old client comes to a women's health clinic for a routine visit with a healing black eye and finger-shaped bruises on both forearms, and says, 'I bruise easily.' The partner who came along answers most of the questions and declines to step out of the room. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Ask the partner directly in the examination room to explain how the bruises happened
Report the situation to the police without telling the client that a report is being made
Tell the client that the relationship is dangerous and that the partner must be left today
Arrange to interview the client alone by giving a routine reason to separate the pair
Assess immediate safety and offer information about a safety plan and community resources
bowtieParams: The client's own statements about safety at home and whether a safety plan is in place
The partner's willingness to attend counseling sessions
Platelet count and complete blood count at every visit
Pattern, location and stage of healing of injuries at each visit
The client's body mass index at each visit
items.rationale: Grip-pattern bruises, an injury the client minimizes and a partner who will not leave the room are cues of intimate partner violence, and screening is valid only when the client is alone. Safety assessment and resources respect autonomy: the client decides when and whether to leave, and directives or reports made behind the client's back can escalate the danger. Reporting rules for a competent adult vary by state, so the nurse follows state law and tells the client what will be reported.

items.stem: A nurse completes a variance report after a client receives a medication intended for a different client. Which information belongs in the report? Select all that apply.
options: An objective description of what happened
The name of the provider notified and the time of notification
The client's response and the assessment findings after the event
The names of the staff who witnessed the event
The date, time and location of the event
The nurse's opinion about which staffing decision caused the error
A note that a copy of the report was filed in the medical record
items.rationale: A variance report records facts that let risk management reconstruct the event: when and where it happened, exactly what occurred, who saw it, how the client responded and who was notified. Opinions about blame turn a safety tool into an accusation and discourage reporting. The report is never filed in or referenced by the medical record, because doing so makes an internal quality document part of the legal chart.

items.stem: A client 1 day after abdominal surgery reports pain of 8 of 10 with guarding and a heart rate of 108. When the nurse calls, the provider says, 'That client is drug seeking. Hold the pain medication,' and ends the call. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates advocacy?
options: Administer the previously ordered opioid anyway, since the order has not been formally discontinued
Document that the medication was held as directed and take no further action
Report the objective findings, request a bedside evaluation, and notify the charge nurse if the pain remains untreated
Tell the client that the provider does not believe the pain is real
items.rationale: Advocacy means putting the client's assessment data in front of the decision maker and escalating through the chain of command when a need goes unmet; guarding with tachycardia after abdominal surgery may also signal a complication that a bedside evaluation would catch. Charting the hold and moving on abandons the problem. Giving a drug the prescriber has just directed be held disregards a change in the order, and repeating the remark to the client damages trust without relieving pain.

items.stem: For each nursing action, click to indicate the ethical principle it best illustrates.
matrixRows: Honoring a client's decision to decline a feeding tube
Having a second nurse independently verify an insulin dose before it is given
Sitting with a frightened client during the wait before a procedure
Assigning staff by client acuity rather than by insurance coverage
Holding a medication the client reports an allergy to until the order is clarified
Arranging an interpreter so a client can weigh the treatment options
items.rationale: Autonomy protects the client's own choice, which is why both honoring a refusal and arranging an interpreter belong to it: a choice made without understanding is not free. Non-maleficence is the duty to avoid harm, seen in independent double checks and in stopping a medication that could trigger an allergic reaction. Beneficence is active good such as comfort and presence, and justice is the fair distribution of care and staff.

items.stem: A nurse discovers that a client received a double dose of metoprolol 2 hours ago. Vital signs are stable, and the provider has been notified. The client asks, 'Did something go wrong with my medicine?' Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: 'You received an extra dose of your blood pressure medicine. The provider knows, and we are checking your vital signs closely.'
'Everything is fine, so try not to worry about the medications.'
'I am not allowed to discuss medication errors with clients.'
'I will ask the provider to explain it to you during rounds tomorrow.'
items.rationale: Veracity requires that clients be told the truth about their own care, including errors, and a client who is asking directly is entitled to a plain answer about what happened and what is being done. Reassurance that hides the event, a claim that disclosure is forbidden, and a deferral to rounds tomorrow all conceal information the client needs to participate in monitoring for effects such as bradycardia and hypotension.

items.stem: A nurse realizes that a client has just been given another client's dose of warfarin. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Assess the client, including vital signs and any signs of an adverse effect
Document the medication given, the assessment findings and the provider notification in the record
Remain with the client and monitor for the effects the provider identifies
Complete the variance report according to facility policy
Notify the provider of the error and the client's condition and carry out any new orders
items.rationale: The client comes first, so the nurse assesses before doing anything else, then notifies the provider, who may order laboratory tests, an antidote or closer observation. Monitoring continues while the effect is possible, and the record then documents the medication given, the assessment and the notification, without ever naming the variance report. The report is completed last because it serves the facility's safety review, not the client's immediate care.

items.stem: A unit practice council reviews the variance reports for client falls on a medical unit. Which conclusion should the council draw from the trend?
options: The rise reflects more thorough reporting rather than any change in client safety
The numbers are within normal variation and no action is needed at this time
Clients identified as high risk should be placed in restraints during evening hours
Falls are rising, cluster in the evening and increasingly occur without a bed alarm, so the evening fall-prevention process needs review
trendHeaders: Bed alarm in use at the time
items.rationale: Variance reports exist to expose patterns, and three months of rising falls concentrated in one time block with falling alarm use point to an evening process problem such as staffing, rounding or handoff rather than to individual carelessness. Injuries are rising with the count, so this is not better reporting or ordinary variation. Restraints increase injury and are never a substitute for a fall-prevention bundle.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the nurses' note that require follow-up by the oncoming nurse.

highlightSegments.text: 0700 A 34-year-old client in the intensive care unit has a nonsurvivable traumatic brain injury; brain death testing is scheduled for 0900.
The client's driver's license carries a donor designation.
The organ procurement organization has not been notified of the imminent death.
The night nurse told the family, 'Donating would be the right thing to do for him.'
Mechanical ventilation and a norepinephrine infusion continue per orders.
The spouse asks, 'What happens next, and who decides?'
The client's mother states that she does not want the body 'cut up.'
A chaplain has been with the family at the bedside through the night.
The night nurse charted, 'Family is being difficult about donation.'
Heart rate 104, blood pressure 92/54, temperature 35.6 C (96.1 F).

items.rationale: Every imminent death is reported to the organ procurement organization, which screens the client and sends a trained requestor; that referral has not happened and cannot wait. Bedside staff do not make the donation request, and urging a family toward donation is coercive. Charting a family as difficult records a judgment rather than a fact; questions and differing views among family members are a normal part of grief.

items.stem: A nurse manager on a 32-bed medical unit wants to redesign shift report. The manager shares data on missed information, asks staff nurses to form a small team to design a bedside handoff, and coaches the team as it pilots and refines the process. Which leadership style is the manager demonstrating?
options: Transformational
Bureaucratic
Laissez-faire
Autocratic
items.rationale: Transformational leaders share a vision, develop staff and invite them to own the change, which is what coaching a staff-led redesign team accomplishes. An autocratic leader would dictate the new process without input, a laissez-faire leader would announce the goal and then provide no direction or support, and a bureaucratic leader would simply apply existing rules and policies rather than redesign the process.

items.stem: Six clients from a highway collision arrive in the emergency department at the same time. The charge nurse immediately assigns each nurse a specific client and task and states that no one is to change assignments without telling the charge nurse. Which statement about this approach is accurate?
options: A directive, autocratic style is appropriate because rapid decisions are needed in a crisis
The charge nurse is misusing authority and should let each nurse choose a client
The charge nurse should have held a group meeting to reach consensus on assignments
A laissez-faire approach would allow staff to work faster during a surge
items.rationale: Autocratic or directive leadership is the style of choice when decisions must be made quickly and lives are at risk, such as a code or a mass-casualty surge; it prevents duplicated effort and clarifies accountability. Consensus building and self-selection take time and leave gaps in coverage, and laissez-faire leadership provides no coordination at all, which is unsafe when demand suddenly exceeds resources.

items.stem: A long-term care unit is short one nurse after a call-out. Which activities may the charge nurse delegate to experienced assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
options: Record oral intake and urine output on the flow sheet
Reposition residents every 2 hours according to the turning schedule
Provide oral care for a resident who receives enteral tube feedings
Teach a resident how to use a newly prescribed insulin pen
Assist stable residents to the dining room for the evening meal
Evaluate a resident who has become confused since the previous shift
Obtain routine vital signs on medically stable residents
items.rationale: Delegation rules allow standard, predictable tasks with a known outcome on stable clients: routine vital signs, ambulation and transport, intake and output recording, hygiene and scheduled repositioning all fit assistive personnel training. Teaching and evaluation of a change in condition require nursing judgment and can never be delegated, and new confusion must be assessed by the registered nurse because it may signal infection, hypoxia or a medication effect.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A cardiac step-down unit must float one nurse to an oncology unit that needs help with routine care and oral medications. The charge nurse should send {{1}} and, before the nurse leaves, should {{2}}.

options: a nurse who has completed cross-training on the oncology unit
the newly licensed nurse who is still working with a preceptor
the nurse who currently has the highest-acuity assignment
the nurse who has floated the fewest times this month
record the float hours as mandatory overtime for the pay period
confirm with the receiving charge nurse that the assignment matches the nurse's demonstrated competencies
instruct the nurse to accept whatever assignment the receiving unit gives
send the unit's telemetry monitors with the nurse in case they are needed

items.rationale: Floating is safe only when the assignment matches what the floated nurse is competent to do, so a cross-trained nurse is the correct choice and the sending and receiving charge nurses confirm the assignment together. An orientee still needs a preceptor, pulling the nurse with the sickest clients disrupts continuity, and rotating floats purely by turn ignores competence, which is the legal standard for assignment.

items.stem: A night-shift nurse believes a newly prescribed dose of IV opioid is unsafe for an older adult client with a low respiratory rate. The prescribing resident dismisses the concern and directs the nurse to give the dose as written. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Chart that the dose was withheld and take no further action until morning
Notify the charge nurse and nursing supervisor and follow the facility chain of command
Administer the dose as prescribed because the provider has the final authority
Ask a more experienced nurse to give the dose instead
items.rationale: A nurse who believes an order is unsafe is accountable for not carrying it out and for escalating through the chain of command, usually charge nurse, nursing supervisor, then the attending provider or medical director. Administering a dose the nurse believes is unsafe transfers no liability away from the nurse, handing it to a colleague simply moves the risk, and withholding a medication without notifying anyone leaves the client's pain untreated and the concern unresolved.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the preceptor's observation note that require immediate correction.

highlightSegments.text: 1000: Observed the newly licensed nurse during the morning medication pass on the medical-surgical unit.
The nurse performed hand hygiene before entering each client room.
The nurse scanned the client's identification band and the barcode on every medication.
For a client on a heparin infusion, the nurse changed the pump rate without an independent double check.
The nurse explained the purpose of each new medication to the client.
The nurse crushed an extended-release metoprolol tablet to give it through the enteral tube.
Each dose was documented immediately after it was given.
A prepared insulin syringe was left on the overbed table while the nurse answered a call light in the next room.
The nurse asked the preceptor to verify an unfamiliar insulin dose before drawing it up.

items.rationale: High-alert medications drive these cues: heparin infusions require an independent double check of the rate, insulin must never be left unattended where another person could give or divert it, and crushing an extended-release tablet delivers the entire dose at once and can cause profound bradycardia and hypotension. Hand hygiene, two-identifier barcode scanning, client teaching, prompt documentation and asking for verification are all correct practices a preceptor should reinforce, not correct.

items.stem: Two nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about how the shift assignments were divided while visitors are in the hallway. Which initial action should the charge nurse take?
options: Submit a written disciplinary report on both nurses to the nurse manager
Tell the nurses to stop and to discuss the problem after the shift ends
Send one of the nurses to work on another unit for the rest of the shift
Move both nurses to a private area and ask each one to describe the concern
items.rationale: Conflict is addressed privately and promptly: moving the nurses away from clients and visitors protects confidentiality and professionalism, and hearing each perspective is the first step toward a collaborative solution. Reassigning one nurse punishes rather than resolves, postponing the discussion lets resentment build and the assignment problem persists for the shift, and beginning with discipline skips the fact-finding a manager needs.

items.stem: A nurse believes the assignment received for the shift is unsafe because it includes more high-acuity clients than the nurse can manage. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Notify the house nursing supervisor that the concern remains unresolved
Bring the recurring pattern of unsafe assignments to the unit practice council
Complete the facility's written assignment-despite-objection documentation
Discuss the specific safety concern and the client acuities with the charge nurse who made the assignment
Ask the nurse manager to review the assignment after the charge nurse cannot change it
items.rationale: The chain of command starts with the person closest to the problem, the charge nurse who made the assignment, and moves up only while the concern is unresolved: manager, then house supervisor. Written objection documentation records that the nurse accepted the assignment under protest while still providing care, and a recurring pattern belongs at the practice council, where staffing standards change. Skipping levels or refusing outright leaves clients and the nurse exposed.

items.stem: The nurse manager of a medical unit reviews the quarterly staffing report. Which conclusion should the manager draw?
options: Rising vacancies and turnover are driving the agency and overtime costs, so retention must be addressed
Agency use is unrelated to the vacancy rate and should be evaluated on its own
The unit is overstaffed, so the number of approved positions should be reduced
The changes represent normal month-to-month variation and need no action
items.rationale: Agency and overtime hours are the symptom; vacancies that more than tripled and turnover that nearly tripled are the cause, so the budget cannot be fixed without fixing retention. Reducing approved positions would deepen the shortage and raise premium pay further. Agency hours track the vacancy line almost exactly, so they are not an independent problem, and a consistent one-direction change across four indicators is a trend, not random variation.

items.stem: During an evening shift a nurse notices that a colleague has slurred speech and an odor of alcohol, has wasted opioids three times without a witness, and has two clients reporting that their pain medication never arrived. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask another nurse to keep an eye on the colleague for the remainder of the shift
Record the observations and raise them at the next unit staff meeting
Speak privately with the colleague at the end of the shift and suggest getting help
Report the observations to the nursing supervisor immediately so the colleague can be removed from client care
items.rationale: Suspected impaired practice is an immediate client-safety emergency: the nurse reports objective observations to the supervisor so the colleague is removed from care and the facility's policy, which usually includes for-cause testing and referral to an alternative-to-discipline program, can be followed. Waiting until the shift ends, delegating observation to a peer or holding the concern for a meeting all leave clients in the care of an impaired nurse and leave unresolved opioid diversion.

items.stem: A hospital activates its emergency operations plan after a multivehicle crash, and the emergency department charge nurse must expand capacity quickly. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask additional staff to report through the facility call-back system
Wait for the incident commander to direct every task before making any change on the unit
Identify clients already in the department who can be safely discharged or moved to an inpatient bed
Use the hospital incident command structure for all communication and reporting
Stop triage and treat clients in the order in which they arrive
Assign arriving staff according to demonstrated competencies rather than the usual rotation
Send client information by personal cell phone text message to speed communication
items.rationale: Surge capacity is created by decompressing the department, matching staff to what they are competent to do, calling in additional personnel through the established system and communicating through incident command so that decisions and resources are tracked in one place. Waiting for direction on every action paralyzes the unit, personal text messaging breaches confidentiality and leaves no record, and abandoning triage means the most salvageable clients wait behind minor injuries.

items.stem: The charge nurse on a medical-surgical unit is making assignments for a team consisting of a registered nurse, a licensed practical nurse and assistive personnel. Select the team member to whom each activity should be assigned.
matrixRows: Develop the plan of care for a client newly admitted with heart failure
Administer a scheduled oral antihypertensive to a stable client
Measure and record intake and output for a client on a fluid restriction
Give the first dose of IV push furosemide
Reinforce previously taught crutch walking with a stable client
Assist a stable client with a bed bath and oral care
items.rationale: Assessment, care planning, client teaching and the first dose of an intravenous medication require the registered nurse's judgment and cannot be assigned away. The licensed practical nurse may give routine oral medications to stable clients and reinforce teaching already provided. Assistive personnel perform standard, predictable tasks such as intake and output and hygiene, while the registered nurse stays accountable for supervision and for evaluating the results.

items.stem: A nurse manager is preparing a request to replace three aging infusion pumps that are expected to last seven years. In which part of the unit budget should this request be placed?
options: Personnel budget
Capital budget
Revenue budget
Operating budget
items.rationale: Capital budgets cover equipment with a long useful life and a cost above the facility's capital threshold, which is exactly what durable infusion pumps are. The operating budget funds day-to-day consumables such as dressings and tubing, the personnel budget funds salaries, benefits and premium pay, and the revenue budget projects income rather than authorizing purchases.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Two home health nurses disagree about how visits are divided across the territory, and one has stopped speaking to the other. The manager who brings both nurses together to build a schedule that answers each nurse's concerns is using {{1}}, which is the best approach here because {{2}}.

options: competing
accommodating
collaborating
avoiding
both nurses have legitimate concerns and there is time to reach a solution both can accept
the disagreement will resolve on its own once the nurses cool down
the manager's authority should settle the disagreement quickly
one nurse should give in so that the working relationship is preserved

items.rationale: Collaborating is the only win-win strategy: both parties' concerns are treated as valid and the solution is built jointly, which is appropriate when the issue matters to both and time permits. Competing imposes the manager's answer and breeds resentment, accommodating simply silences one nurse, and avoiding leaves an active conflict that has already begun to damage communication between team members who must coordinate client care.

items.stem: A preceptor is working with a newly licensed nurse in the second week of orientation on a telemetry unit. Which action by the preceptor best supports the new nurse's development?
options: Complete the more difficult procedures for the new nurse to keep the shift on schedule
Point out the new nurse's mistakes at the bedside so the correction is immediate
Gradually increase the complexity of the client assignment while remaining available for questions
Give the new nurse a full independent assignment now so that confidence develops quickly
items.rationale: Orientation progresses by graded exposure: the preceptor adds complexity as competence is demonstrated and stays accessible so the orientee can ask questions without hesitating. A full independent load in week two exceeds the new nurse's skill and endangers clients, doing the hard tasks for the orientee prevents skill development, and correcting a nurse in front of a client undermines both the client's confidence and the orientee's willingness to ask for help.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the charge nurse log that require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 1900 charge nurse log, 28-bed medical unit staffed with four nurses and one assistive personnel.
Two nurses are carrying seven clients each after a call-out.
A nurse on day 3 of orientation has been given an independent group of six clients.
The unit's only assistive personnel was pulled to the emergency department at 1930.
A client receiving a heparin infusion has no nurse assigned for the required hourly safety checks.
Handoff report was completed with all oncoming staff by 1930.
One nurse has already worked 16 hours and has volunteered to stay for a third consecutive shift.
The crash cart was checked and the log signed at the start of the shift.
Two clients are waiting for intensive care beds to become available.

items.rationale: Three entries create immediate risk: an orientee is not licensed to practice independently and must keep a preceptor, a high-alert heparin infusion with no assigned nurse means required monitoring is not happening, and a third consecutive shift exceeds safe work-hour limits, since fatigue measurably increases error. Heavier ratios, a pulled aide, completed handoff and pending transfers are workload problems the charge nurse manages during the shift.

items.stem: A staff nurse finds current evidence that the unit's peripheral IV dressing-change policy is out of date and may be increasing phlebitis rates. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Ask each provider to write individual orders that override the unit policy
Begin using the new technique immediately and tell colleagues to do the same
Continue to follow the current policy and take no further action
Present the evidence to the unit practice council so the policy can be reviewed and revised
items.rationale: Practice change belongs in the formal review process: the practice or shared-governance council appraises the evidence, revises the policy, and the change is then educated and implemented consistently across the unit. Individual nurses who change practice on their own create variation, are practicing outside policy and cannot be defended if harm occurs. Doing nothing leaves a known risk in place, and provider orders written around a policy do not fix the policy for the next client.

items.stem: A nurse learns that a colleague charted a complete head-to-toe assessment on a client the colleague never entered. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Wait to see whether the behavior happens again before reporting it
Delete the colleague's entry from the electronic health record
Assess the client to determine the client's current status
Complete an occurrence report according to facility policy
Report the finding to the charge nurse or nurse manager
Discuss the colleague's behavior with other staff during the meal break
