Document the nurse's own assessment findings factually in the record
items.rationale: Falsified documentation is both a client-safety problem and a licensure issue, so the nurse determines the client's actual condition, charts factual findings, and reports the falsification through the manager and occurrence-report system, which is how patterns are investigated. A nurse may never delete another clinician's entry; the record is a legal document corrected only by an addendum. Waiting for a second event leaves clients at risk.

items.stem: During a regional disaster the nursing supervisor must staff a surge unit opened in a conference center adjacent to the hospital for clients with minor injuries and stable chronic conditions. Which staffing decision is most appropriate?
options: Pair experienced medical-surgical nurses with ambulatory clinic staff who can provide basic care under supervision
Assign operating room nurses to run the surge unit without additional support
Schedule each nurse for a single 20-hour shift to reduce the number of handoffs
Staff the unit entirely with agency nurses who have never worked in the facility
items.rationale: Surge staffing pairs clinicians whose competencies complement each other so that an experienced inpatient nurse supervises while less-experienced or non-inpatient staff extend capacity, a model that keeps accountability with a qualified registered nurse. Perioperative nurses lack recent general inpatient experience to work unsupported, an all-agency unit has no one who knows the facility's systems, and 20-hour shifts produce fatigue-related errors that outweigh any handoff risk they avoid.

items.stem: An assistive personnel tells the charge nurse that a client who is 2 days post lobectomy "does not look right." The charge nurse finds the client restless and answering in one-word phrases, with a respiratory rate of 30/min, SpO2 88% on 2 L nasal cannula, heart rate 122/min and blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieConditions: Oversedation from the scheduled oral analgesic
Expected fatigue on the second postoperative day
Situational anxiety about the surgical experience
Acute respiratory deterioration requiring rapid response activation
bowtieActions: Ask the assistive personnel to recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes
Document the findings and pass them along in the end-of-shift report
Activate the rapid response team and remain with the client
Notify the surgical provider using an SBAR report
Increase the oxygen flow and reassess the client in 1 hour
bowtieParams: Color of chest tube dressing drainage at the next change
Respiratory rate and work of breathing
Oxygen saturation and level of consciousness
items.rationale: Tachypnea, hypoxemia, tachycardia, falling blood pressure and a change in mental status after thoracic surgery are early-warning cues for acute deterioration, and the concern raised by assistive personnel is a valid cue to act on. The nurse activates the rapid response team, stays with the client and notifies the surgeon with a structured report; progress is judged by respiratory effort, oxygenation and level of consciousness. Delay lets a reversible problem progress to arrest.

items.stem: A charge nurse on a medical-surgical unit is assigning clients to a licensed practical nurse. Which client is most appropriate for this assignment?
options: A client who returned from a thoracentesis 1 hour ago and needs a respiratory assessment
A client who is beginning the first unit of packed red blood cells
A client who arrived 20 minutes ago with new-onset atrial fibrillation
A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who is stable and receiving scheduled nebulizer treatments
items.rationale: Licensed practical nurses care for clients whose condition is stable and whose outcomes are predictable, such as a client receiving routine scheduled respiratory treatments. A new dysrhythmia, the initial assessment after an invasive procedure and the start of a blood transfusion all require registered nurse assessment and judgment because the client's status is changing or a reaction could occur at any moment.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A medical unit begins the night shift two nurses short after unplanned absences. The charge nurse should first {{1}}, and should assign the client who is {{2}} to the most experienced nurse.

options: ask each nurse to choose the clients they would prefer to care for
send the assistive personnel home to reduce the shift's labor cost
review each client's acuity and redistribute the assignments accordingly
take a full client assignment and stop supervising the unit
waiting for a morning discharge with all teaching completed
receiving a continuous insulin infusion for diabetic ketoacidosis
taking oral antibiotics for a resolving cellulitis
ambulating independently on the first day after a hernia repair

items.rationale: Short staffing is managed by acuity, not by an even count of clients: the charge nurse reviews what each client requires and redistributes so the sickest client goes to the most experienced nurse. A titrated insulin infusion demands frequent glucose monitoring and dose judgment. A charge nurse with a full assignment cannot supervise, self-selection creates gaps, and cutting assistive personnel removes the help the team most needs.

items.stem: A nurse manager learns that the unit's supply expenses are 18% over budget for the quarter. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Review a report of supply use by item with the staff and involve them in identifying waste
Transfer the overage to the unit's education fund for the remainder of the year
Lock the supply rooms and require the charge nurse to issue every item
Ask staff to borrow supplies from other units until the next budget cycle
items.rationale: Cost control begins with data and staff engagement, because the nurses at the bedside know which items are opened unnecessarily, stocked in the wrong quantity or charged to the wrong client. Locking supplies delays care and creates workarounds, moving the overage to the education fund hides the problem while cutting staff development, and borrowing from other units simply shifts the expense to another cost center without reducing use.

items.stem: A nurse manager holds a six-week check-in with a newly hired nurse. Click to highlight the statements that indicate unsafe practice requiring the manager's follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: "I have been on the unit for six weeks and I finally feel like I know the routine."
"When an infusion pump alarms and I cannot fix it right away, I silence it and come back later."
"If a prescription is unclear, I call the provider to clarify before I give anything."
"I scan every medication, because the scanner has caught two of my mistakes."
"When the shift gets busy I chart all of my assessments at the end from memory."
"I check with the charge nurse before I accept a client on a drip I have not managed before."
"If I cannot reach the provider, I ask the family what dose the client took at home and give that."
"I stay a few minutes past the shift to finish documentation rather than rush it."
"I asked to be scheduled with my preceptor for my first night shifts."

items.rationale: Silencing an alarm and returning later means a stopped or malfunctioning infusion goes unnoticed, charting assessments from memory hours later produces inaccurate legal records and missed changes in condition, and taking a dose from a family report instead of a prescription is administering a medication without an order. Clarifying unclear prescriptions, scanning, asking before accepting an unfamiliar drip and seeking preceptor support are the behaviors a manager wants to reinforce.

items.stem: A nurse manager reviews unit quality data collected since two positions became vacant. Which conclusion should the manager draw?
options: The data show that the unit has become more efficient with fewer staff
Client satisfaction is declining because of the unit's aging physical environment
Care is being missed as workload rises, and the staffing plan needs to be re-evaluated
The fall rate is within expected limits and the other measures are unrelated to it
items.rationale: Four indicators are moving together in the same direction, which is the signature of missed nursing care: longer call light responses mean clients get up alone and fall, doses are missed because there is no time, and clients notice all of it. Attributing the pattern to the building ignores the timing with the vacancies, calling a rate that has more than doubled acceptable ignores the trend, and worse outcomes are not efficiency.

items.stem: The charge nurse is planning the shift on a surgical unit. Select whether each activity may be assigned to the licensed practical nurse or must be performed by the registered nurse.
matrixRows: Perform the admission assessment on a client transferring from the emergency department
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for a stable postoperative client
Administer an intramuscular antibiotic to a stable client
Create the discharge teaching plan for a client newly prescribed warfarin
Change a sterile dressing on a stable surgical wound
Evaluate whether the plan of care has met the client's mobility goal
matrixColumns: May be assigned to the licensed practical nurse
Must be performed by the registered nurse
items.rationale: The nursing process steps that require judgment, initial assessment, planning teaching and evaluating goal attainment, belong to the registered nurse and cannot be assigned away. Licensed practical nurses perform established procedures on stable clients, including catheter insertion, intramuscular injections and sterile dressing changes, and report data the registered nurse interprets, which is why supervision stays a registered nurse responsibility.

items.stem: A case manager is arranging an interdisciplinary care conference for a client whose rehabilitation goals have stalled. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Facilitate the conference so each discipline reports and the client states personal goals
Reach agreement on measurable goals and assign responsibility for each intervention
Document the revised plan and communicate it to staff at the next handoff
Schedule the conference and invite the client, the family and each discipline involved
Review the client's record and identify the unresolved problems to be addressed
items.rationale: A care conference is only as good as its preparation: the nurse reviews the record first so the discussion targets the actual barriers, then brings together the client, family and the disciplines able to act on them. Reports and the client's own goals precede decisions, because a plan settled before the client speaks is not client centered. Naming who is responsible turns discussion into action, and the revised plan changes care only once it reaches the record and the next shift.

items.stem: At the end of a 12-week orientation, a preceptor documents that a newly licensed nurse still cannot independently manage a client receiving a titrated vasoactive infusion. Which action by the nurse manager is most appropriate?
options: Release the nurse to independent practice and schedule the education at a later date
Extend the orientation with a written plan of measurable goals focused on that skill
Transfer the nurse to a different unit at the end of the week
End the nurse's employment because competency was not achieved on schedule
items.rationale: Orientation is competency based, not calendar based: when a specific skill is not yet demonstrated, the manager extends the orientation with explicit, measurable goals, a timeline and continued preceptor support. Releasing a nurse who cannot titrate a vasoactive drip endangers clients and the nurse's license, transferring the problem hides it from the next manager, and ending employment without a remediation attempt is premature when one focused skill is the gap.

items.stem: A charge nurse is delegating tasks to assistive personnel during a busy shift. Which actions demonstrate the rights of delegation? Select all that apply.
options: Give clear limits, such as the blood pressure value that must be reported immediately
Tell the assistive personnel to use judgment about which clients need vital signs
State the expected outcome and when the results should be reported back
Give the task to whoever is least busy at the moment, regardless of training
Ask the assistive personnel to determine whether the client's pain has improved
Remain available to answer questions while the task is carried out
Verify that the assistive personnel has performed the task competently before
items.rationale: Safe delegation requires the right task, the right circumstances, the right person, the right direction and communication, and the right supervision: the nurse confirms competence, gives specific directions with parameters to report, and stays available to supervise. Choosing a person by availability rather than training ignores the right person, and asking assistive personnel to evaluate pain or decide who needs monitoring delegates nursing judgment, which is never permitted.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse floated from the postpartum unit to a medical unit is assigned a client receiving a titrated heparin infusion, which the nurse has never managed. The nurse should {{1}}, and the receiving charge nurse should {{2}}.

options: tell the charge nurse the limits of the nurse's competency and decline that client
ask the client's family to watch the pump between hourly checks
accept the client and read the protocol during the shift
follow the written protocol and titrate the infusion carefully
reassign the infusion to a competent nurse and give the floated nurse an assignment within scope
report the nurse to the board of nursing for abandoning the client
send the floated nurse back to the postpartum unit for the shift
document that the floated nurse refused an assignment

items.rationale: A nurse who accepts an assignment is accountable for performing it safely, so a nurse without competency in a high-alert titrated infusion must say so rather than learn on the client. The receiving charge nurse reassigns the infusion and gives the floated nurse work within scope. Declining one unsafe assignment while continuing to care for other clients is not abandonment, which requires accepting a client and then leaving without handoff.

items.stem: A client comes to the emergency department reporting a cough for 3 weeks, night sweats, a 5 kg (11 lb) weight loss and blood-streaked sputum. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Keep the client in the waiting area until the sputum results return
Move the client into a negative-pressure room and wear a fit-tested N95 respirator
Place the client in a private room and wear a surgical mask for care
Place the client on contact precautions with a gown and gloves
items.rationale: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with night sweats, weight loss and hemoptysis is a classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis, which spreads by droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air. Airborne precautions begin on suspicion, not confirmation: a negative-pressure room with the door closed and a fit-tested N95 for anyone entering. A surgical mask does not filter droplet nuclei, and the waiting area exposes everyone in it.

items.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who has Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Which action by the nurse demonstrates correct infection control practice?
options: Wearing a fit-tested N95 respirator when entering the room
Using an alcohol-based hand rub after each contact with the client
Washing the hands with soap and water after removing gloves
Requesting a negative-pressure room for the client
items.rationale: Clostridioides difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill, so hand hygiene must be mechanical: soap, water and friction physically remove spores from the hands. The organism spreads by the contact route through hands, equipment and environmental surfaces, so a gown and gloves, dedicated equipment and a sporicidal cleaner such as a bleach solution are used, while respirators and negative-pressure rooms address airborne organisms and are unnecessary here.

items.stem: The charge nurse of a long-term acute care hospital reviews the clients being admitted today. Select the type of precautions required for each client.
matrixRows: A school-age child with confirmed pertussis
An adult with sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis
A resident transferred with untreated scabies
A client with a wound infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
A client with suspected meningococcal meningitis
A client with a well-controlled seizure disorder admitted for observation
A client with a rash and fever diagnosed as measles
items.rationale: Precaution type follows how the organism travels. Large droplets fall within about 2 m (6 feet), so pertussis and meningococcal disease need droplet precautions with a surgical mask. Tuberculosis and measles travel in droplet nuclei that stay airborne, requiring a negative-pressure room and an N95. Scabies and resistant organisms move on hands and surfaces, so gown and gloves apply. A client with no transmissible infection needs standard precautions only.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Put on gloves and pull the cuffs over the gown sleeves
Put on the gown and fasten it at the neck and waist
Perform hand hygiene
Put on the goggles or face shield
Put on the surgical mask and secure it over the nose and mouth
items.rationale: Personal protective equipment is applied from the inside out and from the trunk upward: hand hygiene first, then the gown, then the mask, then eye protection, and gloves last so that the glove cuffs seal over the gown sleeves and nothing already worn is contaminated by gloved hands. Putting gloves on early contaminates the clean equipment still to be applied, and touching the face with gloved hands to adjust a mask defeats the purpose of the barrier.

items.stem: A nurse is orienting a new employee to standard precautions used with every client. Which actions are part of standard precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator for all client care
Offer tissues and hand hygiene to any client who is coughing
Wear gloves when contact with blood or body fluids is anticipated
Place every client in a private room on admission
Dispose of used needles in a puncture-resistant container without recapping them
Use a face shield when a procedure is likely to generate splashes
Perform hand hygiene before and after every client contact
items.rationale: Standard precautions assume that the blood and body fluids of every client may be infectious, so they combine hand hygiene, barriers chosen by the anticipated exposure, safe injection and sharps practices, and respiratory hygiene or cough etiquette. They are used regardless of diagnosis. Private rooms and respirators are transmission-based additions reserved for specific organisms; applying them to everyone wastes resources and isolates clients unnecessarily.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client is 10 days after an allogeneic stem-cell transplant and has an absolute neutrophil count of 180/mm3. The nurse should place the client in {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: a negative-pressure room with the door left open for observation
an airborne infection isolation room vented to the outside
a positive-pressure room with high-efficiency particulate air filtration
a semiprivate room shared with a stable postoperative client
keep a cool-mist humidifier running at the bedside
encourage the client to walk in the unit hallway without a mask
allow a visitor with a mild cough to stay for a short visit
remove fresh flowers and potted plants from the room

items.rationale: A protective environment shields a profoundly neutropenic client from organisms in the environment: air is filtered and the room is kept at positive pressure so that air flows outward when the door opens. Standing water and soil harbor Aspergillus and Pseudomonas, so flowers, plants and humidifiers are removed. Negative pressure protects others from the client and is the opposite of what is needed, and visitors with any respiratory symptoms must be excluded.

items.stem: Click to highlight the actions in the observation note that break surgical asepsis.

highlightSegments.text: 1400: Observed a nurse performing a sterile dressing change on a central venous catheter.
The nurse performed hand hygiene and applied a mask before opening the kit.
The sterile drape was opened by touching only its outer 2.5 cm (1 inch) border.
The nurse reached across the sterile field to pick up the chlorhexidine applicator.
Sterile gloves were applied using the open-gloving technique.
The nurse turned away from the field to answer a visitor's question, then turned back and continued.
Sterile saline was poured into a basin without splashing, with the bottle held outside the edge of the field.
A gauze package that slipped below waist level was picked up and placed onto the field.
The new dressing was labeled with the date, the time and the nurse's initials.

items.rationale: A sterile field is sterile only where it can be seen and only above waist level: reaching across it lets skin scale and clothing fall onto the field, turning away means the field was unobserved and must be considered contaminated, and anything that drops below the waist is contaminated even if the wrapper looks intact. Masking, touching only the 2.5 cm border, open gloving, pouring from outside the field edge and labeling the dressing are all correct technique.

items.stem: An infection prevention nurse reviews data from an intensive care unit after a central line maintenance bundle was introduced. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The infection rate fell because far fewer central lines were used during the period
Rising bundle and bathing compliance is associated with the falling infection rate, so the practice should be sustained
The bundle has produced no measurable benefit and should be discontinued
The increase in line days is what caused the change in the infection rate
items.rationale: The infection rate is already adjusted for exposure because it is expressed per 1,000 line days, and line days actually rose slightly, so the drop cannot be explained by fewer lines. Compliance with the bundle and with chlorhexidine bathing climbed in step with the falling rate, which is exactly the dose-response pattern expected when a prevention bundle works; sustaining audit and feedback is what keeps compliance from drifting back.

items.stem: A nurse is reviewing practices to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infections on a rehabilitation unit. Which action is most effective?
options: Rest the drainage bag on the bed next to the client during transfers
Replace each indwelling catheter routinely every 7 days
Irrigate each indwelling catheter with sterile saline once every shift
Review the continued need for each indwelling catheter daily and advocate for removal as soon as it is not needed
items.rationale: Risk of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection rises with every day the catheter stays in place, so the single most effective intervention is prompt removal, which is why daily necessity review is the core of the prevention bundle. Routine irrigation and scheduled replacement both break the closed system and introduce organisms, and placing the bag on the bed lets contaminated urine flow back toward the bladder; the bag stays below bladder level and off the floor.

items.stem: A home health nurse is scheduled to change the dressing on a wound colonized with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator and keep the client in a separate room during the visit
Take only the equipment needed into the home, wear a gown and gloves for wound care, and disinfect reusable items before leaving
Schedule this client as the first visit of the day so that equipment does not need to be cleaned
Place soiled dressings in the nursing bag and dispose of them at the agency office
items.rationale: Resistant organisms spread by contact, so in the home the nurse limits what enters, uses a gown and gloves for wound care, bags soiled dressings in the home according to agency policy, and cleans or disinfects any reusable equipment before it leaves. A respirator is unnecessary for a contact-spread organism, equipment must be disinfected regardless of visit order, and carrying contaminated dressings in the nursing bag contaminates the bag and the nurse's vehicle.

items.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for removing personal protective equipment in the correct order.
options: Perform hand hygiene
Remove the gloves using a glove-to-glove then skin-to-skin technique
Remove the goggles by handling the headband at the back of the head
Leave the room and remove the mask by its ties without touching the front
Untie the gown, pull it away from the neck and shoulders and roll it inward as it is removed
items.rationale: Removal moves from the most contaminated item to the least: gloves first, then eye protection handled from the back where it is clean, then the gown rolled inward to trap contamination. The mask is removed after leaving the room because the front of the mask and the air inside the room are contaminated, and hand hygiene is always the final step. Removing the mask at the bedside or touching its front transfers organisms directly to the face and hands.

items.stem: A nurse is preparing to care for a client in an airborne infection isolation room. Which action indicates correct use of an N95 respirator?
options: Loosening the straps during long periods of client care for comfort
Selecting any available size because all N95 respirators fit alike
Performing a user seal check each time the respirator is put on
Wearing the respirator over a surgical mask for additional protection
items.rationale: An N95 works only when air passes through the filter rather than around the edges, so every application is followed by a user seal check: exhale and inhale to confirm no leakage at the face. Fit testing determines the specific make and size for each wearer, so sizes are not interchangeable. Layering a surgical mask underneath and loosening the straps both break the facial seal and reduce protection to less than that of a simple mask.

items.stem: A resident of a long-term care facility is diagnosed with influenza A. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator for all routine care
Request transfer to a negative-pressure room
Perform hand hygiene before and after every contact with the resident
Wear a surgical mask when working within 2 m (6 feet) of the resident
Place the resident in a private room or cohort with another resident who has influenza
Place a surgical mask on the resident during transport out of the room
Keep the room door closed at all times to prevent airborne spread
items.rationale: Influenza spreads in large respiratory droplets that fall within about 2 m (6 feet), so droplet precautions apply: a private room or cohorting with the same organism, a surgical mask for staff within that range, a mask on the resident whenever leaving the room, and hand hygiene, which remains the single most effective measure. Negative pressure, a closed door and an N95 are airborne measures needed for organisms such as tuberculosis, measles and varicella, not for influenza.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the triage note that indicate the client should be placed in airborne isolation immediately.

highlightSegments.text: 1015 triage: A 19-year-old client presents with a 4-day illness.
Temperature 38.9 C (102.0 F), heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
The client reports cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes for the past 3 days.
A blotchy red rash began on the face yesterday and has spread down onto the trunk.
The client states, "I was never given the measles vaccine as a child."
The client returned 10 days ago from a 2-week trip abroad.
No known drug allergies and no routine medications.
Lungs clear to auscultation, no neck stiffness and no photophobia.
The client asks how long the wait to be seen will be.

items.rationale: Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward, in an unvaccinated client with recent international travel, is the classic measles picture, and measles spreads by airborne droplet nuclei. Isolation is based on presentation, not laboratory confirmation, so the client is moved at once into a negative-pressure room and staff wear an N95. Normal vital signs and examination findings do not change that.

items.stem: A client is admitted with disseminated herpes zoster involving several dermatomes and scattered vesicles across the trunk. Which action by the charge nurse is correct?
options: Use droplet precautions with a surgical mask for everyone entering the room
Assign the nurse who is pregnant and has no history of chickenpox, because the risk is minimal
Place the client in a private room with contact precautions only
Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room with contact precautions and assign a nurse with documented varicella immunity
items.rationale: Localized zoster in an immunocompetent client needs only covered lesions and standard precautions, but disseminated zoster behaves like varicella: the virus is shed from vesicles and from the airway, so airborne and contact precautions are both required until all lesions crust. Staff without documented immunity, and especially a pregnant nurse who has never had chickenpox, must not be assigned, because varicella in pregnancy can cause severe maternal disease and fetal harm.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client is admitted from the emergency department with suspected meningococcal meningitis. The nurse should initiate {{1}}, which may be discontinued after the client has completed {{2}}.

options: standard precautions alone until the culture result returns
droplet precautions, with a surgical mask for anyone within 2 m (6 feet) of the client
airborne precautions, with a negative-pressure room and an N95 respirator
contact precautions, with a gown and gloves for all care
24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
a repeat lumbar puncture with a negative result
the first dose of the prescribed antibiotic
48 hours without a fever

items.rationale: Neisseria meningitidis is carried in large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions begin as soon as the diagnosis is suspected rather than confirmed, because the first hours carry the highest risk to staff and close contacts. Precautions continue through 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy, when nasopharyngeal carriage is reliably cleared; a single dose is not enough, and fever curves and repeat lumbar punctures do not determine infectivity.

items.stem: Select the minimum personal protective equipment the nurse should wear for each activity.
matrixRows: Performing a venipuncture on a client on standard precautions
Providing perineal care for a client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea
Suctioning the tracheostomy of a client with copious secretions
Irrigating a large abdominal wound that is likely to splash
Changing the bed linens of a client on contact precautions for a resistant organism
Giving an intramuscular injection to a client on standard precautions
matrixColumns: Gown, gloves, mask and eye protection
items.rationale: Protective equipment is chosen by the exposure the task creates, not by the client's label. Brief contact with intact skin or a small amount of blood needs gloves alone; care that soils clothing, or any care for a client on contact precautions, adds a gown; and any task that can spray or splash the face, such as suctioning or wound irrigation, adds a mask and eye protection. Choosing less than the task requires exposes the nurse, while gowning for every activity wastes supplies and time.

items.stem: In which situation must the nurse wash with soap and water rather than use an alcohol-based hand rub?
options: The nurse has just touched the bedside table of a client on standard precautions
The nurse has just removed gloves after taking a blood pressure
The nurse's hands are visibly soiled after a wound dressing change
The nurse is about to enter the room of a client on droplet precautions
items.rationale: Alcohol-based rub is preferred for most moments of care because it is faster and less drying, but it does not remove soil, and organic material blocks its contact with organisms. Whenever hands are visibly soiled or contaminated with body fluids, and after caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile, the mechanical action of soap, water and friction is required. The other situations are routine moments where alcohol rub is fully effective.

items.stem: An infection preventionist reviews monthly data from a medical unit. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Falling hand hygiene and equipment cleaning compliance is associated with rising MRSA transmission on the unit
The increase reflects improved laboratory detection rather than true transmission
Auditing should be stopped because the compliance numbers are not improving
The rise in MRSA cases is unrelated to the compliance measures being audited
items.rationale: Resistant organisms move on hands and on shared equipment, so compliance that falls by about a third while hospital-onset cases rise ninefold over the same period is a coherent, actionable pattern rather than a coincidence. Stopping the audit removes the only feedback that drives improvement. A detection artifact would raise both community-onset and hospital-onset counts and would not track the compliance line so closely.

items.stem: A nurse is setting up a sterile field to insert an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action maintains the sterility of the field?
options: Opening the flap of the sterile package that is nearest to the body first
Keeping the field in view and above waist level throughout the procedure
Treating the entire drape as sterile, including the 2.5 cm (1 inch) outer border
Placing the field on an overbed table that is still damp from cleaning
items.rationale: A sterile field is sterile only while it is above waist level and continuously in view, because contamination that is not seen cannot be corrected. The first flap opened is the one farthest away, so the nurse never reaches across sterile contents. The outer border of the drape is considered contaminated and is where the nurse may touch, and moisture wicks organisms upward from the surface below, so any wet field is contaminated.

items.stem: A nurse assists a provider with the bedside insertion of a central venous catheter. Which actions are part of the insertion bundle? Select all that apply.
options: Plan to leave the gauze dressing in place for 7 days after insertion
Recommend the femoral site in an adult because it is the easiest to access
Ensure the provider wears a cap, mask, sterile gown and sterile gloves
Cover the client with a full-body sterile drape
Stop the procedure and restart if sterile technique is broken
Perform hand hygiene immediately before the procedure begins
Prepare the skin with a chlorhexidine-alcohol solution and let it dry completely
items.rationale: The insertion bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis allowed to dry, optimal site selection and daily review of line necessity, and any observer, including the nurse, is empowered to stop the procedure when technique is broken. The femoral site carries the highest infection and thrombosis risk in adults and is avoided when possible. Gauze dressings are changed every 2 days; only transparent semipermeable dressings may stay for 7 days.

items.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to a pediatric clinic with 2 weeks of paroxysmal coughing followed by an inspiratory whoop and post-cough vomiting. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Keep the infant in the waiting area and wear gloves for all contact
Move the infant and parent into a private examination room and wear a surgical mask for care
Apply contact precautions with a gown and gloves for the examination
Move the infant into a negative-pressure room and wear a fit-tested N95 respirator
items.rationale: Paroxysmal cough with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting in an incompletely immunized infant suggests pertussis, which spreads by large respiratory droplets, so the infant is removed from the shared waiting area into a private room and staff wear a surgical mask within close range. Negative pressure and an N95 are reserved for airborne organisms, gloves alone do not stop droplets, and leaving a coughing infant in the waiting room exposes other unimmunized children.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the rounding note that indicate a breach of infection control practice.

highlightSegments.text: 1330 rounding note, long-term care unit during an outbreak investigation.
A resident on contact precautions for a resistant organism is sharing a room with a resident who has a new surgical wound.
Gowns and gloves are stocked on a cart outside the room door.
A blood pressure cuff used in the precaution room was taken next door and used without being cleaned.
Hand sanitizer dispensers at both room entrances are full and working.
An assistive personnel left the room in the gloves used for perineal care and answered a call light next door.
The resident's dressing is dry, intact and dated today.
Soiled linen was bagged inside the room before being carried to the soiled utility room.
The resident ate lunch in the dining room with the other residents.

items.rationale: Contact spread happens through shared space, shared equipment and hands. Rooming a colonized resident with a resident who has an open surgical wound puts the most susceptible person closest to the source, an uncleaned cuff carries the organism directly, and gloves worn out of the room contaminate whatever is touched next. Group dining during an outbreak investigation defeats the cohorting plan. Stocked equipment, working dispensers and bagging linen in the room are correct.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the trended data for a client recovering from an abdominal hysterectomy. Which findings indicate a developing surgical site infection? Select all that apply.
options: The temperature has stayed below 37.0 C (98.6 F) throughout
The white blood cell count has doubled since day 3
The incision edges have separated and the surrounding skin is erythematous
Drainage has changed from serous to purulent and now has an odor
Incision pain has decreased steadily since day 3
The amount of drainage has decreased since day 3
items.rationale: A surgical site infection usually declares itself between postoperative days 3 and 7 with the combination seen here: rising fever and leukocytosis, drainage that turns purulent and malodorous, wound edges that separate, and pain that increases instead of resolving. The last three options misstate the data, since the temperature rose, the pain rose and the drainage increased; reading the row before judging it is what separates a correct analysis from a guess.

items.stem: A nurse sustains a puncture from a hollow-bore needle just used to draw blood from a client known to have hepatitis C. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the injury to the charge nurse and employee health
Ask the client to consent to additional blood testing
Squeeze the site to express blood and apply an antiseptic
Wash the puncture site with soap and running water
items.rationale: Immediate decontamination of the exposure site is the first step after any percutaneous exposure, so the nurse washes the wound with soap and running water; mucous membrane splashes are flushed with water or saline. Reporting to employee health follows at once so that source testing, baseline serology and any indicated prophylaxis are arranged within the time window. Squeezing the site damages tissue and does not reduce transmission, and the nurse does not obtain the source client's consent.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse inserts an indwelling urinary catheter for a client in the intensive care unit. The nurse should {{1}} during the insertion and, once urine is draining, should {{2}}.

options: disconnect the tubing briefly to confirm that urine flows freely
use clean gloves, because the urinary meatus is not sterile
maintain sterile technique and keep the drainage system closed
irrigate the catheter with sterile saline to verify placement
secure the catheter to the thigh and keep the bag below the level of the bladder
tape the tubing to the side rail so the bag hangs above the mattress
rest the drainage bag on the floor at the side of the bed
coil the tubing on the bed so that urine collects close to the client

items.rationale: Most catheter-associated urinary tract infections come from organisms that ascend the catheter, so the two protections are a sterile insertion and an uninterrupted closed system. Securing the catheter prevents urethral traction that creates a portal of entry, and keeping the bag below the bladder and off the floor allows gravity drainage while preventing reflux of contaminated urine. Disconnecting the tubing, irrigating routinely and looping tubing so urine pools all reintroduce organisms.

items.stem: A client on contact precautions for a resistant wound organism must go to the radiology department for an urgent study. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Remove the gown and gloves worn in the room and perform hand hygiene before pushing the wheelchair
Instruct transport personnel to wear gloves and a gown only if direct client contact is expected
Cover the draining wound with a clean, dry dressing before transport
Cancel the study, because clients on contact precautions may not leave their room
Arrange for the wheelchair and imaging equipment to be cleaned after the study
Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the client for the trip
Notify the radiology department of the precautions before the client leaves the unit
items.rationale: Contact precautions do not confine a client to the room when a study is needed; they shape how the trip is made. The receiving department is told in advance, the source is contained by covering the wound, the nurse changes out of room protective equipment so the corridor and wheelchair stay clean, transport staff wear equipment matched to their contact, and equipment is cleaned afterward. A respirator addresses airborne organisms and has no role here.

items.stem: Two clients are being admitted with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in a surgical wound and no other infection. Only semiprivate rooms are available. Which action by the charge nurse is most appropriate?
options: Place one of them with a client who has Clostridioides difficile, since both need contact precautions
Place the two clients together, because cohorting clients with the same organism is acceptable
Hold both admissions in the emergency department until private rooms open
Place each of them with an uninfected client and keep the privacy curtain drawn
items.rationale: When private rooms are unavailable, clients infected with the identical organism may share a room, because neither client can acquire something the other does not already have. Pairing different organisms cross-infects both clients, and a privacy curtain is not a barrier to organisms carried on hands and equipment, so rooming a resistant organism with an uninfected client is unsafe. Holding admissions is unnecessary when safe cohorting is possible.

items.stem: A client in the intensive care unit has had a nontunneled central venous catheter for 8 days. During an infusion the client develops rigors, temperature 39.1 C (102.4 F), heart rate 126/min and blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg; the catheter exit site is erythematous with purulent drainage and no other source of infection is found. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Hold all antibiotics until the culture results have returned
Apply a warm compress to the exit site and reassess in 4 hours
Notify the provider and prepare for removal of the central catheter
Flush the catheter with heparin and continue to use it for the infusion
Obtain paired blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral site before antibiotics are started
bowtieParams: Temperature and white blood cell count
items.rationale: Rigors beginning with an infusion, fever and hypotension in a client with a purulent catheter exit site and no other source point to a central line-associated bloodstream infection. Paired cultures from the line and a peripheral vein, drawn before the first antibiotic dose, confirm the line as the source, and the infected catheter is removed because it cannot be sterilized in place. Recovery is tracked by fever, white blood cell count and hemodynamics including lactate.

items.stem: A client with active pulmonary tuberculosis must be taken to the radiology department for an urgent study. The transporter asks the nurse what protection is needed. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Leave the client unmasked and have the transporter wear a gown and gloves
Place a surgical mask on the client, notify radiology in advance, and transport without a respirator for the transporter
Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the client and have the transporter wear a surgical mask
Tell the transporter that the study must be postponed until the client is no longer infectious
items.rationale: Airborne transmission is controlled at the source during transport: a surgical mask on the client traps droplet nuclei as they are exhaled, which is why staff outside the isolation room do not need an N95 in open corridors. An N95 protects a wearer breathing contaminated air; it does not filter what the client exhales. Gowns and gloves address contact spread, and an urgent study is not delayed when transport can be done safely.

items.stem: A nurse on a medical-surgical unit receives report on four clients at 0700. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a new colostomy who has refused to look at the stoma since surgery
A client with chronic heart failure whose morning weight is 0.5 kg (1.1 lb) above yesterday
A client with pneumonia whose temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F) and whose acetaminophen is due now
A client 1 day after thyroidectomy who reports tingling around the mouth and cramping of both hands
items.rationale: Perioral tingling and carpal spasm after thyroidectomy signal hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury, which can progress to laryngospasm, so this potential airway emergency is seen first. The fever already has an antipyretic ordered, refusal to view a stoma is an expected early grief response, and a 0.5 kg gain is a small change in a chronic condition. Rank by how fast harm occurs if the nurse delays.

items.stem: Four clients present to the emergency department at the same time. Which client should the triage nurse move to a treatment room first?
options: A 54-year-old with crushing substernal chest pain, diaphoresis, and a blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg
A 7-year-old with an obvious forearm deformity after a bicycle fall and a strong radial pulse
A 30-year-old with a productive cough for 5 days and a temperature of 38.1 C (100.6 F)
A 68-year-old with 2 days of burning on urination and suprapubic tenderness
items.rationale: Crushing chest pain with diaphoresis and a falling blood pressure points to acute coronary syndrome with compromised perfusion, and every minute of delay costs myocardium, so this client is emergent. The deformity has an intact distal pulse, and the cough and dysuria are stable complaints. Emergency triage ranks clients by risk of deterioration, not by arrival time or by how much distress they voice.

items.stem: A nurse assumes care of six clients on a step-down unit. Which items from the outgoing nurse's report require the nurse to go to the client immediately? Select all that apply.
options: A client with type 2 diabetes had a 0600 blood glucose of 148 mg/dL
A client 10 minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells began reporting low back pain
A client who is ready for discharge is waiting for a family member to arrive with transportation
A client 6 hours after cardiac catheterization reports new numbness and coolness in the cannulated leg
A client with an indwelling urinary catheter has averaged 45 mL/hr of urine over the last 4 hours
The chest drainage system of a client with a hemothorax was found lying on its side with the water seal chamber empty
items.rationale: A toppled chest drainage unit with an empty water seal breaks the one-way seal and can collapse the lung, new distal numbness and coolness after catheterization suggests arterial occlusion of the limb, and back pain early in a transfusion is a classic sign of an acute hemolytic reaction. The other three are expected findings: 45 mL/hr is adequate output, 148 mg/dL needs no rescue, and a waiting ride is a logistics issue, not a clinical one.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Eight hours after a bowel resection, a client has a respiratory rate of 30/min, a heart rate of 122/min, a temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F), and new confusion. The nurse should first {{1}}. Because these findings indicate {{2}}, the nurse should {{3}} rather than wait for the scheduled provider round.

options: leave the room to page the surgeon from the nurses' station
stay with the client, apply oxygen, and send a colleague for help
recheck the vital signs in 1 hour and document the change
finish the medication pass and return to the client afterwards
opioid-induced oversedation
an expected postoperative stress response
early sepsis with clinical deterioration
uncomplicated postoperative atelectasis
request a routine chest x-ray for the morning
increase the intravenous rate and reassess at the end of the shift
activate the rapid response team
ask the charge nurse to add the client to the next rounding list

items.rationale: Tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and new confusion after abdominal surgery meet deterioration criteria for sepsis, and confusion is often the earliest sign in this setting. The nurse never leaves an unstable client to make a call; oxygen is applied and help is summoned to the bedside. Rapid response teams exist precisely so a nurse can obtain expert help before arrest, so waiting for rounds, a morning x-ray, or an unordered rate change delays definitive care.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the transfer report that the receiving nurse should follow up on immediately.

highlightSegments.text: 1430 transfer report from the intensive care unit: 72-year-old client, hospital day 4 for aspiration pneumonia.
Weaned from high-flow oxygen this morning and is now on 2 L/min by nasal cannula with a saturation of 94%.
No urine output has been recorded since 0900.
Afebrile for the past 24 hours.
Right internal jugular central line is in place; the dressing is dated 5 days ago and the edges are loose and soiled.
Tolerating a dysphagia diet with thickened liquids.
Ambulated to the chair with one assist this morning.
The client pulled out the nasogastric tube overnight, and replacement has not been discussed with the provider.
Family is at the bedside asking about discharge planning.
Transfer vital signs: temperature 36.9 C (98.4 F), heart rate 88/min, blood pressure 124/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min.

items.rationale: More than 5 hours without documented urine output may signal obstruction, retention, or falling perfusion and must be investigated now. A central line dressing that is 5 days old, loose, and soiled breaches the bundle that prevents bloodstream infection and needs changing immediately. A dislodged feeding tube leaves nutrition and enteral medications unaddressed until the provider is contacted. Stable vitals, successful weaning, tolerating the diet, ambulation, and family questions are all expected.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the shift data for a client admitted with a urinary tract infection. Which action should the nurse take first based on the trend?
options: Encourage oral fluids and reposition the client to promote rest
Document the findings and report the changes at the 1900 handoff
Activate the rapid response team and anticipate fluid resuscitation and blood cultures
Administer the scheduled acetaminophen and reassess the temperature in 1 hour
items.rationale: Across three sets of vital signs the temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate climb while the blood pressure and level of consciousness fall, a pattern of progressive sepsis rather than an isolated fever. This meets escalation criteria, so the nurse summons expert help and prepares for cultures and a crystalloid bolus. Treating the number instead of the trend, offering oral fluids to a drowsy client, or waiting until handoff all allow shock to advance untreated.

items.stem: A nurse is triaging victims at the scene of a building collapse. For each victim, select the triage tag the nurse should apply.
matrixRows: An adult with a deviated trachea and absent breath sounds on one side, respiratory rate 36/min, capillary refill 4 seconds
An adult who remains apneic after the airway is repositioned and has no palpable carotid pulse
An adult with a closed forearm fracture who walked to the collection point and follows commands
An adult with a thigh laceration controlled by a pressure dressing, respiratory rate 20/min, palpable radial pulse, follows commands
An adult who cannot follow commands, respiratory rate 28/min, weak radial pulse, with a boggy area over the skull
An adult with minor facial abrasions who is anxious and asking to help search for family
items.rationale: Disaster triage aims at the greatest good for the greatest number, so red goes to survivable life threats treatable with simple measures: a tension pneumothorax needing decompression and a head-injured victim who cannot follow commands with poor perfusion. A victim who stays apneic after the airway is opened and has no pulse is tagged black because resuscitation would consume resources many others could use. Stable, perfused injuries are yellow, and the walking wounded are green.

items.stem: A nurse has just received report on five clients on a medical unit. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Complete the full assessments and chart the findings for the remaining clients.
Check the medication record for time-critical medications due early in the shift.
Review the report to identify which client has the most unstable or changing findings.
Make a brief safety round on every assigned client, beginning with the least stable.
Delegate routine vital signs and hygiene care to the assistive personnel.
items.rationale: Planning precedes doing: the nurse first sorts the report to find who is least stable, then lays eyes on every client in that order so no deterioration goes unseen. Scanning the medication record next catches time-critical doses such as antibiotics and insulin before they are late. Delegating routine work early lets it proceed in parallel, leaving the nurse free to finish full assessments and documentation, which are the least time-sensitive activities.

items.stem: A home health nurse has five visits planned for the day. Which client should the nurse visit first?
options: A client 3 weeks after hip replacement who needs a gait assessment before discharge from services
A client newly diagnosed with diabetes who needs a second insulin teaching session
A client with a healing stage 2 pressure injury whose dressing change is due
A client with heart failure who telephoned to report waking at night short of breath and a 2.3 kg (5 lb) weight gain in 2 days
items.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with a rapid weight gain indicates fluid overload and impending decompensation of heart failure, a breathing problem that can deteriorate within hours. A scheduled dressing change, a teaching session, and a routine gait assessment are all important but carry no risk of harm if they happen later in the day. Home health visits are ordered by clinical instability, not by geography or by the day's original plan.

items.stem: A nurse is coordinating discharge for a client with heart failure who lives alone and has been readmitted twice in 2 months. Which action is the priority before the client leaves the unit?
options: Give the client the printed discharge instructions and obtain a signature
Confirm that the client has the medications in hand, can state the daily weight plan, and has a follow-up appointment within 7 days
Arrange transportation for the day of discharge
Notify the provider that the client lives alone
items.rationale: Readmission after heart failure is usually driven by medication gaps, unmonitored weight gain, and no early follow-up, so closing those three gaps is what makes the discharge safe. A signature documents that papers were handed over but proves nothing about understanding, the provider already knows the living situation from the history, and transportation matters only once the plan itself is sound. Verify teach-back before the client leaves.

items.stem: A nurse is giving handoff report on a client being transferred to the intensive care unit when the receiving nurse answers a telephone call and turns away. Which action should the transferring nurse take?
options: Pause the report, resume when the receiving nurse can give full attention, and ask for a read-back of the key points
Give the rest of the report to the unit secretary to pass along
Document that report was given and return to the unit
Finish the report and leave a written copy at the bedside
items.rationale: Handoff is a two-way exchange, and a distracted receiver cannot ask questions or confirm understanding, which is where transfer errors begin. Pausing and finishing with a read-back closes the communication loop. A written copy alone, a relay through a secretary, or documenting that report was given all record that words were spoken without ensuring the information reached the person who will act on it.

items.stem: A nurse has activated the rapid response team for a client whose oxygen saturation fell to 84% on room air with a respiratory rate of 32/min. Which actions should the nurse take while waiting for the team to arrive? Select all that apply.
options: Raise the head of the bed to a high Fowler position
Administer the client's scheduled morning antihypertensive
Confirm that the client has patent intravenous access
Bring the medication record, recent vital signs, and code status to the bedside
Apply supplemental oxygen and titrate to the prescribed saturation target
Leave the client to prepare discharge paperwork for another assigned client
items.rationale: While the team is in transit the nurse treats the hypoxemia with oxygen and positioning, secures a route for emergency drugs and fluids, and assembles the record so the team can act on data instead of searching for it. Leaving an unstable client abandons monitoring at the moment it matters most, and an antihypertensive given to a hypoxemic client who may be deteriorating can drop the blood pressure the team is trying to protect.

items.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility reviews findings on a resident who was found on the floor 2 hours ago. Which finding requires the most immediate action?
options: The resident, who takes apixaban daily, is now drowsier and harder to arouse than at baseline
The resident's family has not yet been notified of the fall
A 3 cm bruise over the right hip
The resident rates right shoulder pain as 4 out of 10
items.rationale: A declining level of consciousness after a fall in a resident on an anticoagulant suggests an expanding intracranial bleed, which can be fatal within hours and requires urgent imaging. Bruising and moderate shoulder pain are consistent with a fall and can be assessed and treated next, and family notification, while required, does not change the resident's physiological risk. Neurological change always outranks musculoskeletal findings and administrative tasks.

items.stem: A client on a surgical unit 2 days after total hip arthroplasty suddenly reports sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing. Respiratory rate 32/min, heart rate 124/min, blood pressure 106/62 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 87% on room air, lungs clear, calf on the operative side swollen. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Apply oxygen by non-rebreather mask and keep the client on bed rest
Activate the rapid response team and notify the surgeon
Administer the prescribed as-needed oral opioid for the chest pain
Ambulate the client in the hallway to expand the lungs
Massage the swollen calf to relieve the discomfort
bowtieParams: Respiratory rate and work of breathing
items.rationale: Abrupt pleuritic pain with tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and clear lungs after joint replacement is classic pulmonary embolism, and the swollen calf names the source. The nurse escalates immediately and supports oxygenation while keeping the client still so no further clot dislodges. Ambulating or massaging the calf can send more emboli, and an opioid blunts the respiratory drive. Saturation and respiratory effort are the parameters that show whether the client is improving.

items.stem: At 0900 a nurse on a medical unit has four tasks waiting. Which task should the nurse complete first?
options: Hang the intravenous antibiotic for a client with sepsis whose dose was due at 0830
Complete the admission history for a client who arrived at 0845
Reinforce discharge teaching for a client leaving at noon
Change the dressing on a clean, healing surgical incision
items.rationale: Antibiotic timing in sepsis is directly tied to survival, so a dose already 30 minutes late is the one task with an hourly cost of delay. A healing incision dressing, discharge reinforcement for a noon departure, and an admission history all have hours of slack. Effective time management means identifying which pending items have a hard clinical deadline and doing those before the work that merely feels urgent.

items.stem: A client who had a below-knee amputation is being discharged home to a two-story house with a spouse who works during the day. Which referral is the priority for continuity of care?
options: A peer support group for people living with limb loss
Home health physical therapy for safe transfers, mobility, and prosthetic readiness
A vocational rehabilitation counselor
A dietitian for weight management
items.rationale: The immediate post-discharge risk for a new amputee alone in a multilevel home is falling during transfers and mobility, a physical safety need that outranks psychosocial and long-range needs on Maslow's hierarchy. Home physical therapy also protects the residual limb and prepares the client for a prosthesis. Peer support, nutrition counseling, and vocational planning are valuable, but they are arranged after the client can move safely at home.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the telephone triage note that indicate the client should be directed to the emergency department now.

highlightSegments.text: 1910 after-hours triage call: 58-year-old client with type 2 diabetes.
Reports a sore on the sole of the right foot first noticed 5 days ago.
States the sore now has a foul odor with yellow-green drainage.
Reports an oral temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F) taken 20 minutes ago.
Says the redness has spread from the sole up onto the ankle since this morning.
Checks blood glucose twice daily as usual.
Last reading was 212 mg/dL this afternoon.
States the foot has felt numb for more than a year.
Takes metformin and lisinopril as prescribed.
Reports shaking chills within the past hour.
Asks whether the podiatry appointment next Tuesday will be soon enough.

items.rationale: Purulent malodorous drainage, fever, rigors, and redness advancing up the limb within hours describe a spreading infection with systemic involvement in a client whose neuropathy hides the usual pain warning; this needs same-day intravenous therapy and possible debridement, not an appointment next week. Longstanding numbness, a glucose of 212 mg/dL, and the usual medication routine are baseline data that do not by themselves warrant emergency care.

items.stem: A nurse performs neurological checks on a client admitted after a fall with a head strike. Which conclusion should the nurse draw from the trended data?
options: The client is in pain and should receive the prescribed opioid before the next check
The client is simply asleep, and hourly checks should continue as ordered
The client is having a vasovagal response and needs a fluid bolus
Intracranial pressure is rising and the provider must be notified immediately
items.rationale: A falling Glasgow Coma Scale with a new sluggish pupil, a rising systolic pressure, and a slowing heart rate is Cushing's triad, the late sign of rising intracranial pressure and impending herniation, so the provider is called at once. Sleep does not change pupil reactivity, a vasovagal event lowers rather than raises blood pressure, and an opioid would further depress consciousness and mask the very findings being tracked.

items.stem: A nurse is receiving a client admitted from the emergency department at change of shift. Which actions should the nurse complete before the emergency department nurse leaves the unit? Select all that apply.
options: Complete the full admission database and written plan of care
Obtain the client's signature on the discharge instruction sheet
Review results, treatments, and orders that are still pending or incomplete
Confirm which medications were given in the emergency department and at what times
Confirm the presence, site, and patency of all lines, drains, and infusions
Verify the client's identity with two identifiers against the armband and the record
items.rationale: Anything only the transferring nurse can answer must be settled while that nurse is present: correct identity, the timing of doses that affect the next dose, unfinished results and orders, and the status of every line and drain. The admission database is completed by the receiving nurse afterwards, and discharge paperwork has no place at admission. A handoff is the moment to close information gaps, not to complete unit documentation.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client walks into the emergency department reporting 3 days of vomiting. Heart rate is 126/min, blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg, mucous membranes are dry, and capillary refill is 4 seconds. The triage nurse should classify this client as {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: fast track, because the visit requires only an antiemetic
urgent, because vomiting is uncomfortable but not dangerous
non-urgent, because the client was able to walk in and speak in full sentences
emergent, because the findings show hypovolemia with early shock
collect a urine specimen and have the client wait to be called
send the client to registration and call the next name in the queue
take the client directly to a treatment area for intravenous access and fluid resuscitation
offer oral fluids in the waiting room and recheck the vital signs in 1 hour

items.rationale: Tachycardia with hypotension, dry membranes, and delayed capillary refill are compensated hypovolemic shock from days of fluid loss, and the ability to ambulate does not exclude it, which is why triage relies on vital signs rather than appearance. This client needs intravenous fluids now. Oral fluids, a waiting-room recheck, or routine registration all leave a shocked client unmonitored while perfusion continues to fall.

items.stem: Four students arrive at the school health office at the same time. Which student should the school nurse attend to first?
options: A student with a scraped knee from recess who is crying
A student with a temperature of 38.2 C (100.8 F) and a sore throat
A student whose nosebleed stopped after 5 minutes of direct pressure
A student with a known peanut allergy who has hives on the chest and says the throat feels tight
items.rationale: Hives with a sensation of throat tightness in a student with a known food allergy is early anaphylaxis, an airway emergency that requires epinephrine within minutes. A nosebleed that has already stopped, a febrile sore throat, and an abrasion are all manageable after the airway threat is treated. In any prioritization question, an actual or impending airway problem is assessed and treated before circulation or comfort needs.

items.stem: A nurse in the post-anesthesia care unit is monitoring four clients. Which finding requires immediate intervention?
options: A client shivering 20 minutes after general anesthesia with a temperature of 35.8 C (96.4 F)
A client whose urine output has been 40 mL over the past hour
A client with snoring respirations and an oxygen saturation of 89% after receiving midazolam and fentanyl
A client who rates incisional pain as 6 out of 10
items.rationale: Snoring respirations with desaturation after sedation and an opioid indicate airway obstruction from a relaxed tongue and soft palate, which is corrected immediately with repositioning, a jaw thrust, or an airway adjunct. Postanesthetic shivering, moderate incisional pain, and 40 mL of urine in an hour are all common recovery findings that are managed next. Airway and oxygenation problems always precede comfort and elimination concerns.

items.stem: A hospital uses early warning criteria for activating the rapid response team. Which client situations meet the criteria for activation? Select all that apply.
options: A client whose heart rate rose from 76 to 92/min while walking to the bathroom
A client whose systolic blood pressure has fallen from 132 to 86 mm Hg over 2 hours
A client with a respiratory rate of 8/min after two doses of intravenous hydromorphone
A client with new seizure activity lasting 2 minutes
A client who is newly unable to state the year, with a baseline of alert and oriented
A client with a temperature of 37.6 C (99.7 F) after ambulating in the hallway
A client reporting incisional pain of 7 out of 10 that eases after the prescribed analgesic
items.rationale: Rapid response criteria target acute physiological change: a marked fall in blood pressure, respiratory depression after opioids, new seizure activity, and an acute change in mental status all predict arrest if untreated. A brief low-grade temperature rise and a modest heart rate increase with exertion are normal physiological responses, and pain that responds to the ordered analgesic is being managed successfully. Escalate on change from baseline, not on a single uncomfortable number.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse pages the on-call provider about a client whose urine output has been under 20 mL/hr for 4 hours after a partial nephrectomy. After giving the situation and background, the nurse reports the assessment that the client is {{1}} and recommends that the provider {{2}}. If no new orders are given and the nurse remains concerned, the nurse should {{3}}.

options: anxious about the outcome of the surgery
showing early signs of a urinary tract infection
having an expected response to surgery
developing acute kidney injury or is volume depleted
request insertion of a second urinary catheter
evaluate the client now and consider a fluid challenge and renal studies
raise the oral fluid goal and continue to record output
hold all intravenous fluids until morning rounds
wait and hand the concern to the day shift at report
ask a colleague to page the same provider a second time
move up the chain of command and notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor
chart that the provider was notified and take no further action

items.rationale: Output under 0.5 mL/kg/hr for several hours after renal surgery is oliguria that signals hypovolemia or acute kidney injury, and the SBAR assessment names that concern instead of only reciting numbers. A clear recommendation tells the provider what the nurse wants done. When escalation produces no response and the nurse still believes the client is at risk, the chain of command exists for exactly that gap; documenting alone leaves the client unprotected.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with a new tracheostomy is being discharged home, where the spouse will provide care. Before the discharge is completed, the nurse should confirm that {{1}} and that {{2}} so that care continues without a gap.

options: written step-by-step instructions are in the discharge folder
the spouse has agreed to learn the care once they are home
the spouse has watched the tracheostomy care video
the spouse has independently suctioned the tracheostomy and changed the ties while being observed
a referral has been sent to a tracheostomy support group
home health nursing is arranged and suction equipment and supplies are delivered before the client arrives
a follow-up telephone call is scheduled in 6 weeks
an appointment with the primary care provider is booked in 3 months

items.rationale: Teaching is evaluated by return demonstration, not by exposure to information, because a caregiver who cannot suction independently cannot rescue an obstructed airway at home. Equipment and skilled nursing must be in place before arrival, since a client cannot wait days for a suction machine. Videos, printed sheets, support groups, and distant appointments supplement the plan but none of them keeps the airway patent on the first night home.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Two clients sign in at a walk-in clinic within a minute of each other. One reports a headache that began abruptly 30 minutes ago and calls it the worst headache of their life; the other reports a headache present for 2 days that is partly relieved by ibuprofen. The nurse should see {{1}} first because the presentation suggests {{2}}.

options: the client whose headache started abruptly and is the worst ever experienced
whichever client signed the register first
the client who looks more distressed in the waiting area
the client whose headache has lasted 2 days
a subarachnoid hemorrhage
a medication overuse headache
a tension headache
sinus congestion

items.rationale: A thunderclap headache that peaks within seconds and is described as the worst ever is the classic presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage, which can rebleed and kill within hours, so it outranks a subacute headache that responds to an oral analgesic. Order of arrival and visible distress are unreliable guides; a client with a life-threatening bleed may look calm while a client in ordinary pain appears far more uncomfortable.

items.stem: Click to highlight the entries in the discharge summary that must be resolved before this client can safely leave the hospital.

highlightSegments.text: Discharge summary: 81-year-old client, hospital day 5 for deep vein thrombosis with new atrial fibrillation.
Discharged on apixaban twice daily.
The daughter states she cannot collect the prescription until next week because the pharmacy is closed on weekends.
The client lives alone in a first-floor apartment.
Home oxygen at 2 L/min was ordered, but no supplier has been contacted.
The client correctly repeated the signs of bleeding to watch for and when to call.
Follow-up at the anticoagulation clinic is scheduled for 6 weeks from today.
Physical therapy cleared the client to walk with a rolling walker.
The client states, 'I stopped taking my water pill last month because it made me get up at night.'
A 3-day supply of medications was placed in the discharge bag.
Transportation home with the daughter is arranged for 1400.

items.rationale: A safe discharge requires the medication in hand, the equipment delivered, and timely follow-up. A week without apixaban risks clot extension, ordered oxygen with no supplier means the client goes home without it, and anticoagulation follow-up belongs within about a week rather than 6. The client's disclosure that a diuretic was self-discontinued changes the medication reconciliation and must be reported. Successful teaching, mobility clearance, a bridging supply, and a ride are all resolved items.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the triage note that indicate the client needs immediate evaluation rather than placement in the waiting room.

highlightSegments.text: 1540 triage note: 74-year-old client brought in by a neighbor for abdominal pain.
The pain began abruptly 2 hours ago and is tearing in quality, radiating through to the back.
History of hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history.
Blood pressure 88/46 mm Hg in the right arm and 126/74 mm Hg in the left arm.
Heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 24/min.
Skin is cool, pale, and diaphoretic.
Last bowel movement was this morning and was normal.
The client took an antacid at home without relief.
Denies fever, vomiting, or urinary symptoms.
Reports taking amlodipine and atorvastatin daily.
The neighbor reports the client has not eaten since breakfast.

items.rationale: Abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back, a blood pressure difference of nearly 40 mm Hg between arms, tachycardia with tachypnea, and cool diaphoretic skin describe a dissecting aortic aneurysm with poor perfusion, which can rupture within minutes. Smoking and hypertension are risk factors rather than acute cues, and normal bowel habits, an antacid trial, the absence of fever, and routine medications do not change the acuity assignment.

items.stem: The nurse reviews trended data for a client admitted with a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The data are essentially unchanged, so the plan of care should be revised
The client is deteriorating and should be transferred to a higher level of care
Oxygen should be discontinued today because the client is now ambulating
The client is responding to treatment, and the nurse should begin discharge planning with the case manager
